summaries.summary: Jeremy Jacob was at the beach building a sand castle when a pirate ship came into view. He tried to tell Dad and Mom, but they were busy. The pirates rowed to shore and the head pirate, Braidbeard, asked where they were. Jeremy said they were at North Beach. Braidbeard liked Jeremy’s sand castle and saw that he was a good digger, so he invited Jeremy to join the crew. Jeremy went with the pirates and saw their chest of gold and jewels. The pirates taught him to sing sea shanties and say pirate words. He ate dinner with them and learned pirate manners. Jeremy tried to teach them soccer, but the ball rolled off the deck and a shark swallowed it. Later, Jeremy could not get a bedtime story or tuck-in. When a storm hit, the pirates hurried to work and did not help him feel safe. After that, Jeremy did not want to be a pirate anymore. He helped bury the treasure, and then the pirates sailed away.

One day at North Beach, Jeremy Jacob was making a sand castle when a pirate ship sailed close by. The ship had a skull and crossbones flag, and the pirates were singing. Braidbeard, the head pirate, came to shore and talked with Jeremy. He saw Jeremy’s moat and said Jeremy was a good digger. The pirates asked Jeremy to come with them, and he joined their crew. On the ship, Jeremy learned pirate songs and pirate words. He ate dinner with the pirates, who shouted and talked with their mouths full. Jeremy also tried to play soccer with them, but the ball went off the deck and a shark ate it. At bedtime, Jeremy found that pirates did not tuck him in, read him a story, or give him a kiss good night. Then a storm began, and the pirates rushed around the ship. Jeremy stayed alone. After the storm, Jeremy helped bury the treasure on shore, and the pirates gave him a flag before sailing off.

summaries.summary: Duncan was coloring when postcards arrived from many crayons. The crayons said they had been lost, left behind, broken, melted, or used too much. Maroon Crayon had been broken and fixed by paper clip. Magnificent P Green wanted to run away and see the world. Neon Red had waited eight months after Duncan left him at a hotel pool. Yellow and Orange had melted together in the hot sun. Tan or Burnt Sienna had been eaten by a dog and puked onto the rug. Glow-in-the-dark Crayon was still in the basement after Halloween. Gold Crayon had been made blunt by coloring coins. Turquoise got stuck to a sock in the dryer. Big Chunky Toddler Crayon did not want Duncan’s baby brother using him anymore. Brown Crayon was unhappy about being used for messy brown marks. Duncan felt sad, gathered the crayons, and built a new home for them when they no longer fit in the box.

video_title: 🖍️🏠The Day the Crayons Came Home - Read Aloud - Drew Daywalt

summaries.summary: One day, Duncan was coloring with his crayons when a strange stack of postcards arrived in the mail. The postcards were from crayons Duncan had lost, forgotten, broken, or left behind. Maroon crayon said Duncan lost him on the couch, and paper clip had helped hold him together after Duncan’s dad broke him. P Green said she was changing her name and running away. Neon red crayon reminded Duncan about a family vacation and said he was still waiting to be picked up. Yellow and orange explained that the sun had melted them together. Other crayons wrote too: one had been eaten by a dog, one was stuck to a sock after the dryer, and glow-in-the-dark crayon wanted to be rescued from the basement. Her teacher told her that an Afro could be a sign of pride and a blessing. Keyana loves her thick, soft, curly hair, and today she wears two ponytails that flap like wings.

Julius asks the listener to touch the bones under their skin and notice that everyone has the same hard bones underneath. He says that if people took off their skin and hair, they would look alike. By the end, Julius says that race is not all a person is, and he asks the listener to share something about themselves that cannot be seen just by looking.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: Where Do Chicks Come From? by Amy E. Sklansky, Illustrated by Pam Paparone

summaries.summary: A hen lays eggs, and after a rooster mates with her, one egg can grow into a chick. The hen sits on the eggs to keep them warm. Inside the egg, the chick has food in the yolk, water in the albumin, and air space for its first breath. Over many days, the chick grows. On day three it has a heart. On day five its head, eyes, tail, wings, and legs begin to form. On day seven it is small but already looks like a chicken. On day ten and day eleven it grows more and can open and close its beak. On day fourteen it gets an egg tooth. On day eighteen it is very big and covered with soft down. On day twenty it breathes and pecks a hole. The next day it hatches, rests, and then the hen covers her chicks. Later the fluffy chicks come out and follow their mother to search for food in the barnyard.

An egg starts as a tiny white spot inside the mother chicken. If the rooster’s sperm joins the growing egg, the egg is fertilized. Then yolk, albumin, and a hard shell form. The hen lays the egg and keeps it warm. As the days pass, the chick grows inside. The yolk gives food, the albumin gives water, and the air space helps the chick take its first breath. A breakfast egg cannot become a chick because it was never fertilized. The chick changes every day. It gets a heart, eyes, wings, legs, a beak, and tiny feathers called down. The hen sometimes leaves to find food and water, but she returns quickly. She turns the eggs and clucks to them. By day twenty the chick pecks into the air space and breathes. The next day it pecks the shell, pushes hard, and hatches. The hen warms the new chicks, and soon they run out and look for food with her.

The hen lays several eggs and sits on them to keep them warm. Inside each warm egg, a chick begins to grow. The egg has yolk, albumin, a shell, and an air space. The yolk gives food, and the albumin gives water and more food. On day three the chick has a heart that pumps blood. On day five its head is large, and its wings and legs are forming. On day seven the chick is about one inch long, and its eyes, stomach, brain, toes, and beak have started to grow. On day ten the chick uses more of the yolk, and the hen turns the eggs. On day eleven the chick can open and close its beak. On day fourteen it is curled inside the egg and gets an egg tooth. On day eighteen it is covered with down. On day twenty it breathes. The next day it hatches after pecking and pushing hard. The hen covers the chicks, and later they follow her into the barnyard.

A chick can grow only in a fertilized egg. The rooster mates with the hen, and his sperm joins the egg. The hen lays the egg, and then she warms it. Inside the egg, the chick gets food from the yolk and water from the albumin. As the chick grows, the hen keeps turning the eggs and clucking to them. On day three the chick has a heart. On day five its eyes are very large, and its wings and legs begin. On day seven it is small but already looks like a chicken. On day ten the wings, legs, and beak are fully grown. On day eleven the chick wiggles and tiny bumps appear on its skin. On day fourteen it gets an egg tooth. On day eighteen it is big and covered with soft down. On day twenty it takes its first breath. The next day it pecks, pushes, cracks the shell, and hatches. The hen warms the tired chicks, and they later run out and search for food.

The story begins with an egg that will hatch into a chick in three weeks. First, the egg is formed inside the hen. The rooster mates with the hen, and fertilization happens. Then the hen lays the egg and sits on it to keep it warm. Inside the egg, the chick grows using the yolk, albumin, and air space. The chick changes day by day. It gets a heart, eyes, wings, legs, a beak, and feathers. The hen leaves only briefly to eat and drink, then comes back to warm the eggs again. By day fourteen the chick has an egg tooth. By day eighteen it is so big it touches the shell. By day twenty it breathes and answers the hen with a cheap cheap cluck cluck. The next day it pecks, pushes, and hatches. The hen covers her chicks, and after resting they come out and follow her to find food in the barnyard.

summaries.summary: Mom and a child paddle over a pond and look down at the water. They see lily pads, reeds, and the sky reflected like a mirror. Mom tells the child that under the pond is a hidden world. As they move along, they pass whirlygig beetles, painted turtles, red-winged blackbirds, and a moose eating water lilies. Under the pond, minnows swim, a brook trout waits, a caddisfly larva builds a home, and beavers dive for roots. They also see a goldfinch getting ready to fly, tadpoles changing into frogs, a great blue heron catching a minnow, a woodpecker searching for ants, an otter looking for mussels, and a dragonfly resting. At the end, they head home while the sun goes down and the pond grows dark.

Farther along, a goldfinch stands on a branch and gets ready to fly. Under the pond, tadpoles grow legs, a heron catches a minnow, an otter looks for mussels, and dragonfly larvae catch minnows. Raccoons, mink, and an osprey search for supper too. In the end, they go back to shore as night comes, and the pond becomes a quiet place full of hidden animals.

summaries.summary: Frog runs to Toad’s house in spring and knocks on the door. Toad is asleep and does not want to wake up. Frog goes inside, finds Toad in bed, and pushes him out into the bright sun. Toad says he is too tired and goes back to bed. Frog tells Toad he has been asleep since November and says they can have fun in the spring. Toad asks Frog to wake him in half past May, but he falls asleep again. Frog looks at Toad’s calendar and tears off the old months: November, December, January, February, March, and April. Then Frog runs back and says it is May now. Toad checks the calendar, sees the May page, gets out of bed, and goes outside with Frog to see the spring world.

Frog goes up the path to Toad’s house and calls for him. He says the sun is shining and the snow is melting, but Toad stays hidden in his dark house and bed. Frog pushes Toad outside into the warm light of April. Toad cannot see well at first and wants to go back to sleep. Frog tells him they can skip, run, swim, and count stars together. Toad says he will be too tired and asks Frog to wake him in half past May. Frog feels lonely and looks at the calendar. The November page is still there, so Frog tears off many pages until he reaches April and tears off April too. Then Frog runs back and wakes Toad again. He says it is May. Toad looks at the calendar, sees May, and gets up. At last, Toad and Frog run outside together.

Frog visits Toad because spring has come. He knocks, calls, and walks into the house when Toad does not answer. Inside, Toad is in bed with the covers over his head. Frog pushes him out onto the porch and tells him about the warm April sun and all the spring fun they can have. Toad says he is tired and goes back to bed. He tells Frog to wake him later in May, but he falls asleep at once. Frog checks the calendar and sees that Toad has not changed it since November. Frog tears off the old months one by one until only May is left on top. Then Frog wakes Toad again and says it is May now. Toad looks at the calendar, gets out of bed, and goes outside with Frog to see the spring day.

summaries.summary: Frog ran to Toad’s house in spring and knocked, but Toad did not answer. Frog called for Toad and said the sun was shining and the snow was melting. Inside the dark house, Toad stayed in bed with the covers over his head and told Frog to go away. Frog pushed Toad out onto the porch, where Toad blinked in the bright light and said he could not see. Frog told him that April had come and that they could skip, run, swim, and count stars together. But Toad said he was too tired and went back to bed. He told Frog to wake him again at half past May. Frog felt lonely, so he looked at Toad’s calendar and tore off the pages from November through April. Then he ran back and shouted that it was May. Toad checked the calendar, saw the May page, got up, and went outside with Frog to see spring.

One spring day, Frog went to Toad’s house and tried to wake him. Frog said the snow was melting and that spring had arrived, but Toad stayed hidden in bed under the covers. Frog found him in the dark house and pushed him out onto the porch. Toad did not like the bright sun and said he could not see anything. Frog told Toad about the fun they would have in April, like running in the woods, swimming in the river, and sitting on the porch to count stars. Toad said he was too tired and went back to bed. He asked Frog to come back in half past May. Frog then looked at Toad’s calendar and tore off the old months one by one until he reached May. He rushed back and told Toad to wake up because it was May now. Toad looked at the calendar, saw the May page, and got out of bed. At the end, Frog and Toad went outside together to look at the spring world.

Frog came up the path to Toad’s house and knocked, but no one answered. He called that it was spring, the sun was shining, and the snow was melting. A voice from inside told him to go away. Frog went into the dark house and found Toad in bed with all the covers over his head. Frog pushed Toad outside into the sunshine. Toad blinked and said he could not see, but Frog told him it was the clear warm light of April and that they could enjoy a whole new year together. Frog talked about skipping through meadows, running through woods, swimming in the river, and counting stars on the porch. Toad said he was too tired and went back to bed. Frog asked how long he had slept, and Toad learned it had been since November. Toad said a little more sleep would not hurt and told Frog to wake him at half past May. Frog then tore off the pages of Toad’s calendar until May was on top. He woke Toad again and showed him the calendar. Toad got up, and both friends went outside in spring.

Frog wanted Toad to wake up because spring had come. He knocked on Toad’s door, called out, and said the sun was shining and the snow was melting. Toad kept sleeping in the dark house with the covers over his head. Frog found him and pushed him out onto the front porch. Toad was surprised by the bright sun, but Frog told him that April had arrived and that they could have many fun days together. Frog described how they would play in the meadows, woods, river, and under the stars. Toad said he was too tired and went back to bed. He told Frog to return in half past May. Frog looked at the calendar and saw that Toad had still been sleeping since November. He tore off the old months until the May page was on top. Frog ran back and told Toad it was May. Toad checked the calendar, got out of bed, and went outside with Frog to see the spring day.

Frog ran to Toad’s house in spring and tried to wake him, but Toad did not answer. Frog said the sun was shining and the snow was melting, yet Toad stayed inside his dark house under the covers. Frog found Toad in bed and pushed him outside into the bright light. Toad said he could not see, but Frog told him it was April and that they could start a new year together. Frog said they would skip in the meadows, run in the woods, swim in the river, and count stars on the porch. Toad said he was too tired and returned to bed. He asked Frog to wake him at half past May and then fell asleep again. Frog looked at the calendar and tore off the pages from November through April. When he reached May, he ran back and told Toad to wake up. Toad looked at the calendar, saw that it was May, got out of bed, and went outside with Frog.

summaries.summary: One day in summer, Frog was not feeling well. Toad saw that Frog looked very green and told him to get into bed and rest. Toad made Frog a cup of hot tea, and Frog drank it. Frog asked Toad to tell him a story while he rested. Toad tried to think of a story, but he could not. He walked up and down on the front porch. Then he stood on his head in the house. After that, he poured water over his head. Then he banged his head against the wall. Frog kept asking why Toad was doing these things. Toad said he hoped they would help him think of a story. At last Toad felt terrible, and Frog felt better. Frog said he did not need a story anymore. Then Frog offered to tell Toad a story. Frog told about the frog and the toad, the porch, the head standing, the water, and the wall, and then Toad went to bed while Frog got up.

On a summer day, Frog was sick. Toad said Frog looked very green, even for a frog, and told him to rest in bed. Toad gave Frog hot tea. Frog drank the tea and asked for a story. Toad wanted to help, but he could not think of one. He went to the front porch and walked up and down. He still could not think of a story. Then he went inside and stood on his head. Frog asked why, and Toad said he hoped it would help him think. Toad then poured many glasses of water over his head, but still no story came. After that, he banged his head against the wall. Soon Toad felt terrible, and Frog felt better. Frog said he did not need a story now. Toad asked Frog to get out of bed so he could lie down. Frog then told Toad a story about how Toad had tried to think of a story and could not. When Frog finished, Toad was in bed and Frog was up.

Frog was not feeling well one summer day. Toad noticed and said Frog was very green. He told Frog to get into bed and rest, and he made him hot tea. Frog drank the tea and asked Toad for a story. Toad tried hard to think of one, but he could not. He walked on the porch, stood on his head, poured water over his head, and banged his head against the wall. Each time, Frog asked why he was doing it, and Toad said he hoped it would help him think of a story. After all that, Toad felt much worse. Frog then said he did not need a story anymore. Toad asked Frog to get up so he could rest in bed. Frog offered to tell a story instead. He began, “Once upon a time,” and told about the frog, the toad, the porch, the head standing, the water, and the wall. At the end, the frog was better and the toad was in bed.

summaries.summary: Toad and Frog went for a long walk across a large meadow, through the woods, and along the river. When they got back to Toad’s house, Toad saw that one button was missing from his jacket. Frog said they should go back and look in all the places they had walked. First they searched the meadow and found a black button, but it was not Toad’s. A sparrow brought a button with two holes, but that was not right either. In the woods they found a small button, then a square button from a raccoon, but Toad said each one was wrong. At the river they found a thin button, and Toad got very upset and ran home. There he saw his own white, four-holed, big, round, thick button on the floor. Toad sewed all the buttons on his jacket and gave it to Frog the next day.

Toad and Frog walked a long way together. They went across a meadow, through the woods, and by the river, and then they came back to Toad’s house. Toad was sad because his feet hurt and one button was missing from his jacket. Frog helped him search by going back to each place. In the meadow they found a black button, but Toad said his button was white. A sparrow found a button with two holes, but Toad said his button had four holes. In the woods they found a small button and then a square button, but neither one was Toad’s. At the river they found a thin button, and Toad shouted that it was still wrong. Toad ran home and found his own button on the floor. He felt sorry for making Frog work so hard. Then he sewed all the buttons on his jacket. The next day he gave the jacket to Frog, and Frog was very happy.

After a long walk, Toad and Frog came home to Toad’s house. Toad noticed that he had lost one button from his jacket, and his feet hurt too. Frog said they would return to the meadow, the woods, and the river to look for it. In the meadow Frog found a black button, but Toad said it was not his. A sparrow brought a button with two holes, and Toad put it in his pocket because it was still not the right one. Frog thought it was beautiful and jumped for joy.

summaries.summary: Toad and Frog went down to the river on a nice day. Frog wanted to swim, and Toad said he would go behind some rocks to put on his bathing suit. Toad told Frog not to look because he thought he looked funny in it. Frog closed his eyes, and then Toad came back wearing the suit. The two friends jumped into the water and swam all afternoon. Frog swam fast and made big splashes, and Toad swam slowly and made small splashes. A turtle came by, and Toad asked Frog to tell the turtle to go away so no one would see him when he got out. But then more animals came, like lizards, a snake, dragonflies, and a field mouse. They all wanted to see Toad. Toad stayed in the water until he got cold, shivered, and sneezed. At last he came out, and everyone laughed, including Frog. Toad said, “Of course I do,” and went home with his clothes.

One day, Toad and Frog went to the river. Frog said it was a good day for a swim. Toad went behind some rocks to put on his bathing suit. He told Frog not to peek because he looked funny in it. Frog waited with his eyes closed. When Toad came out, he was wearing the suit, and both friends jumped into the water. They swam for a long time. Frog made big splashes, and Toad made little splashes. Then a turtle came near the riverbank. Toad did not want the turtle to see him, so Frog asked the turtle to go away. But lizards, a snake, two dragonflies, and a field mouse also came and asked to see Toad in his bathing suit. Frog told them to leave, but they stayed. Toad waited in the cold water until he began to shiver and sneeze. He had to come out. Water dripped from his bathing suit, and all the animals laughed. Frog laughed too. Toad said he did look funny and then took his clothes and went home.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: The Moon Seems to Change by Franklyn M. Branley, Ill by Barbara & Ed Emberley

summaries.summary: Look up at the sky at night and you may see the moon. Sometimes it is big and round, called a full moon. Sometimes only part of it shows, like a crescent moon or a quarter moon. The moon seems to change, but it really does not change shape. It changes because it goes around Earth. As it moves, we see more of the lighted half or less of it. This is called waxing when the moon grows bigger and waning when it gets smaller. Half of the moon is always lit by the sun. The moon goes through phases in the same order again and again: new moon, crescent, first quarter, full moon, third quarter, crescent, and back to new moon. A new moon means we cannot see it. A few nights later, a crescent appears, then the moon grows until it is full, and after that it gets smaller again.

The moon goes around Earth in about four weeks. During that time, we see different parts of it. At first, the moon can be a new moon, when the dark side faces us and we cannot see it. Soon after, a small crescent moon appears in the west after sunset. Then the moon gets bigger each night. After about a week, it is a first quarter moon. After another week, it becomes a full moon, and we can see all of the lighted half. Then the moon starts to get smaller. This is waning. About a week later, it is a third quarter moon. After that, it becomes a thin crescent. A few days later, the moon cannot be seen again, and the cycle starts over with a new moon. These changes are called the phases of the moon, and they happen again and again in the same order.

Half of the moon is always bright because the sun lights it. The other half is dark. As the moon goes around Earth, different amounts of the bright side face us. That is why the moon looks like it changes. When we see more of the bright part, the moon is waxing. When we see less of it, the moon is waning. The moon begins as a new moon, when the dark side faces Earth. Then a crescent moon appears. Next comes the first quarter moon. After that, the moon is full and round. Then it changes to the third quarter moon and becomes a thin crescent again. Soon it disappears from view and becomes new moon once more. The moon keeps moving around Earth, so the same pattern of phases happens over and over.

The story explains that a day on Earth is 24 hours long, but a day on the moon is almost a month long. The moon takes about four weeks to go around Earth. As it moves, we see its phases. Sometimes the moon is between Earth and the sun, so the dark side faces us and we see a new moon. A night or two later, a crescent moon appears in the west after sunset. Then the moon grows larger each night. About a week later, it is a first quarter moon. About a week after that, the moon is full. Then the moon gets smaller each night. It becomes third quarter, then a thin crescent, and then new moon again. The same changes happen again and again.

The story gives an experiment with a flashlight, an orange, a pencil, a marker, and a friend. The orange stands for the moon, your head stands for Earth, and the flashlight stands for the sun. You put the pencil in the orange, draw a line, and make an x on one half. Then you hold the orange above your head in a dark room while someone shines the flashlight on it. When the x faces you, you cannot see the lighted half, so it looks like a new moon. When you turn your body, you see a crescent moon. If you keep turning, you see a first quarter moon, then a full moon, then a third quarter moon, and then a thin crescent. After turning all the way around, you have seen all the phases of the orange. The story says the moon works the same way, and the same side always faces Earth.

The story starts by showing that the moon can look different on different nights. It may be full, partly lit, or only a small crescent. The moon does not really change shape. Instead, it moves around Earth, and people see different amounts of its lighted half. The story says that half of the moon is always lit by the sun and half is dark. It explains that a new moon happens when the dark side faces Earth. Later, a crescent moon appears, then a first quarter moon, then a full moon. After that, the moon gets smaller again and becomes third quarter, a crescent, and then new moon once more. The story also gives an experiment using an orange, a pencil, a marker, a flashlight, and a friend to show the phases. At the end, it reminds readers that the same side of the moon always faces Earth.

summaries.summary: Miss Maple flies home to her tall maple tree. All summer long, she has searched for orphan seeds that got lost during spring planting. She brings them home and learns their names: Poppy, wild rice, maple, water lily, pine, bean, impatiens, apple, raspberry, lupine, sunflower, acorn, corn, pea, lentil, buttercup, tomato, honeysuckle, pumpkin, fern, and more. She tells them, “Take care, my little ones. For the world is big and you are small.” Miss Maple takes the seeds on field trips to the river, the fields, and the forest so they can learn where they may grow. She shows them how to stay away from weedy characters. At night, she reads flower tales by firefly light. In winter, everyone stays cozy and shares maple syrup, corn husks, and fruit rinds. When spring rain comes, Miss Maple says the raindrops help them grow. At last, on a windy May morning, the seeds leave to find roots of their own, and Miss Maple goes on to search for more lost seeds.

Miss Maple returns to her maple tree after traveling all summer to find seeds that were lost. She cares for many seeds, each one different. She teaches them about the big world and says, “Take care, my little ones.” She brings them to the river, where some seeds may be carried to muddy soil, and to grassy fields and thick forests, where other seeds may be blown into rich soil. She tells them to stay away from weeds. At night, she reads stories by firefly light. When winter snow comes, Miss Maple and her neighbors stay warm and share food and stories. When spring thunderstorms arrive, she tells the seeds not to be afraid because raindrops help them grow. Then, on a windy May morning, the last spring petals fall, and the seeds set out into gardens, winds, and tides to make new roots. Miss Maple says goodbye, then later drinks green tea in the old maple tree and leaves again to find more lost seeds.

summaries.summary: A long time ago in Lime, an English town, a girl and her mother picked wild blackberries. The mother skimmed cream from the morning and evening milk, then beat it with clean twigs until it became whipped cream. The girl washed the berries from a well, strained out the seeds, and mixed the fruit with sugar and cream. Her mother let her lick the spoon. They took the bowl to an ice pit in the hillside to chill. After supper, they served the blackberry fool in blue dishes to father, the older brothers, and even the baby. Later, the girl licked the bowl clean in the kitchen. A bit more than 200 years ago near Charleston, South Carolina, another girl and her mother made the same dessert with blackberries, cream, sugar, and ice, and the girl also licked the spoon and the bowl clean.

A little over 100 years ago in Boston, Massachusetts, a girl and her mother bought blackberries at a market. They had pasteurized cream waiting at home in glass bottles. The mother checked a recipe book and beat the cream until it became whipped cream. The girl washed the berries from the kitchen faucet and pushed them through a sieve. Then she and her mother mixed the berries with sugar and cream. The mother let the girl lick the spatula. They put the blackberry fool in an icebox to chill. After Sunday dinner, they served it in green dishes to father, the younger brothers, and even the baby. Back in the kitchen, the girl ran her tongue around the bowl. It was a very good dessert.

Just a couple of years ago in San Diego, California, a boy and his dad bought blackberries and organic cream at the supermarket. At home, the man printed a recipe from the internet. The boy beat the cream with an electric mixer until it became whipped cream. The man washed the berries, crushed them in a food processor, and pushed them through a sieve. Together, they added sugar and mixed the fruit with the cream. The boy asked if he could lick the spatula, and his dad said yes. They put the blackberry fool in the refrigerator. Then friends came for dinner and brought food and drinks. After the meal, the man and his son served the blackberry fool in white dishes. Everyone ate it, especially the babies. After the guests left, the boy licked the inside of the bowl. There was hardly any left because it was so delicious.

Many years later near Charleston, South Carolina, another girl and her mother made the same dessert with blackberries from the plantation garden and cream delivered by wagon. They used a whisk, a sieve, and a wooden box of ice. After a large meal, they served the blackberry fool to the master and his family, and the girl and her mother licked the bowl clean in the closet.

In Boston, Massachusetts, a girl and her mother made blackberry fool with berries from the market and cream from glass bottles. The mother beat the cream with cast iron beaters while the girl washed and mashed the berries through a sieve. They mixed in sugar and cream, and the girl was allowed to lick the spatula. They chilled the dessert in an icebox and served it after Sunday dinner to the family, including the baby. The girl then licked the bowl. Later, in San Diego, California, a boy and his dad made blackberry fool with supermarket berries and organic cream. The boy used an electric mixer, and the man used a food processor and sieve. summaries.summary: A little more than 300 years ago in Lime, England, a girl and her mother picked wild blackberries, then went home to make blackberry fool. The mother skimmed cream from the evening milk and added it to the morning cream, beating it with soft twigs until it became whipped cream. The girl drew water from the well, rinsed the berries in muslin, and strained out the seeds. She and her mother added sugar and mixed the fruit with the cream. The girl was allowed to lick the spoon. They carried the bowl to an ice pit in the hillside to chill it, then served the dessert after supper to the father, older brothers, and even the baby. Later, the girl licked the bowl clean in the kitchen and called it a fine dessert.

A little more than 200 years ago outside Charleston, South Carolina, a girl and her mother picked blackberries from the plantation garden. A wagon brought cream from a nearby dairy, and the girl beat it with a metal whisk until it became whipped cream. She washed the berries with well water, crushed them through a ten sieve, and removed the seeds. Then she and her mother added sugar and mixed the berries with the cream. The mother let the girl lick the spoon. They put the mixture in a wooden box in the basement with ice and waited until after supper, when the master and his family ate turtle soup, roast turkey, corn cakes, and sweet potatoes. Later, they served the blackberry fool in yellow dishes. The girl and her mother hid in the closet and licked the bowl clean together, saying it was a fine dessert.

A little more than 100 years ago in Boston, Massachusetts, a girl and her mother bought two wooden boxes of blackberries at an open-air market. At home, they found pasteurized cream in glass bottles waiting at the door. The woman checked a recipe book and beat the cream with cast iron rotary beaters until it became whipped cream. The girl used water from the new kitchen faucet to wash the berries, then smashed them through a sieve with her fingers, turning her hands purple. She and her mother added sugar and mixed the fruit with the cream. The mother let the girl lick the spatula. They kept the blackberry fool in a wooden icebox with blocks of ice, then served it after Sunday dinner of potato soup, roast chicken, and canned asparagus on toast. The whole family ate it, including the baby, and the girl later licked the bowl clean.

Just a couple of years ago in San Diego, California, a boy and his dad bought blackberries and pasteurized organic cream at the supermarket. When they got home, the man printed a recipe from the internet. The boy beat the cream with an electric mixer until it became whipped cream. The man washed the berries in a colander, crushed them in a food processor, and pushed them through a sieve with a plastic spatula. Together, they added sugar and mixed the berries with the cream. The boy asked if he could lick the spatula, and his dad said yes. They put the blackberry fool in the refrigerator while guests arrived with lemonade, grilled vegetables, enchiladas, and tomato salad. After a long dinner, the man and his son served the dessert to everyone, and the guests ate it quickly, especially the babies. After the guests left, the boy licked the inside of the bowl clean and said it was a fine dessert.

Across the story, blackberry fool is made in different times and places by children and their mothers or fathers. In Lime, England, a girl and her mother picked wild blackberries, beat cream with twigs, mixed in sugar and fruit, and chilled the dessert in an ice pit before serving it after supper. Outside Charleston, South Carolina, another girl and her mother used cream from a dairy, a metal whisk, and a basement ice box to make the same dessert for the master and his family. In Boston, Massachusetts, a girl and her mother bought blackberries at a market, used pasteurized cream, and served the fool after Sunday dinner to the family. In San Diego, California, a boy and his dad bought blackberries and cream at a supermarket, used an electric mixer and refrigerator, and served the dessert to guests after a long dinner. In every version, the child is allowed to lick the spoon, spatula, or bowl, and the story ends by saying the blackberry fool was very delicious.

summaries.summary: A tiny sea snail lived on a black rock with other snails. She looked at the sea and the ships and said she wanted to sail. The other snails told her to sit still and stay put. But the tiny snail wanted to travel, so she climbed onto the tail of a great big gray blue humpback whale. The whale sang to her about ice, coral caves, stars, and waves, and he carried her across the sea. They saw big waves, caves with fish and sharks, and a sky that was sometimes sunny and sometimes stormy. Then the whale lost his way. Fast boats scared him, and he swam too close to shore. The tide went out, and the whale was stuck on the sand. The tiny snail asked him to move, but he could not. She crawled to the school, where children saw her trail and called the firemen. The children helped keep the whale cool, the tide came back, and the whale and snail returned safely. Back on the rock, the snail told her tale, and many snails rode on the whale’s tail.

This is a story about a tiny snail with an itchy foot and a great big humpback whale. The snail sat on a black rock and watched the sea. She wanted to sail and said, “I’ll hitch a ride!” One night the whale came when the tide was high and the stars were bright. He sang to the snail and asked her to come sail with him. The whale carried the snail on his tail over the sea. They saw icebergs, far lands, waves, caves, fish, sharks, and a big sky with sun and storms. The snail felt very small. Then speed boats raced by and made the whale swim too close to shore. The tide went away, and the whale was left on the sand. He could not move on land. The snail crawled away and left a silver trail that said, “Save the whale!” Children saw her, called the firemen, and helped with water. The tide came back, and the whale and snail went safely home. After that, the whale held out his tail, and many snails climbed on to sail too.

summaries.summary: In the meadow, an old mother turtle lived in the sand in the sun with her little turtle. The mother said, “I dig,” and the little turtle said, “I dig too.” So he dug all day in the sand in the sun. Then an old mother fish lived where the stream runs blue with her little fishes. The mother said, “Swim,” and the little fishes said, “We swim.” So they swam and leaped in the blue stream. Next, a mother blue bird lived in a hole in a tree with her little birdies three. The mother said, “Sing,” and the three birdies said, “We sing.” So they sang in the hole in the tree.

Over in the meadow, a mother muskrat lived in the reeds on the shore with her little ratty’s four. The mother said, “Dive,” and the four said, “We dive.” So they dived and burrowed in the reeds on the shore. Then a mother honeybee lived in a snug bee hive with her little honey’s five. The mother said, “Buzz,” and the five said, “We buzz.” So they buzzed and hummed near the bee hive. After that, a black mother crow lived in a nest built of sticks with her little crows six. The mother said, “Catch,” and the six said, “We catch.” So they caught and called in the nest built of sticks.

In the meadow where the grass is so even, a gay mother cricket lived with her little crickets seven. The mother said, “Chirp,” and the seven said, “We chirp.” So they chirped cheery notes in the grass. Then by the old mossy gate, a brown mother lizard lived with her little lizards eight. The mother said, “Bask,” and the eight said, “We bask.” So they basked in the sun by the gate. Next, a green mother frog lived where the clear pools shine with her little froggies nine. The mother said, “Croak,” and the nine said, “We croak.” So they croaked and jumped by the clear pools.

In the soft shady glen, a mother firefly lived with her little flies ten. The mother said, “Shine,” and the ten said, “We shine.” So they shone like stars in the soft shady glen. Before that, many other mothers and little ones lived in the meadow too. The old mother turtle and her little turtle dug in the sand in the sun. The mother fish and her little fishes swam and leaped in the stream. The mother blue bird and her little birdies sang in a hole in a tree. The mother muskrat and her little ratty’s dove and burrowed in the reeds.

summaries.summary: Babushka lived alone in Adasha and was famous for the beautiful eggs she painted. Every day through the long winter, she decorated eggs with stars, flowers, triangles, and circles. After a snowstorm, she went outside and saw caribou coming to eat because the snow covered their grass. Then a goose fell from the sky. Babushka found that a hunter had hurt the goose, so she carried it home, fed it, and kept it warm in her best basket. She named the goose Rashinka. As Rashinka grew stronger, she laid eggs and explored the house. One day she knocked over Babushka’s paint jars and then the basket of painted eggs, and all the eggs broke. Babushka and Rashinka were sad. The next morning, Babushka found a new, brightly colored egg in Rashinka’s basket. For 12 mornings, more beautiful eggs appeared. Babushka took them to the festival in Moscow, won first prize, and came home. That night she found one last egg hatch, and the little goose stayed with her always.

Rashinka grew better and laid an egg each morning. Then she jumped on Babushka’s work table, spilled the paint, and knocked over the basket of painted eggs. The eggs shattered, and Babushka could not go to the festival. The next morning, however, she found a shining egg in Rashinka’s basket. Every morning for 12 days, another beautiful egg appeared. Babushka gathered enough eggs for the festival in Moscow. There she showed the judges her eggs, and they chose them as the best. She won a featherbed quilt as first prize. When she returned home, Rashinka was gone, but later Babushka heard a tiny sound and found a special egg hatching in the basket. The goose stayed with her always.

Babushka was sad, but the next morning she found a beautiful egg in Rashinka’s basket. Rashinka laid another egg each day for twelve days. Babushka took the eggs to Moscow, won first prize, and shared tea, kulik, and poshka with Rashinka before leaving. After Babushka returned home and found Rashinka gone, she heard a sound in the basket and discovered a special egg that opened into a little goose. Rashinka stayed with her always.

The wool is washed, combed, spun, and knitted into warm clothes. Party dresses can be made from silk, which comes from silkworm cocoons. At the end, the story says old clothes can be reused or recycled instead of thrown away.

Fleece jackets can be made from recycled plastic bottles. Rain boots are made from rubber from rubber trees. summaries.summary: Ember the dragon loved gold and wanted treasure of his own. He saw other dragons with gold, so he tried to get some from villagers. He puffed a big scary flame, but it was only a tiny flame. At dusk, the other dragons flew home with their spoils, and Ember stayed behind. In the foggy village, he saw golden light and thought it was gold, but it was a street lamp and then a window. Ember was tired and curled up in the warm light. Then a storm came. A baker told Ember to come inside and help in the bakery. Ember washed, pushed dough, and used his small flame to light the stove. He watched the dough change into golden bread. Ember took some home and found it tasted buttery, crunchy, and soft. Soon, other dragons wanted a taste. Ember wanted more, and the baker said people did not like dragons who stole. In the end, Ember learned that baking gold was better than taking it, and sharing it was best of all.

Then he saw the dough turn into shiny gold bread. Ember took some home and ate it. It was rich, crunchy, and soft. The smell brought more dragons, and they asked for a bite. Ember did not plan for such big bites. After that, he wanted more, and the baker let him come back. The story ends by saying that baking gold is better than taking it, and sharing is best of all.

summaries.summary: A brave Knight wanted Glory and Treasure, so he went on a quest with a fierce and friendly detective. At first, they lost the treasure map and searched for it. They found it folded in the Knight’s pocket, and then the Knight led the way. They rode on his Noble rocket and went into space, but they did not find any treasure. On the way back to Earth, the rocket spun and crashed into the ocean. The Knight and the detective stayed safe, climbed onto a pirate ship, and met Pirates who were ready to Dance. The Pirates gave them a ride, and the Knight traded his gleaming pants for borrowed pantaloons. When they reached the Sandy Dunes, a fierce fire-breathing armadillo blocked the treasure chest. The Knight used a pillow to distract it, and the detective tickled it. The Beast moved away, and they opened the chest. Inside, they found more treasure maps and started a new quest.

summaries.summary: Butterflies soar in the sunlight, and moths flutter under the moon and stars. They have lived on Earth since the time of the dinosaurs and are found on every continent except Antarctica. Butterflies and moths are closely related insects. Both can fly, both have antennae, and both are the only insects with scaly wings. They also begin life as wingless, wiggly caterpillars. Their life has four stages: egg, caterpillar, pupa, and adult. This change is called metamorphosis. A baby caterpillar hatches from an egg on a leaf and eats the host plant. As it grows, its hard skin does not grow with it, so it molts and sheds the old skin. Caterpillars spend their time eating and growing, but many predators want to eat them. Some hide with camouflage, some look poisonous, and some use stinky smells or scary tricks. Others spin silk to bungee jump away. When they are big enough, they become a pupa inside a chrysalis or cocoon. Inside, the body changes and a new body with wings is made. Then the adult butterfly or moth comes out and flies.

Butterfly pupae are inside a chrysalis, and most moth pupae are inside a silk cocoon. Inside, the old body changes into a new one with wings, big eyes, and a different mouth. summaries.summary: On a Sunday morning, a little egg rested on a leaf. When the warm sun rose, a tiny caterpillar came out. She was very hungry and looked for food right away. On Monday she ate one apple, but she was still hungry. On Tuesday she ate two pears. On Wednesday she ate three plums. On Thursday she ate four strawberries. On Friday she ate five oranges. Each day she kept eating, but she was still hungry. On Saturday she ate many foods, like cake, ice cream, pickle, cheese, salami, lollipop, cherry pie, sausage, cupcake, and watermelon. That night she had a big stomach ache. The next Sunday she ate one green leaf and felt much better. She was no longer hungry. She had become a big, fat caterpillar. Then she built a cocoon and stayed inside for more than two weeks. After that, she made a hole, pushed out, and became a beautiful butterfly.

Ling tried to stop him, but a great tigress appeared and stood between them. Myoshan climbed onto the tigress, and they disappeared into mist. For nine years Ling did not see her sister. During that time the king became ill, and the kingdom grew sad. Then one spring morning Ling smelled Myoshan’s fragrance again. It led her to Fragrant Mountain, where Myoshan sat on a giant lotus in deep meditation. Ling ran into her arms, and Myoshan said they would never be apart again because she had promised to stay in the world and help all beings.

After Ling found Myoshan on Fragrant Mountain, she said that anyone could call for her and she would come. Ling felt relieved and said they should share the story with others so children could learn that love is the greatest power in the world. Then the king arrived and asked if Myoshan was the wise healer who had saved his life. Myoshan said she had sent medicines because she had heard he was sick. The king knelt down and cried, saying he had been cruel and asking forgiveness. Myoshan told him that the only thing she wanted was for him to rule his kingdom with kindness. After that, the king became a good and just ruler. He built a beautiful temple on Fragrant Mountain for his daughter, and happiness spread through the kingdom. The story ends by saying that Princess Myoshan became the immortal Kuan Yin, who hears the cries of the world. People still call on her in prayer when they need love, compassion, or help finding light in difficult times.

Princess Ling woke each morning to see her sister, Princess Myoshan, meditating by her bed. One day Myoshan left through the window before breakfast, and Ling realized she was trying to escape the marriage plans of the princes waiting at the palace. When the king asked where Myoshan was, Ling lied to protect her and sent the search party toward the fish pond. Ling then went into the forest and found Myoshan under a willow tree, where wild animals rested peacefully around her. Myoshan said the scene was possible through the power of love and explained that she wanted a spiritual life instead of marriage. The king ordered her to White Sparrow nunnery, but there she was made to do hard work instead of becoming a nun. When Ling visited, Myoshan was plowing a barren field. The sisters made a wish for all beings, and a dragon, birds, and seeds helped revive the land. Myoshan later grew food and medicine there, while Ling learned from her about caring for all life equally.

Myoshan’s work at the nunnery and in the garden helped many people, but the king stayed angry until he came to take her away. Before he could reach her, a tigress appeared, and Myoshan escaped with the animal into the mist. Years passed, and Ling missed her deeply while the king grew weak and the kingdom became darker. Then Myoshan returned to Ling through her fragrance and led her to Fragrant Mountain. There Ling found her sister sitting on a giant lotus, shining with calm light. Myoshan told Ling that she had promised to remain in the world after finishing her meditation so she could help Ling and all other beings. As they rejoiced, the king arrived again, but this time he had come to thank Myoshan because she had sent medicines that saved his life. He begged her forgiveness, and she asked him to rule with kindness. The king changed, built a temple on Fragrant Mountain, and the kingdom became happy. On the way, he found a leprechaun making fairy boots. Jamie caught him and asked for a pot of gold. The leprechaun offered a wish instead, and Jamie wished for the biggest potato in the world. Jamie planted the seed, and a giant potato grew so big that it pushed up the garden shed and part of the cottage. The villagers came to see it and helped dig it out. The potato blocked the road, so everyone cut it up and shared it. All winter they ate the potato, and in spring the villagers promised to help Jamie and Eileen always have food if he did not plant another giant potato.

Jamie O'Rourke hated work, especially potato work. Eileen warned him that they would have nothing to eat in winter if he did not dig the potatoes, but Jamie stayed in bed and made her do the work. Then Eileen hurt her back, and Jamie became afraid they would starve. He went to church in the night, but on the hill he heard singing and found a leprechaun. Jamie grabbed the little man and asked for his pot of gold. The leprechaun said he had only a little gold and offered a wish. Jamie wished for the biggest potato in the world. It rolled down the hill and blocked the road, so the villagers cut it into pieces and ate it all winter. In spring, Jamie said he would plant the seed again, and the villagers promised to give Jamie and Eileen food if he would stop.

summaries.summary: The child says, “This is my body. It belongs to me.” The child learns the names of body parts like belly button, vulva, butt, elbows, penis, and nipples. The child says, “I am the boss of my body,” and talks about doing things that feel good. Grown-ups still make some choices to keep the child safe and healthy, like putting on helmets. Sometimes the child does not like these choices and feels upset. It feels better when grown-ups ask first or explain what is happening. The story says everyone is different, and some people like hugs while others do not. Asking if something is okay is called asking for consent. When someone says yes, it means consent. When someone says no, or shows no in many ways, we must listen and stop right away. People can change their mind, and their body choices matter.

A child talks about body parts and says the body belongs to them. The child learns that they are the boss of their body, even though grown-ups sometimes make choices to keep them safe and healthy. The story shows children putting on helmets for safety. It also explains that people like different things, such as hugs, kisses, or getting dressed. To know what someone wants, we ask for consent. A question like, “Can I pick you up?” may get a yes or a no. If the answer is yes, we can do it. If the answer is no, we must stop. No can sound like “Stop,” “Not really,” or “Maybe later,” and it can also be silent. A yes can turn into a no, and that change must be respected. The story ends by saying everyone has the right to make choices about their own body.

video_title: How to Catch Santa - Read Aloud with Author Jean Reagan | Brightly Storytime Together

summaries.summary: The story starts with a child on Christmas Eve, ready to try to catch Santa. The child can ask many questions about Santa’s work, the reindeer, the elves, the cookies, and the letters. The child can also say important things, like trying to be good, thanking Santa for gifts, and telling him what the parents want. Santa may also get little gifts, such as a headlamp, a nose warmer, pictures, and homemade decorations. The story says not to use big tricks like lassos, candy canes, or nets. Instead, the child should be clever and gentle. The child can leave glitter notes so Santa leaves a trail, scatter carrots for reindeer clues, bake cookies, draw arrows, and hang bells and chimes. The family waits, listens for Santa sounds, and keeps the tree lights on. Before sleep, the child checks the window one last time. Santa will come only when the child is asleep, and if he is not caught, next year is another chance.

summaries.summary: On Christmas Eve, the story says this is the best time to catch Santa, but only if you plan ahead because he is very busy. It suggests thinking of questions to ask him, like how he fits down chimneys, how the reindeer fly so fast, and whether elves ride in the sleigh. You can also tell Santa that you are trying to be good, thank him for the presents, and mention what your parents want. The story says you may give him gifts too, like a headlamp, a nose warmer, drawings, or decorations for Mrs. Claus. It warns not to do wild tricks like lassoing Santa or setting traps. Instead, be clever and gentle. On Christmas Eve, you can leave glitter notes, carrots, riddles, cookies, arrows, and bells. Then wait, listen, and stay awake as long as you can. If you do not catch Santa, there is always next year.

The story begins by saying that after waiting for many days, Christmas Eve arrives, and that is when you can try to catch Santa. Because Santa only stays for a short time, you should plan what to do before he comes. The story gives ideas for questions, such as how Santa gets down chimneys, how the reindeer fly, and whether elves ever ride along. It also suggests things to say to Santa, like that you are trying to be good and that you are thankful for the presents. You may even give him gifts, such as a headlamp, a nose warmer, drawings, and decorations for Mrs. Claus. Next, the story warns against rough traps and says to be crafty, clever, and gentle. It then offers ways to spot Santa, including glitter notes, carrots, riddles, cookies, arrows, and bells. At night, listen for Santa sounds, and remember he comes only after you are asleep.

This story is about getting ready for Santa on Christmas Eve. It says you should think ahead because Santa is busy and will not stay long. First, you can prepare questions for him about chimneys, reindeer, elves, toys, letters, and cookies. Then you can tell him important things, such as that you are trying to be good and that your family thanks him for the gifts. The story also says you can make presents for Santa, like a headlamp for dark chimneys or a nose warmer for cold sleigh rides. After that, it tells you not to use wild plans like nets or traps. summaries.summary: The story explains that mindfulness means paying attention to the present moment, both inside our bodies and around us. It says breathing is the main tool for practicing mindfulness. First, it shows how mindfulness can help with focus, stress, and calm. Then it teaches a game called Rainstorm. Children rub their hands for wind, tap slowly for rain, clap for lightning, stomp for thunder, and then slow down until everything is quiet. After that, it shows Funny Breath, where children sit tall, make bunny paws, and take quick bunny breaths. Next comes Scrunch and Let Go, where children squeeze their toes, legs, belly, arms, hands, and face, then breathe out and relax. It also teaches Hot Chocolate, where children blow on an imaginary cup, and Bear Breath, where children breathe slowly like a bear in a cave. At the end, it asks children to think of kind things they have done and kind things they can do next time.

The next exercise is Funny Breath. Children sit up tall, hold still, make bunny paws, and take quick breaths in through the nose before letting the air out. Then comes Scrunch and Let Go. Children squeeze their toes, legs, belly, arms, hands, and face, then breathe out and relax their whole body. After that, Hot Chocolate helps children calm down by pretending to blow on a hot cup. After that, Llewellyn and Evelyn collected more wonders together, like rainbows, the sound of the ocean, the wind before snow, and the seasons of winter, spring, and summer. Their jars filled Llewellyn’s house. Then Evelyn’s family moved away, and Llewellyn felt very sad and empty. Later, he collected a meteor shower in a jar and sent it to Evelyn. Evelyn sent back sounds, crowds, and bright night lights from her new home. When autumn came, Llewellyn went to collect a jar full of golden leaves for Evelyn, and a boy named Max was there too.

Mommy says many women in her family have mooche, or mustaches, and that hair grows on many parts of the body. Papa tells Lakshmi that hair can protect people and keep them warm. They also talk about the hair between her eyebrows and compare it to Frida Kahlo and a caterpillar. That night, Lakshmi dreams of tigers and butterflies. Noah asks if he has one, and Lakshmi draws a much on his lip. Soon many children line up to show real or drawn mooches.

summaries.summary: The lupine lady was once a little girl named Alice who lived in a city by the sea. She loved listening to her grandfather, an artist, tell stories about faraway places. Alice said she would grow up, travel, and someday live by the sea. Her grandfather told her she must do a third thing too: do something to make the world more beautiful. When Alice grew up, she left home and worked in a library in another city. People called her Miss Rumphius. She traveled to many places, including a tropical island, mountains, jungles, deserts, and the land of the lotus eaters. She met kind people, saw animals, and collected beautiful shells. At the land of the lotus eaters, she hurt her back and decided it was time to live by the sea again. There she planted lupine seeds, and the flowers grew and spread. Soon fields and roads were covered with blue, purple, and rose-colored lupines, and people called her the lupine lady.

Alice lived in a city by the sea with her grandfather, who made and painted beautiful things. In the evenings, she listened to his stories and promised to go to faraway places and live beside the sea when she was old. Her grandfather said she must also do something to make the world more beautiful. Alice grew up, moved away, and worked in a library, where she helped keep books in order. She traveled to warm islands, beaches, mountains, jungles, and deserts. She met the bapa raja and his wife in a fishing village, and he gave her a shell with a bird of paradise painted on it. Later, in the land of the lotus eaters, she hurt her back and returned to live near the sea. She planted lupine seeds in her rocky garden. When she could not plant more, the wind and birds spread the seeds. The next spring, lupines grew everywhere, and Miss Rumphius had done the third thing her grandfather asked.

summaries.summary: I am not a unicorn. I am not a fish. I am a narwhal, and I am a kind of whale. My family includes the beluga whale, the dolphin, and the porpoise. I live in the cold Arctic waters with my pod, which means my family. I can dive very deep and hold my breath under the ice for a long time. In spring, narwhals swim to warmer bays. This is called migration. When we get there, we lie on the water and rest. This is called logging. Long ago, people found narwhal horns on the beach and thought they were unicorn horns. My horn is really a big front tooth called a tusk. It grows in a spiral through my upper lip. It helps me taste salt and find food. I can stun cod fish or squid with my tusk and then eat them. I make clicking and knocking sounds, and my family knows what I mean.

summaries.summary: It was the night before Easter, just before dawn. Sister and I were in bed, and our Easter baskets were on the table. We waited and hoped the Easter Bunny would come. Then the hens in the barn made a loud clatter, and I got up to see what was happening. I saw a big fuzzy rabbit with a crook in his ear. He walked on two legs and came to the house with chocolates and striped lollipops. The bunny wore a checkered vest and a bow tie. He filled our baskets with chocolates, chicks, and lots of candy. Some sweets spilled onto the floor. Then he chose eggs and hid them around the house on couches, chairs, the mantle, the bookshelf, and under the stairs. When the rooster crowed, the bunny hurried away in his cart. I read his note: “Happy Easter to all, and to all a great day.”

summaries.summary: There were three bears: papa bear, mama bear, and baby bear. They lived in a little house in the forest. They had three chairs, three bowls, and three beds. The big chair was too hard, the middle chair was too soft, and the baby chair broke. Then she tasted the porridge. The big bowl was too hot, the middle bowl was too cold, and the little bowl was just right, so she ate it all. Goldilocks went upstairs and tried the beds. The big bed was too hard, the middle bed was too soft, and the little bed was just right, so she fell asleep. The bears came home, saw what happened, and found Goldilocks in the baby bear’s bed. Goldilocks woke up, saw the bears, jumped out the window, and ran home.

The leaves on all the trees turned yellow, red, and orange, and one by one they fell. Little tree kept holding them. Spring came, and the other trees grew bright new leaves. The seasons kept changing, and little tree still would not let go. At last, after another summer and autumn, he saw the other trees growing tall. Then he let his last leaf fall to the ground for the first time.

Kim told him she was nervous too because it was her first job away from home. Rick and Kim held hands, and Rick stayed for the rest of the week. He had fun doing races, crafts, and a play, and by Friday he wanted to come back next summer.

summaries.summary: Harvey Milk was an ordinary man with a big dream. He wanted everyone, including gay people, to have equality and to live and love as they pleased. Harvey spoke to people about his dream, and in 1977 he became one of the first openly gay people elected to political office in the United States. He and his friends planned marches against unfair laws. Before one march, Harvey asked artist Gilbert Baker to help make a symbol for their group. Gilbert said they needed a flag. Volunteers helped him dye, cut, and sew bright fabric into a flag with eight colorful stripes. On June 25, 1978, the flag flew in San Francisco as Harvey and others marched for equality. Five months later, Harvey and Mayor George Moscone were killed. Many people marched silently with candles. After that, more rainbow flags were made, and the flag became a sign of equality, pride, and hope.

He asked Gilbert Baker for help, and Gilbert said, “We need a flag.” Volunteers worked together with dye, cloth, scissors, and thread to make a flag with eight stripes. On June 25, 1978, the rainbow flag flew in San Francisco while Harvey and others marched for equality. Later, Harvey and Mayor George Moscone were assassinated. People then held candle marches. The rainbow flag kept going after that. More flags were made, the colors changed to six stripes, and people in many places around the world began to carry and display the flag as a symbol of love and equality.

summaries.summary: Peep was old enough to go on the rooftops with her big brother Hoot. Hoot wanted to teach Peep his owl wisdom, and Peep wanted to sing about the Moon beams. Hoot told Peep that owls say only “who,” and he said “who” can mean hello, goodbye, good morning, and good night. But Hoot forgot that owls never shout. Peep listened for a while, then flew away when Hoot would not listen to her. Hoot thought Peep would not listen to his wisdom, and Peep thought Hoot did not believe in singing about mystery and magic. After Peep left, Hoot missed her songs. He heard Peep’s sweet voice on the wind and learned that little sisters have their own owl wisdom. Hoot asked Peep to teach him her song. Soon Hoot and Peep sang together in their own special ways, and the night felt perfect.

One night, Peep joined Hoot on the rooftops. Hoot tried to teach her how owls speak. He said owls say “who” first, then always “who,” and at last only “who.” He also said “who” can mean many things, like hello and good night. Peep did not like only saying “who.” She liked whispering to the wind and singing with the waves and Moon beams. Because Hoot would not listen to Peep, she flew away. Then Hoot saw that he missed her. Without Peep, saying “who” did not feel good anymore. He heard Peep singing in the wind and knew he had made a mistake. Hoot asked Peep to teach him her song. After that, the two owls sang together. Hoot used his owl sounds, and Peep used her own song. The night wind carried their music, and they thought it was a perfect night.

summaries.summary: Lightning McQueen wanted to rest, but Mater wanted to go tractor-tipping. Mater honked at two sleeping tractors, and they tipped up on their back tires. Mater drove away, but his hook caught on the gate and tore part of the fence. Frank chased Lightning and Mater toward town. They hid behind the new race track, and Frank drove past them. When they went home, their tires were soft and sticky from wet asphalt. They had driven on the street while it was being paved. Doc saw the tire tracks and was not happy. Lightning and Mater fixed the road with Bessie. Then Doc asked Mater to fix Frank’s broken fence. Mater started the job, but he fell asleep. While he slept, the tractors got out and wandered away.

The next day Lightning went to look for Mater and the tractors. The tractors were gone, and the road had been messed up. Sheriff asked Mater if he let the tractors out, and Mater said they kind of let themselves out. Sally said the road would not be ready in time for the race. Mater felt bad and said he would fix the road again, even if he had to work all night. Lightning said he would help. Mater pulled Bessie, and Lightning practiced for the race. The next day, cars came from all over for the big race. The road to the new racetrack was smooth and ready. Lightning’s friends were there to watch, but Mater was not with them. He had brought the tractors to see the race. Lightning told him to go get them. When the green flag waved, Lightning raced fast and took the lead. He won the race.

summaries.summary: One quiet evening in Radiators, the town folk rode down Main Street and waited for dark so they could go to the drive-in movie. Mater did not want to go alone, so Lightning McQueen and Sheriff went with him. When they saw glowing lights in the caves, Mater got scared and wanted to go back. Sheriff said there were no ghosts and shined his headlights into the cave. Then they found Goodman, the Swedish racer, who had many headlights and a funny accent. Goodman asked McQueen to race in the caves. Sheriff put night vision goggles on McQueen, and McQueen and Goodman raced through the dark cave all night. In the morning, the mystery was solved, and the friends went back to town. McQueen wanted to race again, but Sheriff said next time he would stay for the movie.

summaries.summary: A fish tells about life in a bowl day by day. At first, the fish swims around the bowl and even thinks about napping, but fish do not sleep, so it keeps swimming. Then a new fish named Mr. Bubble arrives, but he only bubbles and says almost nothing. Soon the bowl changes more and more. Plants appear, so the fish waters them. A snail named Marvin joins in, then a crab named Fred comes and makes the bowl feel crowded. After that, a sunken pirate ship, two guppies named Rhonda and Clark, and an angelfish named Cha-Cha all move in too. The fish can hardly swim without bumping into something, and Rhonda and Clark say they will have babies. On day 12, the fish gets upset and shouts that it wants its bowl back. On day 13, it gets a tiny bowl all to itself, but it soon feels lonely and worries about the others. On day 14, everyone comes back together in a big tank, and the fish is happy to be part of a family.

summaries.summary: One morning, the child woke up and saw that a pet unicorn had silly spots all over her body. The child used a doctor bag and a magnifying glass to look closely at the spots. The child thought the spots came from telling knock knock jokes the day before. Then the unicorn sneezed, and spots flew out of her nose and went everywhere. The child tried to fix the problem by putting band-aids on each spot, but when the band-aids came off, the spots were still there. Next, the child tried washing the spots off, but that did not work either. The child and the unicorn grew tired, so the child covered the unicorn with a blanket and went to sleep. When the child woke up, the unicorn was gone. After searching the room and house, the child found the unicorn in the hallway making spots into art. The story ends by saying the spots were hard to remove, but they showed the healing power of art.

summaries.summary: The book speaks to a dear girl and gives her many kind reminders. It tells her to keep her arm raised when she has smart things to say. It says she may sometimes feel pink and sparkly, and other times feel the opposite. She is told to look in the mirror and thank the things that make her special, like freckles, a birthmark, and red hair. The book says it is okay to cry, to need a friend, to be alone, or to need a tissue or a bucket. It says she can ask as many questions as she wants and can write down her thoughts. She should make her room awesome, make her bed, keep her wonder, and stop to dance sometimes. She is also told to find people like her and unlike her, say no when needed, color outside the lines, listen to her brave side, and know she can always turn to the book and to the person who loves her.

video_title: All About Weather -  A First Weather Book for Kids By Huda Harajli MA

summaries.summary: Weather is what the sky and air are like outside. The sky may be blue, the air may feel warm, and the weather can change all the time. Weather helps people decide what to do each day. Weather also changes through the year, and these changes are called seasons. Many places have four seasons: spring, summer, fall, and winter. In spring, the weather is warm and rainy, and flowers bloom. In summer, it is hot and sunny. In fall, the air gets cooler and leaves change color. In winter, the air is cold and there may be snow. Near the middle of the earth, there are two seasons: rainy and dry. Thermometers show how hot or cold the air is. The sun gives light and warmth, and it helps make the weather on Earth.

The sun can make the air feel hot, and then people can enjoy a sunny day outside. They may ride a bike in the park or go to the beach to cool down. When the air moves, it is windy. Wind cannot be seen, but it can be felt, and it can blow a hat away. On a windy day, people can fly a kite or blow bubbles. Windmills can turn wind into electricity. Sometimes the sky is cloudy. Clouds form when tiny water droplets rise up because of warmth from the sun and stick together. Clouds can be called cumulus, stratus, cirrus, or nimbus. People can look at clouds and see different shapes. Clouds are very heavy, even if they look light and fluffy.

Sometimes it rains outside, so people need an umbrella. Rain is water that falls from clouds. Rain helps plants grow because it gives them water. A drop of water can spend 9 days in the sky before it falls to the earth. On a rainy day, a child can read a book near a window and listen to the raindrops. Sometimes rain freezes and turns into snow. Snow is icy and wet, and snowflakes all have six sides, even though they can look different. On a snowy day, children can make snow angels or try ice skating. A snow day is cold, so people should lace up their boots. Weather can change from rain to snow when the air is cold enough.

Sometimes there is a thunderstorm. If people hear thunder and see lightning, it is a thunderstorm. Thunderstorms can bring rain and sometimes wind. They happen when cold air and warm air meet. During a storm, people should move the picnic inside and stay safe indoors away from windows. They can play games with their family while they wait. They can also count the seconds between lightning and thunder to see how far away the storm is. After a thunderstorm, people may see a rainbow. Rainbows form when light shines through raindrops. The rainbow has seven colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet.

People can get ready for weather by choosing the right clothes and items. On a cold snowy day, they may need warm things. On a rainy day, they may need two items, like an umbrella and boots. On a sunny and bright day, they may need things for sun. Looking at what people wear can help tell if it is spring, summer, fall, or winter. Weather changes, and each season has its own kind of sky, air, and clothes. After learning about sunny days, windy days, cloudy days, rainy days, snowy days, and stormy days, a child can become a weather expert. The story ends by asking which kind of weather is your favorite.

video_title: We Are Water Protectors by Carole Lindstrom and Michaela Goade   Story Time Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Nakomis tells the child that water is the first medicine and that people come from water. She says water is sacred and that they stand with their songs and their drums. The child hears that the river’s rhythms run through their veins and their people’s veins. Then the story tells of a black snake that will destroy the land, spoil the water, poison plants and animals, and wreck everything in its path. Long ago, people said it would come many years later, and now it is here. Its venom burns the land and makes the water unsafe to drink. The child says they must keep the black snake away from the village’s water and bring the people together to stand for the water and the land. They must also protect the winged ones, the crawling ones, the four-legged, the two-legged, the plants, trees, rivers, lakes, and the earth. The story ends with the people standing as water protectors and saying, “We are still here.”

The story begins with Nakomis teaching that water is the first medicine and that water nourishes people before birth and after. She says water is sacred, and the people stand with songs and drums. The child feels the river’s rhythms in their own body and in their people. Then they remember the black snake, a danger that was foretold long ago. Now it has come, and its venom hurts the land and poisons the water, plants, and animals. The child feels tears and says they must keep the black snake away from the village’s water. They call their people to stand together for the water and the land. Nakomis says water has a spirit, water is alive, and water remembers ancestors. In the end, the people stand as stewards of the earth and water protectors, and the black snake must face their fight.

summaries.summary: A narrator dreams of “you,” and then the two are together. They carry gifts in a backpack and cross a bridge that is like the universe. They say goodbye, “Adios corazon,” and reach the other side. There, they cannot go back, and they become immigrant migrants. The sky and the land welcome them with words they do not know. They do not understand many things and feel afraid to speak. They make many mistakes. Then they become caminantes, walking thousands and thousands of steps across the land. One day, they find a new place that is strange and surprising. In that place, they do not need to speak. They only need to trust, and they do. Books become their language, their home, and their lives. They learn to read, speak, write, and make their voices heard. In the end, they are stories, two languages, lucha, resilience, hope, and dreamers, “sonyadores of the world.”

video_title: Different is Good by Rebecca J. Jackson

summaries.summary: Ashura loved summertime because the days were long, the world looked golden, and school was out. But he also felt sad because the children at school called him names and made him feel unwelcome. One night, his mother told him to go to the park the next day, and Ashura was scared because he thought the other children would hurt his feelings again. That night, he prayed to the stars for help. A strange purple creature named Cleo came through his window and said the stars had sent him. Cleo promised to go with Ashura to the park. The next day, Cleo showed Ashura many children who were different in skin color, hair, clothes, faith, language, and family. He explained that all of them were special. Ashura listened, played with Bella and her friends, and learned that he belonged too. He went home happy and wished for morning so he could return to the park.

When summer came, Ashura enjoyed the warm weather, but he worried about how other children treated him. He lived with Mama, Baba, Samira, and baby Milo, and his family looked different from the neighbors on the street. One evening, Mama said he should go to the park the next day because his friends would be there. Ashura agreed, even though he was afraid. At night he could not sleep, so he asked the stars for help. Then Cleo, a small purple creature with blue spots, appeared at his window and told him the stars had sent him. The next morning, Cleo met Ashura at the park and showed him that every child was different and important. He pointed out children with different clothes, hair, food, languages, and families. Ashura learned not to be ashamed of his skin or his family. He spent the day playing with Bella and others, then returned home smiling and feeling proud.

Ashura felt nervous and prayed to the stars so he would not have to face the other children alone. A magical creature named Cleo came to his window and promised to help him. The next morning, Cleo waited for him at the park.
