summaries.summary: The ballots were counted, and Splat the cat became the new student body president. At first, he gave a speech and promised new pencils, better fish food for the class goldfish, and quieter quiet reading time. But at lunch, he heard classmates grumbling that they did not want the new pencils, and his afternoon felt rough. Mrs. Wimpy Dimple told Splat to think about what the kids really wanted and to share new ideas the next day. That night, Splat thought hard on the bus and at the dinner table. The next day, he made big promises about race cars for school, pizza and ice cream every day, and robot teachers to do homework and tests. Mrs. Wimpy Dimple later explained that Splat could not promise things he could not keep. She told him to look for something he could change. Splat then suggested fixing up the school library, and everyone painted, sorted books, and set up displays. The library project was a big success.

summaries.summary: A calerie pear tree lived for more than 20 years on the World Trade Center Plaza in New York City. On September 11, 2001, the Twin Towers fell near her and covered her with debris. For a month, she lay under smoking rubble. Then workers saw a few green leaves showing through the gray ash and concrete. They carefully uncovered the tree and found that many branches were gone, only a few roots were left, and her trunk was burned and scarred. Still, the leaves gave them hope. The workers took her by truck to a nursery. The tree felt scared as the city grew smaller behind her. At the nursery, workers put her in rich soil and fertilizer. Richie, a city parks worker, touched her trunk and said he would help her heal. The tree felt sad, but she began her long recovery.

Before the tree lived at the World Trade Center Plaza, she had grown in a quiet nursery from a seed to a tall sapling. She remembered her first trip to New York City on a chilly spring day, when she saw tall buildings, traffic, music, bright lights, and many people. She was excited about her new home, but when she was hurt years later, she remembered those feelings while riding to the nursery. At the nursery, workers placed stone blocks near her in a memorial shaped like the World Trade Center. Richie came every day to care for her. In spring, he pruned away damaged parts of her branches, even though she did not like it. One day he found twigs in her limbs, and soon a dove came with twine and built a nest. Richie felt hopeful. Not long after, he saw green buds on the tree and knew she would survive.

As spring warmed the nursery, the calerie pear tree began to change. The ground softened, the air grew warm, and birds sang around her. She shook off the winter cold and opened into small white blossoms. Richie kept visiting and caring for her, bringing fertilizer and trimming the damaged parts. One day, when he came with fresh fertilizer, the tree dropped a shower of petals onto his hair, and he laughed. The tree also remembered a sunny day at the World Trade Center Plaza, when the sky was bright and the clouds moved slowly. Her memories and the care she received helped her keep growing. The tree went through many years of healing after the attack. In time, she became strong enough to return to the 9/11 Memorial Plaza. There, she stood as a sign that she had survived and was home again.

summaries.summary: Red and Lulu lived happily in their evergreen tree. Their nest was safe in the branches, and the tree kept them cool in summer and cozy in winter. In winter, people decorated the tree with lights and sang, “Oh Christmas tree, oh Christmas tree, thy leaves are so unchanging.” Red and Lulu loved to listen and sometimes sang too. One cold morning, Red went to find breakfast while Lulu stayed in the tree. When Red came back, the tree was gone. It had been cut down, placed on a big truck, and driven away with Lulu inside. Red flew after it, but he could not catch up. He searched for days in a strange place and felt tired and hungry. Then he heard the song again and followed it to Lulu. Later, workers took the tree away again, and Red and Lulu stayed in a new home in a park. Every year, they still visit the Rockefeller Center Christmas tree and listen and sing.

summaries.summary: A gingerbread man began as batter in a bowl. Children in a classroom mixed ginger, cinnamon, molasses, butter, and eggs, then rolled and shaped him like a man and added sweets. He baked in a warm oven until the teacher called recess and the class ran out, leaving him behind. The gingerbread man popped off the pan and ran through the hall, saying he wanted to be with the children. He met the coach, who helped when his toe came off. Then he met the nurse, who fixed his toe with glue and a bandage. After that, he slid down a handrail, landed in the art teacher’s lunch bag, and asked for help again. The art teacher sent him to the principal. Principal Peacock showed him a missing poster from room 23. At last, the class came back, cheered, and made him a gingerbread desk, chair, and house. He stayed with them and looked happy.

summaries.summary: In the wild wild west, a Rancher and his wife lived on a ranch. Every morning, the Rancher fed the cattle and saddled his horses, while his wife baked breakfast biscuits. One day, she got tired of biscuits and made gingerbread dough instead. She cut out a gingerbread Cowboy with boots, a hat, and a big belt buckle, then gave him raisins, candies, and nuts for eyes, mouth, and vest. She put him in the oven to bake. When the Rancher peeked inside because he was hungry, the gingerbread Cowboy jumped out and ran away. He laughed, “Giddy up giddy up as fast as you can. You can't catch me. I'm the gingerbread man.” He ran past a Road Runner, havelinas, longhorn cattle, and Cowboys, and each one wanted to catch him or eat him. At the river, a coyote offered help. The coyote carried him across, then tricked him, tossed him up, and swallowed him. That was the end of the gingerbread Cowboy.

summaries.summary: A cookie lives in a bakery near a river and tells about feeling unsure at school. The cookie goes to a gingerbread house school with kind Miss biscotti, but does not raise a hand, finishes tests last, and often makes mistakes. One day Miss biscotti gives the class a homework task: make something completely original. The cookie tries cooking, building, and sculpture, but each idea fails. Then the cookie watches the rain on the river and gets an idea to write a poem called “my crummy days.” The cookie writes it and feels proud. The next day, the cookie reads the poem aloud to the class. The other children listen, nod, laugh at the funny parts, and clap at the end. Miss biscotti says the poem is completely original. After that, the cookie feels more confident, starts speaking up, and learns that being smart can mean many different things.

The poem was called “my crummy days,” and the cookie worked on it until it was finished. The next day, the cookie shared the poem in class. The children reacted with smiles, nods, and applause. Miss biscotti praised the poem, and the cookie felt smart, began raising a hand, and kept writing.

Then he took all the gifts and food to the top of Mount Crumpet and waited to hear the Whos cry. But the Whos woke up and sang together anyway. The Grinch was surprised and thought Christmas did not come from a store. His heart grew three sizes, and he brought everything back to Hooville.

Animals got ready for cold weather. Bear ate all day and said winter was too cold, so he stayed inside. Raccoon said Bear would sleep through all the fun. Bats went into a cave, caterpillars closed their cocoons, and Hedgehog said, “See you in Spring,” before going into his warm winter home. Then snow came and covered the forest. Little Owl watched the frozen pond and saw fish swimming under the ice. Later, he missed Hedgehog and asked Mama how long until spring. Mama said snow was like a special secret and told him to enjoy it while it was there. Little Owl listened to the quiet forest and heard a tiny drip from an icicle.

summaries.summary: In a big house high on a hill lives a family: a mama, a papa, a boy, a girl, and a baby. On the mantle in The Parlor sits a snow globe that nobody notices anymore except baby. Inside the snow globe lives a tiny family with the same members, and they are having tea and crumb cake too. The little family loves the snow that covers their world all year. They build snowmen, skate on a pond, throw snowballs, and make snow angels. They wish someone would shake the snow globe hard so they could have a hill for sledding. The little children ask their papa for stories about the big snowstorms from long ago, and he tells them there used to be big storms, but now only a small flurry comes sometimes. One evening, a real blizzard begins outside. The big family goes sledding, but baby stays inside. Baby climbs to the mantle, sees the little baby, grabs the snow globe, and shakes it hard. The little family rushes outside to sled, and later everyone sleeps and dreams of the next snowstorm.

They play in the snow, make snow angels, and hope for a big snowstorm so they can go sledding on a hill. Sometimes they call out, but the big family does not notice them. The little children ask their papa about old snowstorms, and he says the house used to shake and dishes flew around, but now only a gentle flurry comes once a week. They all enjoy the snow and go to sleep dreaming of more snow.

summaries.summary: Martin Luther King Jr. was born in Atlanta, Georgia, on January 15, 1929. He grew up with his father, who was a pastor, his mother, who had been a teacher, and his sister Willie Christine and brother Alfred Daniel. As a boy, Martin liked baseball, football, basketball, riding his bicycle, and singing in his father’s church. One day, two friends said they could not play with him anymore because they were white and he was black. Martin cried and did not understand why skin color mattered. His mother explained that black people had been treated unfairly for a long time. Martin learned to read at home and read books about black leaders. He finished high school early, went to Morehouse College, studied in Boston, and married Ketta Scott. Later, as a pastor in Montgomery, he led peaceful protests after Rosa Parks was arrested. He helped lead the bus boycott, the March on Washington, and other peaceful protests. In 1964 he won the Nobel Peace Prize. In 1968 he went to Memphis to march for fair pay, and there he was killed.

He was sad and confused, and his mother told him that black people had been treated unfairly for many years. Martin learned to read at home and studied books about black leaders. He worked hard in school, finished high school early, and entered Morehouse College when he was only 15. After college he studied in Boston, met Ketta Scott, and married her in 1954. He became a pastor in Montgomery, Alabama. The next year, Rosa Parks was arrested for not giving up her bus seat, and Martin led a bus boycott. People stopped riding the buses for almost a year until the white-only bus sections ended. Later he moved back to Atlanta and led peaceful protests and marches. In 1963 he gave his famous “I have a dream” speech. In 1964 he won the Nobel Peace Prize. In 1968 he went to Memphis to march for equal pay, and James Earl Ray shot him.

summaries.summary: Audrey Fay Hendrix lived in Birmingham with her Mama C, Daddy, and family. Mama told her to hush, but Audrey kept listening to meetings at Fred’s church, where people sang, shared stories, and heard Mike say segregation was wrong. Mike asked people to protest and fill the jails, but many adults were afraid. Then Jim said children should go instead. Audrey said she wanted to go to jail, and her parents let her join the protest. She marched from 16th Street Baptist Church, was arrested, and spent days in juvenile hall with hard beds, little food, and strict guards. After more children were arrested, the jails filled up, the protests worked, and Birmingham later ended segregation laws.

Audrey Fay Hendrix grew up in Birmingham during segregation. At home, she heard Mike, the name her family used for Martin Luther King Jr., talk with the adults about unfair laws. Mike preached that segregation was sinful and said people should disobey unjust laws by sitting in, marching, and getting arrested. The adults were afraid, so they did not go. Then Jim Bevel said children could fill the jails instead. Audrey asked to go, put on her best clothes, and marched with the children from 16th Street Baptist Church. Police arrested her and sent her to juvenile hall, where she faced hard beds, bad food, and strict rules. After many children were jailed, the city could not keep arresting more people, and segregation in Birmingham ended.

Today, St Patrick’s Day is a day for worship and celebration. Many people go to church to give thanks for St Patrick’s work in Ireland. They also wear green to honor an old Irish custom. Long ago, people in Ireland burned green branches in March and spread the ashes in fields to help the land grow. Green decorations are placed on doors and windows, and shamrocks are used often. A shamrock is a plant with three leaves, and it is a symbol of St Patrick and Ireland. People also remember leprechauns, tiny magic creatures from Irish stories, and some say they can lead a person to gold. The harp, one of Ireland’s oldest instruments, is another decoration. Families may send cards, share food, and wear green carnations or pin shamrocks to their clothes. There are often songs, Irish dances, games, and parades with flags, pipers, fiddlers, and many green costumes.

St Patrick’s Day was first celebrated in the United States in Boston in 1737. Since then, many people have celebrated it each year. The holiday is especially important to the Irish, but other people join in too. On this day, some people go to church, while others enjoy parties and parades. They sing Irish songs, dance Irish jigs, and play games. In many places, there are green hats, green banners, and costumes. People may give flowers, cakes, cookies, and other goodies to family and friends. Some families spend quiet time together and share meals. St Patrick’s Day is a time for both worship and celebration, and many people enjoy feeling a little bit Irish for the day.

Many legends are told about St Patrick. One story says he got rid of all the snakes in Ireland by beating his drum and frightening them into the sea. Another says a wizard tried to kill him by putting poison in his drink, but St Patrick turned it into ice and threw it from his cup. A different story says a friend borrowed St Patrick’s cloak, and when a fire broke out, the friend was safe because he was wearing it. Another legend says St Patrick used the shamrock to explain the Holy Trinity, showing one God as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Other stories say fish rise from the sea on March 17th and pass his altar, and that when St Patrick died, the sun stayed in the sky for 12 days and nights.

He studied religion in France, and in 432 the Pope named him patricius. After that, he became a priest and then a bishop. Bishop Patrick sailed to Ireland, preached there, and built churches and schools across the country. People trusted him because of his kind ways, and he spent the rest of his life caring for the Irish people. He died on March 17th in 461, and people honor him on that day.

summaries.summary: Audrey Fay Hendrick lived in Birmingham with her mama and daddy. When Mike, also called Martin or Dr. King, came to town, her family cooked ribs, greens, sweet potato, and hot rolls. Audrey listened when grown-ups talked about segregation, which kept black and white people apart. She said she wanted to eat inside Newberries, sit downstairs at the Alabama, and use the nice books, seats, and fountains like white children. On Monday nights, she went to Fred’s church with her family and sang, “Black and white together, we shall overcome.” She heard Mike say that unjust laws should be broken and that people should fill the jails. When the grown-ups would not go, Jim said children should go. Audrey raised her hand and said she wanted to go to jail. Her mama said okay, and Audrey went with other children to protest.

Audrey got ready to go to jail in clean clothes. Her daddy bought her a game, and her parents told her teachers she would be gone for a while. Miss Wills hugged her, and her grandparents told her she would be fine. Then her mama and daddy took her to 16th Street Baptist Church. There were many children there, singing freedom songs. Audrey was the youngest child and did not know anyone. She stood with the others, held a protest sign and her game, and marched out singing, “Ain't going to let nobody Turn Me Around.” A white policeman stopped her and sent her to juvenile hall. A matron locked her in a day room with older girls. Audrey sat alone, played with her game, and cried when the matron scolded her. Jail was hard, and Audrey was hungry, tired, and lonely.

In jail, Audrey ate grits, slept on a thin sheet, and had no fresh clothes or toothbrush. She was taken to a room where four white men asked her questions. Audrey said she was not against America and that the meetings were about freedom. She said she marched because she wanted to go places and do things like everybody else. More children came into the day room. Some were wet because firefighters had sprayed them with hoses, but they kept marching until they were sent to jail too. By Audrey’s fifth day, the police could not fit any more people in the jail. Audrey heard, “We filled up all the rooms!” and felt proud. On television, she saw black people walking into stores and restaurants. No more children could be sent to jail, and things had changed.

After seven days, Audrey went home. Her mama and daddy hugged her and washed the jail off her. She ate hot rolls baptized in butter for dinner. Two months later, Birmingham took segregation laws off the books. Audrey later ate her ice cream at the Newberries counter, just like everybody else. Black and white people could be together there. The story shows Audrey speaking up, marching, and going to jail with other children so unfair laws could change.

She knew the unfair rules for buses, stores, elevators, and schools. At church, she heard Mike say that people should disobey unjust laws and fill the jails. When the adults would not go, Jim said children should go instead. Audrey chose to go. She marched from 16th Street Baptist Church, was arrested, and spent seven days in juvenile hall. Jail was cold, hard, and lonely, but more children came after her. The jail filled up, the protests continued, and black people began entering stores and restaurants. Later, Birmingham changed its laws, and Audrey could sit at the Newberries counter.

summaries.summary: St Patrick’s Day is celebrated on March 17th. It honors St Patrick, who lived many years ago. He was born in Britain and was raised in a Christian family. When he was a boy, people took him to Ireland and made him a slave. He had to herd sheep, and he prayed for help. Six years later, he escaped and went back to Britain. There he thought and prayed and decided he wanted to return to Ireland to teach people about God. He studied religion in France. In 432, the pope gave him the name Patricius, and he became a priest and then a bishop. Bishop Patrick went back to Ireland, preached, and built churches and schools. People trusted him and loved him. He died on March 17th in 461, and later he was called Saint Patrick. Today people celebrate with church, green clothes, shamrocks, cards, songs, dances, parades, and food.

summaries.summary: The story tells about 13 American women who did not give up when people said they could not do big things. Harriet Tubman was born into slavery, but she escaped and led her family, friends, and strangers to freedom. Helen Keller was blind, and some people did not think she could learn, but she learned to read, write, and speak. Clara Limi worked in a factory with terrible conditions and helped workers get better treatment. Nellie Bly became a reporter and told the truth about how people were treated, even when it was risky. Virginia Apgar became a doctor and made the Apgar score for newborn babies. These women kept going even when others tried to stop them.

Maria Tallchief was teased for being Native American, but she kept dancing and became the first Great American Prima ballerina. Claudette Koven was told to give up her seat on a bus, but she stayed seated and took a stand for justice. Ruby Bridges had to walk through protesters to go to school, and she helped integrate an all-white elementary school in New Orleans. Margaret Chase Smith became both a U.S. Representative and a U.S. senator, and then she kept working for women’s rights, free speech, and space exploration. Sally Ride believed women could do math and science jobs, and she became the first American woman in space. She also helped young girls imagine themselves in those careers.

Florence Griffith-Joyner heard her father tell her to run fast like a jack rabbit, and she believed she could do it. She kept training and became the fastest woman ever at the 1988 Summer Olympics. Oprah Winfrey’s grandmother expected her to become a maid, but Oprah knew she wanted a different life. She kept going and became a media superstar who hosted the highest rated talk show of all time. Sonia Sotomayor watched fictional judges on television and wanted to be a real judge. She persisted and became a Supreme Court Justice and the first Latina on America’s highest court.

The story begins by saying that girls may hear that their dreams are impossible, but they should not listen. It then shows many women who persisted. Harriet Tubman escaped slavery and helped others reach freedom. Helen Keller learned to read, write, and speak after becoming blind. Clara Limi fought for better factory conditions. Nellie Bly became a reporter and exposed unfair treatment. Virginia Apgar created a score that hospitals still use for newborn babies. These women all kept working toward their goals, even when people doubted them or made things hard.

More women in the story kept going and reached important goals. Maria Tallchief ignored teasing and bad advice and became a famous ballerina. Claudette Koven refused to give up her bus seat and helped inspire others to stand for equal rights. Ruby Bridges walked through angry protesters to attend school and help open the school to African-American students. Margaret Chase Smith kept speaking up after becoming a U.S. Representative and senator. Sally Ride became the first American woman in space and helped girls dream about science. Florence Griffith-Joyner became the fastest woman, Oprah Winfrey became a TV star, and Sonia Sotomayor became a Supreme Court Justice.

summaries.summary: Mr Fish wanted to buy presents for his friends, but he kept looking for gifts that were big, bright, perfect, and full of meaning. He went to one store and saw many shiny things, but nothing felt right. At the next store, he found a sign for the season’s hottest item, but it had already sold out. At the final store, he arrived first in line, but the store was closed. Mr Fish felt sad and thought he would miss the party and let his friends down. Then Miss Shimmer told him that the best gift was the one and only him. She said it was not too late to make gifts from the heart. Mr Fish made gifts with his own fins and gave them to his friends at the party. Everyone laughed, sang, shared, and enjoyed the happy day together.

The student and the teacher swam to a new fish door, and Miss huitt greeted the class. She said they would have a spectacular year and told them three things: they were smart, they could get it, and they belonged. The class listened, tried their work, and everyone could do it with her help. Later, Mr Fish and his pals were playing in the park when a shark came along and told them to move aside. The shark kept being mean, and Mr Fish felt scared and did not know what to do. The friends tried to play again, but the shark returned and kept causing trouble. Then Mr Fish had an idea. He turned back, faced the shark, and spoke up about what had happened. The friends stood together, and the shark was told to leave until he was ready to treat them with respect. After that, the park was happy again, and everyone played kindly together.

One day in the ocean park, Mr Fish and his friends were having fun when a shark came and scared them. The shark growled, used bad names, and took a guppy’s lunch. Each time the shark came back, Mr Fish shrank and felt afraid. The park stopped feeling happy, and Mr Fish did not know what to do. Then he realized that words can make a difference when things go wrong. He turned around and spoke clearly to the shark about what was happening. The shark was told to leave until he could be respectful. After Mr Fish spoke up, the friends felt stronger and less scared. They began taking turns and using empathy, and the park filled with joyful play again. Mr Fish learned that one fish can help by speaking up and caring about others. Everyone was able to enjoy the ocean park together once more.

Mr Fish saw one friend feeling unhappy, and then two friends, then three, then four, and soon the whole class was in a bad mood. No one was smiling or laughing, and Mr Fish felt sad and did not know what to do. He thought that one fish could not change this, but then he had an idea and tried it. It worked. He tried it again in a new way, and it worked again and again. Mr Fish kept trying, and every time his kind idea helped. Soon the feeling spread from one friend to two, then three, then four, and the whole class became happy again. Mr Fish said, “I can be kind,” and the class said, “We all can be kind.” The bad mood went away, and everyone felt better together.

Late one quiet evening, Mr Fish could not get to sleep. He said his mind was busy and his fins were full of energy, so he could not drift into Dreamland. First, Miss clam gave him a tip: smooth his seaweed bed, imagine fluffy sheep, and count them. Mr Fish tried, but he still could not sleep. Then Mrs squid gave him another plan: widen his eyes, blink four times, and slowly close his lids. Mr Fish tried that too, but he still stayed awake. After that, Mr Fish made his own bedtime routine. He smoothed his seaweed bed, hugged his snoozy snuggly, cleared his busy head, and moved gently in the ocean. Then he closed his eyes, tucked in his fins, and tried to drift right off to sleep.

Mr Fish and a class of students swam to a door marked brand new fish, where Miss Huitt welcomed them. She said they would have a spectacular year and told them three facts: they were smart, they could get it, and they belonged. The class got to work, and Miss Huitt helped them. They listened, tried, and were able to do the work. Later, Mr Fish gave a grin goodbye. After that, he was at the park with his pals and buddies, enjoying happy play when a shark came along and told them to move aside and scram. The shark kept being mean, using bad names and stealing a guppy’s lunch. Mr Fish felt scared and did not know what to do. Then he realized that words can make a difference. He turned back, spoke up, and told the shark to leave until it was ready to treat everyone with respect. The friends grew stronger, felt less scared, and the park became happy again.

One day, Mr Fish saw that one friend was unhappy, then two, then three, then four, and soon the whole class was in a bad mood. No one was smiling or laughing, and Mr Fish felt upset because he did not know what to do. He thought that one fish could not change things, but then he had an idea. He tried it, and it worked. He tried again in a new way, and it worked again. He kept trying, and each time his idea worked. Mr Fish learned that it was not hard to be kind. His kindness spread from one friend to two, then three, then four, until the whole class was in a good mood. Mr Fish said, “I can be kind,” and the class answered, “We all can be kind.”

Late one quiet evening in the deep ocean, Mr Fish could not get to sleep. He said his mind was busy and his fins were full of vim, and he could not drop into Dreamland or slide into snooze. First, Miss Clam offered tips. She told him to smooth his seaweed bedding, imagine fluffy sheep, and count them to one hundred, but Mr Fish still could not sleep. Then Mrs. Squid gave another plan. She said to widen his eyes, blink four times, and slowly close his lids for automatic 40 winks, but that did not work either. After that, Mr Fish decided to make his own routine. He planned to settle in his spot, smooth his seaweed bed, hold his snoozy snuggly, clear his busy head, move gently in the water, close his eyes, and drift right off to sleep.

Mr Fish began with a pout because he wanted presents that were big, bright, perfect, and meaningful for his friends, but time was running out. He searched stores one by one and found shiny items, a sold-out hot item, and then a closed store, so he ended with no gift at all. He felt sure he would miss the party and let his friends down. Miss Shimmer then told him that he only needed to bring himself and that the best gifts come from the heart. Mr Fish made presents with his own fins and brought them to the party. His friends loved the gifts, and everyone was happy, laughing, talking, and singing. They shared the season and the goodwill it was bringing, and Mr Fish joined them with peace, joy, and love.

summaries.summary: There was once a triangle that was always busy. It held up roofs, supported bridges, made music in an orchestra, caught the wind for sailboats, and could also be slices of pie and halves of sandwiches. Its favorite thing was to fit into the shape people made when they put their hands on their hips. The triangle liked to hear the latest news and tell it to its friends. One day, the triangle felt bored and said there must be more to life. It went to the local Shape Shifter and asked for one more side and one more angle. Poof! The triangle became a quadrilateral. The quadrilateral was happy with its new jobs, like being a baseball diamond, a checkerboard space, a screen, or a window frame. Its favorite thing was being the pages of a book. But after a while, it also grew dissatisfied and went back to the Shape Shifter for another change.

The quadrilateral asked the Shape Shifter for one more side and one more angle, and it became a pentagon. The pentagon could be home plate on a baseball diamond, a part of a soccer ball, or the shape inside a five-pointed star. Its favorite job was being the headquarters of the United States military near Washington DC, where it heard top secrets. It could not tell those secrets to its friends, and the friends felt left out. After some time, the pentagon became restless and unhappy again. It returned to the Shape Shifter and asked for one more side and one more angle. Poof! It changed into a hexagon. The hexagon could be floor tiles, houses, patios, fancy crackers, and parts of bolts and branches. Its favorite thing was being a cell in a beehive, where it watched bees buzz in and out.

The hexagon spent so much time in the beehive that it was too busy to talk to its friends. The friends missed it and felt ignored. Soon the shape became restless and unhappy again, and it went back to the Shape Shifter for more sides and more angles. The Shape Shifter agreed and changed it into a heptagon, then an octagon, a nonagon, a decagon, and more shapes after that. At last, the shape had so many sides and angles that its sides were very small and it had trouble keeping its balance. Its friends could not tell which side was up and began to avoid it. One day, while going down a hill, the shape rolled faster and faster. It crashed into fences and trees, hit bicycles, and scared walkers. Finally, it stopped and felt tired, dizzy, lonely, and sad.

The shape knew it could not keep its balance and that its friends did not want to be near it. It also could not remember why it had once been unhappy as a triangle. Very carefully, it went back to the Shape Shifter. When the Shape Shifter asked if it was happy yet, the shape said it wanted to be a triangle again. The Shape Shifter was not surprised and said, Poof! The shape became a triangle again. The triangle was delighted to have its old shape back. It became busy once more, doing the same things it had done before: holding up roofs, supporting bridges, making music, catching wind, and becoming pieces of food. Its favorite thing was still slipping into place when people put their hands on their hips so it could hear the latest news.

The triangle told its friends the news again, and they were glad it was back in shape. The story shows how the triangle changed into many shapes because it kept wanting more sides and more angles. First it became a quadrilateral, then a pentagon, then a hexagon, and later many-sided shapes. Each time, the new shape had different jobs, but it still felt dissatisfied after a while. The more sides it had, the harder it was to balance, and the less it could be with its friends. After rolling down a hill and feeling tired and sad, it asked to be a triangle again. The Shape Shifter changed it back, and the triangle returned to its busy life, happy to do its old jobs and hear the latest news.

summaries.summary: There was a triangle that was always busy. It held up roofs, supported bridges, made music, caught wind for sailboats, and was slices of pie and halves of sandwiches. Its favorite thing was to fit when people put their hands on their hips, so it could hear the latest news and tell its friends. But one day the triangle felt tired of the same old things. It went to the shape shifter and asked for one more side and one more angle. Poof! The triangle became a quadrilateral. The quadrilateral could be many things, like a baseball diamond, a checkerboard space, a screen, or book pages. Then it wanted one more side again and became a pentagon, then a hexagon, and then more and more shapes. At last it had so many sides that it rolled down a hill, crashed, and felt dizzy and sad. It went back and asked to be a triangle again. The shape shifter said yes, and the triangle was happy and busy again.

A cone called to the other shapes, and stars, cubes, and the Pentagon parade came too. But they all got trapped. A trapezoid took pictures, and a parallelogram felt sick. Then a straight and narrow line came with a clever plan. She asked for help, and a prism and a sphere joined her. The sphere jumped on the count of three, and the circle popped out. All the shapes were saved, and the line made the jungle gym wider so no little shapes would get stuck again.

She made a clever plan. A prism and a sphere helped her. The sphere jumped at the count of three, and the circle popped out. The lever worked, and all the shapes were saved. Then the line told the jungle gym to make wider spaces so the shapes would not get stuck again.

summaries.summary: A square had four equal sides and four matching corners, and it was happy. On Monday, it was cut into pieces and poked full of holes, so it changed into a fountain that babbled and giggled and clapped. On Tuesday, it was torn into scraps, so it became a garden. On Wednesday, it was shredded in strips, so it became a park. On Thursday, it was shattered, so it became a bridge. On Friday, it was snipped into ribbons, so it became a river. On Saturday, it was crumpled and ripped and wrinkled, so it became a mountain. On Sunday, the square waited and waited for something else to happen, but nothing did. Its sides felt confining and its corners felt rigid and cramped. Then it changed into a window that looked out on the mountain, the river, the bridge, the park, the garden, and the fountain.

The show has space for all of them.

Escaro digs through the snow and asks about jokes and facts while he searches for spring. Soon he sees that the snowbank is not a snowbank at all. It is a bunny rabbit. Escaro does not want the bunny in his book and says he will go on alone. The bunny stays, so Escaro goes into his shell and then agrees to have a hopping contest. He hops very high, all the way to the Moon, and wins. After that, Escaro realizes he may not have unwe after all. He may just be hungry. Then the sun shines, the birds sing, the snow melts, and flowers appear. Escaro invites the bunny to eat the flowers with him.

summaries.summary: Nikki spent one summer at her Grandma’s cottage in the North Woods after her dad drove away to work at the plant. Nikki felt sad at first because there were no other kids and no TV. But Grandma was busy and full of surprises. Her house was filled with books, fish charts, fishing poles, and a half-finished bear carving. She gave Nikki chores like stacking firewood, cleaning gutters, and fixing the truck. Then she taught Nikki to fish for bluegills near the lily pads. Nikki did not catch anything at first and thought the river had no fish. The next day, while waiting on the dock, Nikki found an old raft floating toward her with drawings of animals on it. Grandma helped her use the raft, and many birds and animals came close. Nikki began to draw what she saw. She spent the summer exploring, swimming, and learning about the river. On her last day, she helped a deer fawn stuck in mud, drew it on the raft, and Grandma painted over the drawing so Nikki would always be part of the river.

Under the leaves, Nikki found drawings of animals like a rabbit, bear, fox, and raccoon. She tied the raft to the dock, and Grandma later helped her use it on the river. Birds, turtles, raccoons, foxes, and other animals came close to the raft. Nikki started drawing them. She also swam, camped on the raft, and listened to Grandma’s river stories. At the end of summer, Nikki rescued a deer fawn from mud and painted its picture on the raft with Grandma.

video_title: When I Was Young in the Mountains (beauty of a simple, rural life) #kidsbooks #reading #education

summaries.summary: The child lives in the mountains with grandfather and grandmother. Grandfather comes home from the coal mine covered in black dust, and only his lips are clean when he kisses the child’s head. Grandmother cooks hot cornbread, pinto beans, and fried okra. One night she walks with the child through the grass to the Johnny house and holds the child’s hand in the dark. The child then promises not to eat more than one serving of okra again. This opening shows the family’s daily life in the mountains and the small lessons learned there.

The family walks across the cow pasture and through the woods with their towels to reach the swimming hole. The water is dark and muddy, and sometimes snakes are seen, but they jump in anyway. On the way home, they stop at Mr. Crawford’s house for a mound of white butter. Mr. Crawford and Mrs. Crawford look alike and smell like sweet milk. The story shows how the child and family travel through the mountain land for swimming and then stop for food on the way back.

To take baths, the family pumps pails of water from the well at the bottom of the hill. They heat the water and pour it into round tin tubs. After their baths, they stand in front of the old black stove, shivering and giggling while grandmother heats cocoa on top of it. This part tells how the family gets water, washes, and warms up together in the mountain home.

On Sundays, the family goes to church in the schoolhouse. Sometimes the congregation walks through the cow pasture to the dark swimming hole for baptisms. The child’s cousin Peter is laid back into the water, and his white shirt sticks to him. When this happens, grandmother cries. The story then shows more life in the mountains, with frogs singing at dusk, cowbells in the morning, and a black snake in the yard. Grandmother threatens the snake with a hoe, and if it does not leave, she kills it. Once, four people even draped a dead long snake across their necks for a photograph.

In the evenings, the family sits on the porch swing. Grandfather sharpens the child’s pencils with his pocketknife. Grandmother shells beans and braids the child’s hair. The dogs lie nearby, the stars shine overhead, and a bobwhite whistles in the forest: Bob, Bob, Bob White. At the end, the child says there is no wish to go to the ocean or the desert or anywhere else. The mountains are enough, and the child wants to stay there always.

summaries.summary: The chairs tell about how people sit on them in many rough ways. Kids sit pretzel style, sit down hard, lean back until the chairs fall, drag them by their backs, swing them around, and smear food on them at lunch. The worst part is when someone sits on a chair and lets out a fart. One day, the chairs decide they have had enough. They gather in the classroom at night and write a strike letter to the teacher. They say they want respect and kindness before they go back to work. In the morning, the children cannot find their chairs and must stand in class all day. They can still do their schoolwork, but they do not like it. Then the children write letters back, saying they are sorry and will treat the chairs better. The chairs read the notes, return to the classroom, and the children keep their promise.

summaries.summary: On Monday, Simon had a cold, but he still wanted the best week ever. He kissed his family, ate his favorite breakfast, and rode the bus to school. On Wednesday, he went on a field trip. On Thursday, recess was fun, and on Friday, he looked forward to a big kickball game. On the bus ride home, Simon heard germs talk to him. They said they spread sickness when people do not wash hands or cover mouths. Simon then covered his mouth when he sneezed and coughed, used a tissue, threw it in the trash, and washed his hands with warm, soapy water. The germs went away. Simon rested all weekend, drank lots of fluids, and by Monday he felt good again and was ready to go back to school.

summaries.summary: Principal Nancy tells Pete and his class they are going on a class trip. They ride a bright yellow bus to the firehouse. Pete and the other kids see the big red firehouse, two fire trucks, and the firefighters’ tools. The firefighters show the children around and let them ring the brass firebell and slide down the pole. Then the kids try on firefighter gear. Pete puts on black overalls, tall boots, a yellow jacket, and a black helmet. The gear is very heavy, and he can barely move. The children also look inside a fire truck. Cie honks the horn, and Pete turns on the sirens and lights. Then the fire alarm rings. The firefighters hurry to get ready, jump into the truck, and drive to a fire in town. They connect the truck to the hydrant, use the hose, and spray water on the fire. Pete helps aim the hose. When they hear grumpy toad on the roof, they raise a ladder and help him climb down. The fire goes out, everyone is safe, and the firefighters tell Pete, “Good job, Pete!”

There, Rapunzel saw the lanterns, learned she was the Lost Princess, and later went back to the tower. Mother Gothel hurt Flynn, but Rapunzel’s magic saved him. Rapunzel went home to her real parents, the King and Queen.

summaries.summary: On Christmas Eve, a boy lay in bed and listened for Santa’s sleigh bells. He thought Santa was real, even though a friend said there was no Santa. Then he heard steam and saw a train outside his house. A conductor invited him aboard the Polar Express and took him to the North Pole. Many children in pajamas rode with him, sang Christmas carols, and ate candy. The train raced through dark forests, high mountains, icy plains, and a frozen desert until it reached the North Pole, a city full of toy factories and elves. At the center, Santa chose the boy for the first gift of Christmas. The boy asked for a silver bell from Santa’s sleigh. Santa gave him the bell, but it fell through a hole in the boy’s pocket on the way home. On Christmas morning, his sister Sarah found the bell in a box with a note from Mr. C. The boy could hear the bell, but others could not. As years passed, only he could still hear it.

summaries.summary: The story tells a child that today is their day and they are off to great places. The child has brains in their head and feet in their shoes, so they can choose where to go. They look at roads and streets and decide not to go down some of the bad ones. Then they go out of town where many things can happen. As they keep going, they may fly high, join the High Flyers, and take the lead. But sometimes they will not be first, and sometimes they will get hung up, left in a Lurch, and fall into a slump. They may come to a place with no signs and feel confused about which way to go. They may also find the Waiting place, where everyone is just waiting for things. The story says they will escape that place, keep moving, face scary things, and go on until they succeed and reach their mountain.

The child is told to start out and choose where to go. They can look around and decide not to walk down streets that are not good. When they leave town, exciting things can happen, and they should keep going without worry. The story says they may rise up high and become one of the High Flyers. They may win games, score points, and be famous, but sometimes they will not win. At other times, they may be alone and play lonely games against themselves. They may also meet scary things on the road and feel afraid to keep going. Even so, the story says they will walk on through bad weather, through enemies, and through rough places. They must step with care and keep their balance. In the end, the story says they will succeed, move mountains, and get on their way to great places.

summaries.summary: One quiet starry night, a boy went out to sea in a little boat called La Luna with Papa and Grandpa. They took him to work for the first time. The Moon lifted him onto its surface, where he saw Stars shining all around. The sea was high, so he anchored the boat to the Moon. Then a star fell beside him and sang when he touched it. Papa and Grandpa came to sweep up the fallen stars. They argued about how to do the work when a huge star crashed into the Moon and stuck there. The boy touched it, heard its song, and tapped it with a hammer. Many stars fell down. Together, the three of them cleaned the Moon. When the work was done, they went home and said good job to the boy.

summaries.summary: Pete goes on a bug safari with his friends to look for bugs. Cali finds a tiny black ant building an ant hill. Gus sees a round red ladybug in the mint patch with nine spots. Marty spots a big black spider that caught a fly. Then Pete finds a green caterpillar in a flower pot and says he will bring it home to show Mom and Dad. At home, Mom and Dad help Pete make a home for the caterpillar in a big jar. Dad makes little holes in the lid, and Pete adds leaves and a twig. The next morning, the caterpillar is gone, but Mom and Dad show Pete that it is inside the jar as a pupa. Pete waits while Cali, Gus, and Marty visit and ask if it has come out yet. One day, the pupa wiggles, cracks open, and a butterfly comes out. Pete, Mom, Dad, and his friends watch it fly away. Pete says they should find a new caterpillar.

summaries.summary: Franklin could count by twos, tie his shoes, zip zippers, and button buttons, but he felt worried about his first day of school. He woke up very early and told Godi his fish, “It’s my first day of school.” He packed his new pencil case with a ruler, a pencil, an eraser, and 12 colored pencils. Then he woke his parents and said he could not be late. His mother and father told him it was too early and made him a good breakfast. Franklin said his tummy felt like it had jumping frogs. On the way to the bus stop, he wanted to go home. His parents hugged him and showed him his friends waiting for the bus. On the bus, Franklin and the other children worried, too. At school, Mr. Owl welcomed them, showed them where to go, and gave them fruit. Franklin learned, drew, built with blocks, sorted money, and asked Mr. Owl to help him read his favorite book. He had a wonderful day. When he got home, he had forgotten his jumpy tummy and gave his parents two pictures and big hugs.

Then he woke his mother and father and said he must not be late. They laughed because it was still very early. Franklin was not hungry, but his father said he needed a full tummy for school. Franklin said his tummy felt full of jumping frogs. His mother hugged him and said the feeling would go away. When it was time to leave, Franklin still felt unsure and said he did not want to go. At the bus stop, he saw many friends and their families waiting. The bus came, and Franklin hugged his mother and father before getting on. On the bus, the children asked questions about school. At school, Mr. Owl kindly showed them coats, seats, the bathroom, and fruit. Franklin stayed in his seat at first, then drew, colored, and learned many things. He asked Mr. Owl to help him read his favorite book. After school, Franklin rode home happy. His parents asked about his tummy, and Franklin said it was empty. He gave them pictures and hugs.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: I Need My Monster by Amanda Noll

summaries.summary: The child found a note saying Gabe had gone fishing and would be back in a week. The child wanted a monster under the bed to help with sleep, so the child knocked on the floorboards and waited. First came Herbert, who had a soft voice, no claws, and did not seem scary enough. Then came Ralph, who had neat fur and shiny claws with nail polish, but he also was not scary enough. Next came Cynthia, a girl monster with sharp claws and a slimy tail, but the child said a boy monster was needed. After that came Mac, who had scruffy fur, claws, and a long tongue, but he still did not feel right. Then Gabe came back from fishing. Gabe had green ooze, a spiked tail, and scary claws. The child said no other monster could scare like Gabe. Gabe stayed under the bed, and the child pulled up the blanket and got ready to sleep.

One night the child found that Gabe, the monster under the bed, had gone fishing for a week. The child could not sleep without Gabe’s ragged breathing, whistling nose, claws, and green ooze. So the child quietly knocked on the floorboards and called for a new monster. Herbert arrived first, but he sounded too polite and did not have scary claws. Ralph came next, but his claws were smooth and even had nail polish. Then Cynthia appeared with sharp claws and a tail, but the child said the monster had to be a boy. After Cynthia left, Mac showed up with scruffy fur and a long tongue, but that still did not work. At last Gabe returned and said fishing was not fun because the fish were too easy to scare. Gabe showed his drool, ooze, tail, and claws, and the child said Gabe was the only monster who could really scare the child. With Gabe back under the bed, the child pulled up the covers and was ready for sleep.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: Goodnight, Little Bear by Igloo Books

summaries.summary: The first snow fell, and Mommy bear told little bear it was time to hibernate. She said hibernate means to find a cozy place and sleep all winter. Mommy bear made a bed of dry leaves in a cave under a rock. Little bear lay down beside her, but he could not sleep. He felt something was missing, so he got up quietly and walked into the dark forest. He saw wood cutters carrying heavy wood. When they saw him, they shouted, “Help a bear!” and ran away, leaving their wood behind. Little bear kept walking. Soon he found a small wooden house by a frozen pond. Inside was an old lady. She did not shout. She said, “Come in. Come and warm yourself by the fire.” She stroked his head, gave him honey, washed him, and then gave him a teddy bear. Little bear went back to Mommy bear and slept with the teddy bear at last.

summaries.summary: A hare boasted to the other animals that he was very fast and that the tortoise was very slow. One day, he laughed at the tortoise and said he could never win a race. The tortoise said he could beat the hare, so they chose a race to the foot of the mountain. The squirrel said, “Ready!” The mouse said, “Set!” The raccoon said, “Go!” The hare ran far ahead right away. The tortoise moved slowly but steadily. The hare looked back and saw the tortoise was far behind. He stopped to eat carrots and lettuce and talk with friends. Then he lay down in a pumpkin patch and went to sleep. While he slept, the tortoise kept going and passed him. At last, the tortoise crossed the finish line before the hare woke up and ran back. The story says, “Slow and steady wins the race.”

The blue knight then welcomed Gareth and the lady, and Gareth explained that he was riding to rescue a fair lady’s sister from the Red Knight of the Red Plain. Gareth and the Red Knight fought in the valley near the castle. They broke spears, fell from their horses, and battled on foot with swords and shields. On the way, they saw friends by the river and invited them to come for pancakes. At the market, A dika saw Camila at her plantain stand and invited her too. Mama bought flour at the flower stand and asked more friends to come. She also bought a chili pepper, and another friend gave her the best one. When they went home, A dika counted the guests and said they had invited all their friends. Mama cooked the pancakes while the children fetched water and helped with the fire. Soon friends arrived with milk, butter, fish, plantains, flour, salt, and cardamom. They shared the meal together, and after eating, Kaya played the thumb piano while everyone enjoyed the feast.

summaries.summary: A long time ago in Africa, Navarro lived in a village with his two beautiful daughters, Manyara and Niasia. Manyara was often mean to Niasia and said she would one day be queen, while Niasia stayed kind and worked in her garden. One day a messenger came from the king’s city and said the king wanted a wife. Navarro prepared to send both daughters, but Manyara tried to go first. On the road, she met a hungry boy, an old woman, and a grove of laughing trees, but she was rude and did not help them. Niasia later met the same boy and gave him food, gave the old woman seeds, and was polite to the trees. When the party reached the city, Manyara ran out in fear and warned Niasia about a monster. Niasia went inside and found Nyoka, the garden snake, who changed into the king and chose her as his wife. Manyara became a servant in the queen’s household.

Navarro had two daughters, Manyara and Niasia, who were both very beautiful. Manyara was jealous because people praised Niasia’s kindness. Niasia grew millet, yams, sunflowers, and vegetables, and a small garden snake named Nyoka stayed beside her in the garden. One day a messenger came from the king and said the most worthy and beautiful daughters should come to the city so the king could choose a wife. Manyara tried to go alone, but Navarro said both daughters must go. That night Manyara hurried ahead through the forest and was rude to a hungry boy, an old woman, and laughing trees. The next morning Niasia joined the wedding party and was kind to the same boy and old woman. She also passed the trees politely. When they reached the city, Manyara ran out crying and said a monster had frightened her. Niasia went into the chamber, where Nyoka became the king and asked her to marry him. She agreed, and a great wedding feast was held.

video_title: Little Larks 12 - Personal Leadership - The Most Magnificent Thing

summaries.summary: A girl and her best friend do many things together. One day the girl decides to make the most magnificent thing. She hires an assistant, gathers supplies, and starts working. She tinkerers, hammers, measures, saws, glues, twists, and paints, while her assistant helps by pouncing, growling, chewing, circling, and tugging. But each time they finish, the thing is wrong. It is square, round, fuzzy, long, short, rough, smooth, big, small, and even smells like stinky cheese, but it is still not magnificent. The girl gets angrier and works faster until she hurts her finger and shouts that she quits. Her assistant takes her for a walk. As they walk, she sees that some parts of her wrong things are actually good. By the end of the trail, she knows how to make it right. She works carefully again, and this time she makes the most magnificent thing.

This is a story about a girl and her best friend in the whole wide world. They race, eat, explore, relax, and make things together. The girl wants to make one very magnificent thing, so she gets an assistant and gathers her supplies. They work in a quiet place. She builds and measures, and her assistant helps in his own wild way. But when they look at the thing, it is not good at all. The girl tries again and again. She changes it many ways, making it square, round, fuzzy, long, short, big, small, and more. Still, it does not match the thing in her mind. She gets upset, works too fast, and hurts her finger. She says she quits. Then her assistant suggests a walk. While walking, she notices that some parts of the wrong things are actually right. She gets new ideas and returns to work. At last, after careful making, she finishes the magnificent thing and rides it with her assistant.

When she is done, it leans a little left and is heavier than she thought, but it is just what she wanted. They take it for a spin.

She and her assistant ride it together, and it is magnificent.

summaries.summary: A child has a tiny elephant for a pet. Every day they walk together, and the elephant does not like the cracks in the sidewalk. The child helps the elephant over the cracks. One day, they walk to number 17 for pet club day. The child says, "Come along," and helps the elephant the last few feet. But on the door there is a sign that says, "strictly no elephants." The tiny elephant leads the child back to the sidewalk. Then the child talks with a girl. She says the sign did not mention skunks, but the child says they still would not want them there. The girl says the elephant does not stink. The child agrees. Then the child asks, "What if we start our own Club?" The child tells the elephant to come along, and they make a new place to play. A new friend helps make signs for the club. The signs say, "strictly no strangers, no spoil sports, no exit out, all are welcome."

summaries.summary: On a bright Saturday morning, Lucy and her little brother Max went with their parents, Sarah and James, to the city zoo. They brought a picnic basket and arrived early. First, they saw the African Savannah with tall giraffes. Max laughed when a giraffe looked at him and tasted the leaves in his hand. Then they went to the lion’s den and saw lions resting in the sun. They also saw a leopard on a rock. After that, they visited the reptile house and looked at snakes, a big python, and color-changing chameleons. At the bird aviary, parrots, peacocks, and hummingbirds were busy and bright. The family later ate ice cream at the zoo cafe and watched flamingos. They saw monkeys, apes, and chimpanzees, and a monkey tried to grab Max’s red cap. They watched the elephant show, then saw red pandas, tigers, bats, and owls. At the petting zoo, Lucy petted a rabbit and Max fed a goat. They went home with a stuffed giraffe and a toy lion.

summaries.summary: In a small village, six Blind Men heard that a huge elephant had come to town. They had never met an elephant before, so they went to learn about it by touching it with their hands. The first man touched the side and said the elephant was like a wall. The second touched a tusk and said it was like a spear. The third touched the trunk and said it was like a snake. The fourth touched a leg and said it was like a tree. The fifth touched an ear and said it was like a fan. The sixth touched the tail and said it was like a rope. Soon they began to argue because each one thought only his answer was right. A wise old man came and told them they were all correct. He explained that each man had felt only one part of the elephant, so each description was only part of the whole. The Blind Men stopped arguing and understood that they had to listen to each other to see the full truth.

Six Blind Men lived in a small village. When the villagers told them about a huge elephant, they went to find out what it was like. Because they could not see it, they used their hands to feel different parts. One felt the side and said, "An elephant is like a wall." Another felt a tusk and said it was like a spear. Another felt the trunk and said it was like a snake. One felt a leg and said it was like a tree. One felt an ear and said it was like a fan. The last man felt the tail and said it was like a rope. The men argued loudly because each one believed his own answer. The villagers watched them bicker. Then a wise old man came and told them that they were all right, because each had touched only one part of the elephant. He said the elephant was all of those things together. The Blind Men then understood that only by joining their ideas could they know the whole animal.

summaries.summary: Percy was a humble pencil in a small town. He lived in a cozy stationery shop with pens, markers, and glittery gel pens, but he felt ordinary. Percy watched children come in for school supplies and heard them talk about dreams. One day, he heard a little girl named Lily wish for a special pencil that could help her write the best story ever. Soon after, Lily came to the shop with her mom, saw Percy, and picked him. Percy was very happy. At home, Lily used Percy every day to write stories about magical lands, brave knights, and talking animals. Percy felt alive as Lily wrote, laughed, and sometimes cried. Later, Percy wore down and felt discouraged. Then Lily sharpened him and said, “I can't write Without You Percy.” Percy became sharp again and helped Lily finish her biggest story. She entered it in a school contest, read it to her class, and won first place. Lily hugged Percy and said, “We did it together!”

She used him every day to write about magical lands, brave knights, and talking animals. As Percy grew dull, he felt he was not special. But Lily sharpened him and said, “I can't write Without You Percy.” After that, Percy could help again. Together they finished a story about a pencil saving a kingdom from a terrible monster. Lily entered the story in a contest, won first place, and kept Percy on her desk even when he became too small to use.

summaries.summary: Rapunzel lived in a tall tower with very long hair. Every day, Mother Gothel called, “Rapunzel, let down your hair!” Rapunzel pulled her up. Mother Gothel used Rapunzel’s magic hair to stay young and beautiful. Rapunzel did not know Mother Gothel had taken her from the king and queen. Rapunzel could not leave the tower, but she had a friend named Pascal. On her birthday, she saw shining lights in the sky and wished to see them. Then Flynn, a thief, climbed into the tower to hide. Rapunzel thought he wanted her hair, but he did not. She asked him to take her to the lights, and he agreed. They ran from guards, escaped a cave with her glowing hair, and reached the kingdom. Rapunzel learned she was the lost princess. Mother Gothel took her back, but Flynn came to save her. Rapunzel cut her hair, Mother Gothel withered away, and Rapunzel went home to the king and queen.

summaries.summary: Raya went into the chamber of the dragon gem. Her father, Chief Benja, tested her, and she beat the masked warrior, who was really him. Benja was happy that Raya became a guardian of the dragon gem. He made a meal with food from Fang, Talon, Spine, Tale, and Heart. Benja turned to stone. Raya and Tuktuk escaped with one shard, and the other chiefs took the rest.

summaries.summary: Summer came to Arendelle, and the day was very hot. Olaf was very happy because he loved warm weather. He ran to Anna and asked her to go outside and play. Anna said it was hot and sticky, but she smiled at Olaf. Olaf and Anna went to find Elsa. They saw Elsa in the great hall with a dignitary. Olaf said hello and told Elsa he liked warm hugs. He asked to play in the sunshine. Elsa said yes and asked what they should do. Anna said they could have a picnic on the shores of the fjord. Olaf loved that idea. The three friends went to the royal kitchen for picnic food. Olena was there, trying to stay cool in the icebox. She said it was too hot for baking. Elsa suggested ice cold lemonade, and Olaf was very pleased.

Anna, Elsa, and Olaf went to the royal gardens for their summer day. Some children were lying on the grass because it was too hot to play. Olaf ran to them and said hello. He asked if they loved summer. The children liked Olaf, and he chased butterflies and blew on dandelion fuzz. Anna and Elsa joined in too. After a while, Anna sat down and said she was ready for the picnic. Elsa said they should go to the docks and sail to the fjord. Olaf was excited because he had always wanted to sail. At the docks, Anna and Elsa chose a sailboat, and they set off on the water. Olaf sang happily. When they reached shore, he even got to steer the boat. Then Anna began setting up the picnic for everyone.

At the fjord, Olaf could not stay still. He talked about sand on his snow and asked Anna to make sand angels. Anna put a toe in the sand and found it very warm. She tiptoed to the water instead, where the cool water felt better. Olaf, Anna, and Elsa spent the whole afternoon outside in the summer sun. They built sand castles and sand people. They chased waves on the shore. They danced with seagulls. When they were tired, they had their picnic on the shores of the fjord. Olaf said it was the best day of his life. Then they sailed back to Arendelle as the sun went down and filled the sky with pretty colors. Olaf wished he could hug the summer sun, and Anna told him he might need a bigger snow flurry for that.

Back at the docks, Kristoff and Sven were waiting for Anna, Elsa, and Olaf. They had spent the afternoon harvesting mountain lakes. Their sled was full of ice. The ice jumped out of the boat as they came in. Anna was very happy to see the cold ice, and she lay on the blocks. Olaf told Kristoff and Sven all about the picnic, the garden, the boat, and the games at the fjord. He said he wished it could always be summer. Elsa smiled and said summer was wonderful. Then she looked ahead and said that tomorrow there would be a chance of snow.

summaries.summary: Just me and my mom went to the city. Mom gave me money to buy train tickets, and I wanted to help her get on the train, but the steps were too high. Mom helped me instead. Then the conductor came, and the tickets were gone, so Mom paid him more money. The city was busy, and I held Mom’s hand. We went to the Museum of Natural History and saw rooms full of old dinosaur bones. I picked up a little dinosaur egg to show Mom, but someone took it away. I tried on costumes for Mom, and a museum guard did not like that. Next we went to the aquarium and saw fish and seals. Mom got mad because she could not find me. I ran to the front to see the seals better. We also went to an art museum, had lunch, bought a hot dog, and went to a store where I tried on clothes. We took a taxi back to the train station, and Mom bought the tickets this time. We went home, and I stayed awake almost all the way.

After a sunny day that comes after the rainy day, the person goes outside to look. The brown is gone, and now there is green all around. Spring has come.

They saw him turn water into wine, calm stormy seas, fill nets with fish, heal sick people, and bring dead people back to life. Then it was time for Jesus to go to Jerusalem. Two friends found a donkey for him to ride. Jesus rode toward the big city while his friends walked and sang, “Hooray!” More people joined them. They waved palm branches and shouted, “Praise Jesus! He is our king.” Some people did not sing, and the Pharisees were jealous. Jesus told them the singing could not be stopped. In Jerusalem, Jesus and his friends ate supper together in an upstairs room. Jesus broke bread and shared a cup of wine to help his friends remember him and trust him. After supper, Judas came with soldiers. They took Jesus away, put a robe and thorny crown on him, and made fun of him. They nailed Jesus to a cross, and he died. His friends buried him in a tomb, but on Sunday an angel said Jesus had risen. The women told the friends, and Peter and John saw the empty tomb.

After that, Herbert finished things, listened well, and obeyed better.

video_title: The Story of St. Nicholas by Cheryl Odden - Children's Book Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Nicholas was born in Lysia to rich parents, but when he was still young, both of them died and left him their money. Nicholas decided to use it to help poor people. He heard about a father who had three daughters but did not have enough money to help them marry. At night, Nicholas secretly climbed the house and threw a bag of gold into the daughters’ room three nights in a row. On the third night, the father stayed awake, caught Nicholas, and learned it was a young man helping them. Nicholas asked him not to tell anyone, and the father promised. Later, Nicholas traveled to the Holy Land, prayed in Bethlehem and in Jesus’ empty tomb, and then returned by ship. A storm came, Nicholas prayed, and the sea became calm. When the ship reached Meera, the church leaders chose Nicholas to be bishop.

After Nicholas became bishop, the emperor Dialesian said Christians were a danger and ordered that God’s word and other writings about Jesus be found and burned. Many Christians hid their scriptures, and some were sent to prison. Nicholas was noticed because of his Christlike actions, so he was arrested too. He sat in a cold prison and refused to bow to the emperor. He said he would bow to no one but God. Later, a new emperor named Constantine took the throne and ordered all Christians to be released. Nicholas was freed from prison. After that, a church leader named Arias taught that Jesus was created, and his songs made fun of God. This caused trouble among Christians, so Emperor Constantine called a meeting of church leaders. Nicholas was angry when Arias sang his shameful song and slapped him.

The church leaders were shocked when Nicholas slapped Arias. They knew Arias had spoken wrongly about Jesus, but they also wanted Christians to live in peace. So they told Nicholas that he could no longer preach. Even after losing his job as bishop, Nicholas kept helping others. He lived among poor people, cared for sick people, and started orphanages. He did these things until he died, and some people believe he died in the year 343. Many years later, stories about Nicholas helped lead to the Santa Claus legend, with a white beard, a red suit, and reindeer that deliver presents on Christmas Eve. In some places he is called Santa Claus, and in Italy he is called Bobo Natalie. The story says Nicholas should be remembered because he suffered for Jesus and stood up for him when others made fun of him.

Nicholas was a generous boy who gave his inherited money to people in need. One important time, he helped a poor father with three daughters by secretly giving gold for three nights. This saved the daughters from living on the streets and helped their father find them good husbands. Later, Nicholas traveled to Bethlehem and the Holy Land, where he prayed and said Jesus was Emmanuel, God with us. On the ship ride home, a storm shook the boat, but Nicholas prayed and the water calmed. When he reached Meera, he rushed to the church to give thanks. There, the church leaders chose him as bishop because he was the first person to enter the church. After that, Nicholas was arrested under Emperor Dialesian for helping Christians and refusing to bow to the emperor. He stayed faithful, and later Constantine freed him. Nicholas then kept serving the poor and the sick.

Long ago, about 200 years after Jesus was born, Nicholas grew up in Lysia with wealthy parents. When his parents died, he chose to help poor people with the money they left him. He learned about a father whose three daughters needed help, so Nicholas secretly gave gold to the family for three nights. The father caught him on the third night and promised not to tell. Later, Nicholas visited Bethlehem and the empty tomb of Jesus, then sailed back home. A storm hit the ship, Nicholas prayed, and the sea became calm. The crew reached Meera safely, and the church leaders made Nicholas their bishop. Much later, Emperor Dialesian punished Christians, Nicholas was put in prison, and he refused to bow to the emperor. After Constantine became emperor, Nicholas was freed. When Arias made fun of Jesus, Nicholas slapped him, and the church leaders stopped Nicholas from preaching. Still, he kept helping the poor until he died.

summaries.summary: In a cave in the woods, a great brown bear sleeps through the cold winter. He sleeps all day and all night while the wind blows outside. A tiny mouse comes into the cave from the snow. It is dark and damp, so Mouse makes a small fire. The bear keeps snoring. Then Hair comes in, and Mouse asks who is there. Mouse and Hair pop corn and drink black tea. Badger comes next with honey nuts, and they share the food. Gopher, Mole, Ren, and Raven also come into the bear’s den. They talk, sing, and eat while the bear keeps sleeping. Hair stokes the fire, and Mouse cooks stew. A pepper flake makes the bear sneeze, and he wakes up very angry. Mouse tells Bear not to worry and offers more corn and tea. Bear eats and feels happy. When the sun comes up, the bear cannot sleep, but his friends are all snoring.

summaries.summary: Laura traveled across the giant Prairie in a covered wagon with her paw, ma, big sister Mary, little sister Carrie, and their bulldog Jack. They were looking for a place to build a house. One morning Laura and Mary woke before the sun, ate cornmeal mush, and helped ma wash the dishes. Then paw drove the wagon until he stopped and said this was the place for their house. Paw and ma unloaded the wagon while Laura, Mary, and Jack watched. Paw then drove away to bring back logs from the creek bottom. Laura felt frightened without the wagon, but she helped ma while Mary watched baby Carrie. For many days paw hauled logs and made piles for the house and stable. When there were enough logs, paw and ma began building the house together. Later paw met Mr. Edwards, who lived across the creek. Mr. Edwards came to help finish the house, and he and paw worked fast, cut a door and windows, and then stayed for supper. That night paw played his fiddle, Mr. Edwards danced, and the family sang under the big moon.

Mr. Edwards came to help, and in one day they built the house walls higher, cut a door, and made windows. Laura looked inside and saw sunlight through the cracks. summaries.summary: Winter came, and Anna needed a new coat because her old blue coat was too small. Her mother had once hoped to buy one after the war, but the stores were still empty and there was no money. So Anna's mother thought of a way to trade special things for what they needed. First, she and Anna went to a farmer and asked for wool from his sheep. The farmer said they must wait until spring, so Anna visited the sheep often, asked if their wool was growing, fed them hay, and gave them hugs. In spring, the farmer sheared the sheep, and Anna's mother traded a gold watch for the wool. Then they traded a lamp to an old woman for yarn, red lingan berries made the yarn red, and a weaver traded cloth for a garnet necklace. At last a tailor made the coat, and Anna wore it home. At Christmas, the helper trades were remembered, and everyone shared cake and joy.

summaries.summary: One sunny spring day, Tigger and Rue bounced to Christopher Robin. Christopher Robin told them that tomorrow was Mother’s Day. Roo wanted to give Mama, Kanga, something extra special. Christopher Robin said they could have a surprise party and everyone could bring a present. So Christopher Robin, Roo, and Tigger invited all their friends in the Hundred Acre Wood to bring gifts for Kanga. The next morning, Roo woke up and remembered he had forgotten to get Mama a present. Before he could finish thinking, Kanga knocked and then opened the door. Everyone shouted, “Happy Mother’s Day!” Kanga smiled and came inside. Roo told her to sit down while they celebrated her. Then the gifts began: Eeyore gave flowers, Tigger gave a huge bunch of flowers, Christopher Robin brought muffins, Rabbit brought fresh vegetables, Piglet brought a cake, and Pooh brought honey. Roo also said a poem about Kanga. At the end, Roo felt sad because he had forgotten her present, but Kanga said he had already given her the best present ever. Roo gave her a big Mother’s Day hug.

Tigger had a striped kite, Rabbit had a carrot kite, Owl had a kite shaped like a book, Roo had a green kite, and Pooh had a sticky kite because of honey. Eeyore’s kite was missing its tail, but Roo found it and gave it back. On festival day, the wind was very weak, and the kites would not fly well. Roo ran with his kite, Tigger tried to bounce his up, and Owl got tangled in a tree branch. Everyone felt disappointed. Then Kanga said the wind comes and goes. The friends went off to do other things until the wind returned. Later, strong wind blew through the wood, and the friends hurried back to the festival. This time, the wind lifted them and their kites high into the air.

summaries.summary: Olal Lakota Native American boy grows up on Pine Ridge reservation with his family. He remembers cold winters, shared homes, and a giveaway where people bring gifts to share. After his mother dies, his father tells him to step inside a circle and says he must dig deeper and keep going. The boy works hard, runs from bullies, and thinks about stories of Native Olympians. He sweeps floors, builds grain elevators, and goes to Haskell Institute, where he is first told he is too slow for track. He keeps training with cans of concrete and later earns a team jersey. He wins records and dreams of the Olympics, but his body feels weak in races. A coach gives him honey, which helps. He gets a college scholarship, faces unfair treatment, and keeps running. After medical help, new training, and more hard work, he goes to Tokyo. There he gets shoes, runs the 10,000 meter race, and wins the gold medal. At the end, he is honored with songs, drums, a feather headdress, and a new name.

He listens while they call out answers and say things like “Hey,” “that’s mine,” and “vanilla please.” Even when he is quiet, Nathan has many thoughts. He thinks about puddles outside and about digging in the schoolyard. The story shows that people can share what they feel in many ways, not just with talking. At the treasure chest, they meet a fierce fire-breathing armadillo. The Knight uses a pillow to distract it, and the detective tickles it. The beast curls into a ball and falls down. The heroes move it away, open the chest, and find treasure maps inside. They take the new map and begin another Quest.
