summaries.summary: In a tree by an old stone wall, two birds named Peter and Paul built nests. Paul looked at Peter’s nest and wanted to know whose was best. Paul said he had soft feathers in his nest, and Peter said he had strong sticks from a vine. Paul got upset and made his nest stronger with mud while Peter was away. Then Peter made his nest into a veranda with a straw roof. Paul made his nest into a fortress with a drawbridge, turrets, and cannons. Peter then built a hot tub, a home cinema, and a games room, with a ferris wheel, merry-go-round, and log flume outside. A storm came, and both big nests were too heavy. They fell apart and landed in a broken, soggy pile. An owl took Peter and Paul into her tree trunk home, gave them food and drink, and kept them dry. After that, Peter and Paul built a smaller home together in a hollow tree and welcomed other animals there when rain flooded their homes.

summaries.summary: Mark was a hammerhead shark in Bubbleton. He was big and had sharp teeth, but he was gentle and shy. The people in the village were afraid of him and closed their shops when he swam by. One day, Mark saw a lonely little plant pot outside a shop. The shopkeeper was so scared that he told Mark to take it and go away. Mark did not want to hurt anyone. He paid for the plant and took it home. Mark cared for the plant every day. Soon it grew into a big Christmas tree. Mark decorated it with bright coral. The lights and colors made his house glow. The fish in Bubbleton came to see the tree. Mark asked them to help decorate, and they brought lights and seaweed decorations. More fish came, and they all said hello to Mark. After that, decorating Mark’s Christmas tree became a yearly event, and the village learned not to judge him so quickly.

Sammy shouted threats, but Kevin answered back. They both dug tunnels until their heads bumped. Then they started planning a fort together.

video_title: This Little Explorer: A Pioneer Primer

summaries.summary: Many little explorers went on big adventures. Leif Erikson was a Viking who sailed to North America and was the first European to land in America. Marco Polo went to China with his dad when he was a teenager. He rode camels, saw wild animals, met a rich Emperor, and later wrote a book about his travels. Christopher Columbus sailed from Spain on the Nina, the Pinta, and the Santa Maria in 1492. He wanted to reach Asia, but he landed in America instead. Ferdinand Magellan showed that the world was round by sailing around it. These explorers traveled on oceans and across lands to find new places and learn new things.

Some explorers helped other people travel and learn. Sacagawea was a Native American guide for Meriwether Lewis and William Clark in the American West. Matthew Henson and Robert Perry searched for the North Pole in the cold Arctic for many years. Jacques Cousteau went deep under the sea to study ocean life and film it for TV. He showed plants and animals in the ocean so people would protect them. Edmund Hillary climbed through ice and snow to the top of Mount Everest, the highest mountain in the world. These explorers went to hard places and kept going, even when the land, sea, or ice was difficult.

Some explorers used planes and rockets to go far away. Amelia Earhart was a famous pilot who did flying tricks and broke speed records. She was the first woman to fly an airplane alone across the Atlantic Ocean. Neil Armstrong was an astronaut who walked on the moon and put a flag there. He said, 'one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.' The story also says that Yuri Gagarin was the first astronaut to go into outer space, Sally Ride was the first American woman in outer space on the space shuttle Challenger, and Mae Jemison was the first African American woman in outer space on the Space Shuttle Endeavour. These explorers reached the sky and beyond.

Annie Londonderry was the first woman to ride a bicycle around the world. These explorers traveled by sea, land, and bike, and they visited places that were far away and new to them.

summaries.summary: Little Morer Mouse looked outside and saw only brown. He wanted to see green. He ate the shells off his sunflower seeds and listened when the big people said it was springtime and “Garden time!” They explained that seeds could be planted in dirt with water and sunshine and grow into many more seeds or vegetables. Morer was unsure, but he decided to plant his last sunflower seed. He found a sunny place, dug a hole, dropped in the seed, covered it with dirt, and watered it from an acorn cap. The next day it rained, and Morer found soggy dirt. He wanted to dig up the seed, but he waited after a quiet voice said, “Wait.” He waited through more rain. On the third day, sunshine came, and two green leaves appeared. Morer cared for the plant, pulled weeds, and watered it until it grew into a giant sunflower full of seeds. He thanked God, saved the seeds, and fell asleep beside a spider friend.

summaries.summary: One wonderful day, Jim pansy woke up and thought everything was wrong. The sun was too bright, the sky was too blue, and the bananas were too sweet. Jim did not know what was happening. Norman from next door said Jim might be grumpy, but Jim said he was not. On his walk, Jim met Marabou, then lemur, then snake. Norman kept saying Jim was grumpy, and the others pointed out Jim’s hunched body, bunched eyebrows, and frown. Jim tried to fix these things by loosening up, raising his brow, and smiling, but he still did not feel happy inside. Many animals asked Jim to sing, swing, roll, stroll, lie in the grass, stomp, take a bath, hug, laugh, nap, eat, jump, sit in the sun, and dance. Jim did none of it. He shouted, stormed off, and felt sorry. Then Jim found Norman again. Norman was grumpy too because he had danced with porcupine and got hurt. Jim asked if Norman was okay, and Norman said he would feel better soon. Jim said he was still grumpy too, and Norman said it was a wonderful day to be grumpy. Jim agreed and felt a little better.

summaries.summary: A little butterfly wants to reach a group of migrating butterflies and find the flowers, but the trip is 200 miles long. The butterfly worries about flying so far and asks if it can take a plane, a hot air balloon, or a blip, but the answer is no. It remembers life as a caterpillar, when it built a chrysalis, waited, and then started the journey with friends. Now it is lost and alone, and it fears storms and animals like snakes, birds, dragonflies, frogs, and spiders. A whale also appears, and the butterfly jokes about living in its stomach, but the whale spits it out. The butterfly keeps hearing, “Keep trying,” and starts flying again. It travels mile by mile, though wind blows it back and it feels discouraged. At last, after 200 miles, it reaches the flowers and says it can do many things when it believes in itself. Then it is told to eat up before going dormant for winter.

It keeps moving until it reaches 200 miles and finds the flowers. Then it is told to eat before it goes dormant for winter.

summaries.summary: Taco was a cat who lived a happy life with his humans in a warm house with good food and love. When he was a tiny kitten, a man threw him from a car near a Mexican restaurant, and Taco got stuck in a bush. He cried in the rain and cold until two big hands came through the bush and picked him up. A girl hugged him, and the humans took him home. They made him a cozy bed and fed him from a bottle until he grew strong. As Taco got bigger, he became a brave cat who went on many adventures, like walking outside, visiting the lake, wearing costumes on Halloween, and helping with Christmas. When Taco was 17, his humans brought home Bean, a dirty yellow kitten from under a dumpster. Taco hissed at first because he did not want to share. Then the girl reminded him how he had been saved too. Taco understood, shared a toy with Bean, and decided to be a good big brother.

In the end, they learn that the sign was right, and one dinosaur says he has an itch too.

video_title: Yertle the Turtle

summaries.summary: On the far away island of Salamasand, Yertle the Turtle was king of a small, clean pond where the turtles had plenty to eat and were happy. But Yertle wanted to see more and be higher than everyone else. He ordered nine turtles to swim to his stone and stand one on top of another, making a nine-turtle stack for his throne. Yertle climbed up and bragged that he could now rule cows, mules, a house, a blueberry bush, and a cat. Then Mac, the turtle at the bottom, said his back, shoulders, and knees hurt. Yertle did not listen and ordered many more turtles to pile up. Mac and the others obeyed, and Yertle rose even higher. Mac asked for rights and food, but Yertle shouted back. When the moon rose, Yertle wanted to go higher still. Then Mac burped, the throne shook, and Yertle fell into the pond. Yertle became king of the mud, and all the turtles were free.

He saw cows, mules, a house, a blueberry bush, and a cat, and he kept shouting that he was a great king. After a while, the turtle named Mac, who was stuck at the bottom, told Yertle that his back and knees hurt. Yertle told him to be quiet and demanded even more turtles for a taller throne. The turtles from the pond came and built the stack higher. Mac groaned again and said they were in pain and needed food. Yertle still wanted more height, but then Mac burped. The throne shook, Yertle fell into the pond, and the turtles were free.

The man said the kitten might be lost, so they looked for her owner, but no one was found. They took the kitten to the animal shelter so the people there could care for her. At the shelter, the director thanked them and told them to be careful because one puppy was missing. George saw many animals, but he wanted to find the barking he heard. He went into a room with dogs and saw puppies. When he opened the door, the mother dog ran out, and all the puppies got loose. The dogs, cats, and bunnies became noisy. The man with the yellow hat and the director put the puppies back. Then George opened another door and found the missing puppy. Everyone was happy, and the director gave the puppies and their mother a snack.

George walked with the man with the yellow hat and found a frightened kitten in the park. They searched for the kitten’s owner, but the kitten was alone, so they brought her to the animal shelter. The director of the shelter took the kitten and told George and the man to watch their step because one puppy had escaped. George stayed behind while the man signed papers. Soon George heard barking and followed it to a room full of dogs. He saw the puppies and wanted to pet one. When George opened the door, the mother dog rushed out, and the puppies ran everywhere. They hid under a desk, barked at the bunnies, and made the other animals noisy too. The director and the man with the yellow hat came back and helped put the puppies in their cage. One mother dog was still barking, and George opened a door to find the missing puppy. The director was glad, and she gave the mother dog and puppies a snack.

video_title: Can I Play Too?

summaries.summary: A snake asks, “Can I play too?” The others are playing catch with their arms, but the snake has no arms. He says, “I do not have arms,” and then tells them he was teasing. The snake says he is a snake. The friends ask if a snake can play catch. The snake says he can try. One child throws the ball, but it bounces off the snake’s head. They try again, and it bonks him again. The friends think they need a new idea. They throw more and more balls, but the balls just hit the snake because he cannot catch them. The snake says he cannot play catch. Then the friends say he is their friend and they will all play catch. An elephant helps with a new idea by throwing the snake, and the snake says, “Wee.” Piggy says he loves playing catch with friends.

video_title: How Do Dinosaurs Stay Friends?

summaries.summary: A dinosaur and his friend have a terrible fight. The story asks many times if the dinosaur will do mean things, like write a bad note, ruin a towel, tear a book, throw a lunch box, kick a bike, or tell lies. But the dinosaur does not do these things. Instead, he sends a nice note and takes most of the blame. He is surprised to find that his friend does the same. Then the dinosaur invites his friend over to share and play. He lets his friend choose the first toys. He also brings a toy dragon and knight to school with a card that says he does not want to fight. Later, he gives his friend cookies he helped his mom bake. He wraps up a favorite bear with a bow and brings it as a gift. In the end, the friends make things right and stay friends with good hugs and more.

A dinosaur and his best friend have a big fight, and it might end their friendship. The story says the dinosaur does not scribble a mean note, wipe muddy feet on a towel, tear up a book, throw a lunch box in the lake, or do other bad things. He does not scream, spit, or tell a lie to the new teacher. Instead, he sends a kind note and says most of the fight was his fault. Then he sees that his friend has also sent a note taking blame. After that, the dinosaur asks his friend over to share toys and play. He lets his friend pick the first toys. He brings a toy dragon and knight to school with a card that says, “Really, I don’t want to fight.” He also shares cookies he helped bake with his mom and gives a wrapped bear as a gift. The story ends with the friends making up.

summaries.summary: Duck knocked on Hippo’s door and asked him to walk in the rain. Duck twirled her umbrella and said, “It’s spring, spring, spring!” Hippo was worried about the weather, but Duck said he could come if he shared her umbrella. Hippo put on his big rubber boots and went outside. At first, there was no room for Hippo. He tried walking in front of Duck, and then behind her, but that did not work. Then Duck stood on Hippo’s feet while Hippo held the umbrella, and that worked just fine. They jumped in puddles, splashed through mud, and dropped a stick into the creek. Duck wanted to sail down the creek, so Hippo helped her into the water. Again, there was no room for Hippo, so Duck sat on Hippo’s lap. They swirled around boulders and a crocodile, then twirled into a pond. Duck could not find Hippo, but Hippo was under her, and Duck was sitting on his head. At the end, they went home, shared the umbrella again, and Hippo invited Duck in for tea.

summaries.summary: It was spring, Pinkalicious’s favorite season. She loved the cotton-candy sky at sunset and the garden full of blossoms. She believed fairies came to the yard and made the plants grow with fairy dust. One spring, she decided to build a house for the fairies so she could see them. Peter helped her gather twigs, leaves, and shells. Together they made a little house in the garden, added buttercups around the door, and made a shell path. Pinkalicious also made a pond, a boat, and a slide. She watched and waited, but the fairies did not come. Peter tried to cheer her up, but Pinkalicious still wanted to see them. Then she thought the fairies might come at night, so Mommy and Daddy let her and Peter camp outside. She left honeysuckle and berries for the fairies and stayed awake as long as she could, but she fell asleep. In the morning, the flowers were blooming and the snack was gone. Pinkalicious saw bright morning light and knew the fairies had come.

At last Pj decided he really wanted to be a bunny. He hurried home, and his family was happy to see him. Pj ate his cooked carrots, played with his brothers and sisters, and was glad to be a bunny again.

summaries.summary: One morning Paddington went into the Browns’ garden with paper and pencil and made a list of the nice things about being a bear and living with the Browns. He wrote about having his own room, a warm bed, and marmalade for breakfast. He soon remembered another very nice thing: the garden. The Browns’ garden was quiet and lovely, but it took hard work to keep it nice. Mr. Brown mowed the lawn, Mrs. Brown weeded the flower beds, and Mrs. Bird helped too. Mrs. Bird suggested that Jonathan, Judy, and Paddington each have a piece of the garden. Mr. Brown agreed, and the children began their work. Paddington bought a garden book, looked at the building site, and accidentally left his marmalade jar on a platform. Builders poured concrete over it, but when the jar came back, Paddington found a way to use the broken concrete. He made a rock garden, won praise, and later received a gold star from Mr. Lionel Trug on National Garden Day.

summaries.summary: Ping was a young duck who lived with his big family on a wise-eyed boat on the Yangtze River. Every morning they crossed a little bridge to the shore to look for food, and every evening they went back to the boat. Ping always tried not to be last, because the last duck got a spank on the back. One evening Ping was busy catching a little fish and did not hear the call. His family crossed the bridge without him. Ping hid in the grasses so he would not be last, but the boat sailed away in the dark. In the morning Ping was alone and swam down the river to find his family. He met strange fishing birds and ducked underwater. Then he found crumbs leading to a houseboat, where a boy grabbed him. The boy’s family took Ping onto the boat, but later the boy set him free. Ping swam back just as his family returned, and he was spanked for being last. At last he was home again.

summaries.summary: Once there was a peddler who sold caps. He carried many caps on his head: his checked cap, then gray caps, brown caps, blue caps, and red caps on top. He walked through town calling, “Caps! Caps for sale!” One morning, nobody wanted to buy any caps. The peddler grew hungry, so he went for a walk in the country and came to a big tree. He sat down, leaned back, and fell asleep. When he woke up, his caps were gone. He looked all around, then looked up into the tree. Monkeys were sitting in the branches, and each monkey wore a cap. The peddler shook his finger and stamped his feet, but the monkeys copied him. At last he threw down his own cap. Then all the monkeys threw down the caps too. The peddler put them back on his head and walked back to town calling, “Caps! Caps for sale!”

summaries.summary: Straw was part of a big family with many colors and stripes. He had many friends, and he loved to be first. One day, Straw got a bad brain freeze from drinking too fast. His head hurt, and he felt sad. A glassmate saw him and asked him to play. She showed Straw how to blow bubbles. Straw tried it and learned quickly. He laughed and played with the bubbles. Then his friend told him that not everything is a race and that some things should be savored. Straw had not thought about that before. That night, after bedtime story, Straw talked about the strawberry swirls in the whipped cream and the rainbow inside a tiny bubble. He stayed in bed and thought about the day until he fell asleep. After that, Straw still sometimes wanted to be first, but most of the time he wanted to make good things last.

summaries.summary: Scribble had crossing, wiggly lines and could change into many bright colors. He liked green, baby blue, and other crazy colors. One day, Scribble walked to a house and said hello. He asked if they could play. The house was curious, but it was grumpy and asked, “What are you anyway?” Scribble said he was just a scribble. The house said Scribble did not look right because his lines were not straight and his colors were too bright. Scribble asked for a chance, but the house told him to go away. Scribble felt very sad and cried, then changed his colors and kept walking. Soon he met the sun and the clouds, but they also told him to go home because his lines were messy. Scribble said being different did not make him bad. The next day, the house, the clouds, and even rainbow asked him to play. Scribble forgave them, and they all made beautiful art together.

summaries.summary: On Saturday morning, Henry, the narrator, Mom, and Grandpa sat at the kitchen table for pancake breakfast. Mom squeezed oranges, Henry and the narrator guessed how many pancakes they could eat, and Grandpa flipped the pancakes. Then one pancake flew up, hit the ceiling, and landed on Henry. After they saw it was only a pancake, they kept eating breakfast, and even the pancake that hit Henry was eaten. That night, Grandpa told a tall tale about the town of Chew and Swallow. In that town, food came from the sky at breakfast, lunch, and dinner. It rained juice, snowed peas, and sometimes blew hamburgers. People carried plates and forks outside. At first, the town enjoyed all the food, and the sanitation workers cleaned up the extra food after every meal.

In Chew and Swallow, the food weather got worse and worse. One day it was only Gorgonzola cheese, then only broccoli, and then brussels sprouts with peanut butter and mayonnaise. Later, a pea soup fog made it hard to see, and the food kept getting bigger. Huge storms brought bread and rolls that damaged roofs and filled the sea with floating rolls. Another morning, pancakes fell in a storm, and one huge pancake covered the school, so school had to close. Then cream cheese and jelly sandwiches fell in deep drifts, and people ate so much that they got sick. After that came a bad salt and pepper wind and a tomato tornado, and the town became a mess. The sanitation workers could not keep up, and everyone grew afraid.

The storms in Chew and Swallow became so wild that giant meatballs started damaging houses and stores. School stopped, and the town could not stay safe. So the people decided to leave Chew and Swallow. They glued giant pieces of stale bread together with peanut butter, took only the things they needed, and sailed away on rafts. After a week on the water, they reached a small coastal town that welcomed them. The bread was still strong enough for them to build temporary houses. The children went back to school, and the adults looked for places to live and work in the new town.

In the new town, the people had to get used to buying food at a supermarket. They thought it was strange to see food on shelves, in boxes, cans, and bottles, and to find meat in big refrigerators. Nothing came down from the sky except rain and snow. There were no more fried egg clouds, and no one got hit by a hamburger again. The people did not go back to Chew and Swallow to see what had happened there, because they were too afraid. Grandpa finished his story, and Henry and the narrator stayed awake until the end. Then they went to sleep after Grandpa kissed them good night.

The next morning, snow was falling outside the window. Henry and the narrator ran downstairs for breakfast and ate quickly so they could go sledding with Grandpa. While they slid down the hill, they thought they saw a giant pad of butter at the top. They could almost smell mashed potatoes. This matched Grandpa’s story about Chew and Swallow, where food came from the sky and then became too big and dangerous. The story began with a pancake at breakfast, moved into Grandpa’s tall tale about the food weather town, and ended with the family enjoying snowy weather and thinking about the strange foods they had heard about.

One time, she even pulled a steamroller out of a pond. People said, “Nothing can stop her.” One winter, snow began as a drizzle, then rain, then deep snow. The truck plows went out first, but the snow got deeper and the wind made big drifts. Soon the roads were blocked, and the city stopped. Schools, stores, trains, mail, police, and even the doctor and fire department could not move. Then Katie went out. She plowed the city center, helped the police, the postmaster, the telephone and electric workers, the water department, the doctor, and the fire chief. She also cleared the airport runways. At last she finished the side streets and went home to rest.

video_title: Where Do Babies Come From? - Kids Read Aloud Audiobook

summaries.summary: A baby starts growing inside a mother’s body. When a woman has a baby growing inside her, she is called pregnant or expecting a baby. The baby grows in the womb, which is below the stomach and keeps the baby safe. To begin a baby, two things are needed: a sperm from the father’s body and an egg from the mother’s body. When the sperm and egg come together, a tiny seed may start to grow in the womb. The baby gets food from the mother through a special tube called the umbilical cord. This cord helps the baby grow bigger. Babies usually grow for 9 months. When the baby is ready, it is born through the birth canal. After birth, the umbilical cord falls off and leaves a belly button.

The story says every living thing has a way to make a baby. A baby begins when the father’s sperm and the mother’s egg come together. The sperm comes from the father’s body, and the egg comes from the mother’s body. In one way, the father’s penis fits inside the mother’s vagina, and the sperm swims to find the egg. In another way, doctors can help by mixing eggs and sperm outside the body in invitro fertilization, then placing the fertilized egg back in the mother’s womb. A single fertilized egg can start a brand new baby. As the baby grows, it gets food through the umbilical cord. After about 9 months, the baby is ready and is born through the birth canal at home or in a hospital.

The story explains that many people can help bring babies into the world. A fertility specialist can help the sperm and egg come together at the beginning. Midwives can help the mother before, during, and after birth. A family doctor may help deliver the baby too. If a baby cannot be born through the vagina or birth canal, an obstetrician can help by doing a surgery called a cesarian section. The story also says babies can be adopted. An adopted baby starts like any other baby, from a fertilized egg. Sometimes a birth parent cannot care for the baby and gives the baby to another family. Then the baby belongs to the adopted family and is loved there.

Babies can be born into many kinds of families. Some babies have one mom or one dad. Some have two moms or two dads. Some families have a baby with the help of a doctor, and some families choose to adopt a baby. The story says babies are loved very much in every kind of family. It explains that no matter what shape or size a family is, a baby can be welcomed and cared for. Babies who are adopted come from a fertilized egg, just like other babies. When a birth parent cannot care for a baby, the baby may go to another family. Then that family raises the baby as their own.

A baby starts when a sperm from the father and an egg from the mother come together. The sperm finds the egg, and a tiny seed begins to grow into a baby. The baby gets food from the mother through the umbilical cord while it grows. Babies usually take 9 months to grow, and when they are fully developed, they are born through the birth canal. The umbilical cord then falls off and leaves a belly button. The story ends by saying that each person started life as a little seed that became them.

The fourth finds a melon bed, the fifth sails the garden pool, and the sixth is carried off to school. The seventh meets a hungry red, the eighth is frightened by a hen, and the ninth falls into the sea. The tenth climbs an apple tree and hangs there patiently until by and by it becomes a butterfly. After the story, each caterpillar is named. Number one is a morning cloak caterpillar, number two is a buckeye caterpillar, and number three is a cabbage looper caterpillar. Number four is a yellow bear caterpillar, number five is a yellow neck caterpillar, and number six is a monarch caterpillar. Number seven is a painted lady caterpillar, number eight is a woolly bear caterpillar, number nine is a common wood nymph caterpillar, and number 10 is a tiger swallowtail caterpillar.

video_title: Slowly, Slowly, Slowly, Said the Sloth - Kids Read Aloud Audiobook

summaries.summary: Slowly, slowly, slowly, a sloth crawled along a branch in a tree. Slowly, slowly, slowly, the sloth ate a leaf, fell asleep, and then woke up. All day long and all night long, the sloth hung upside down in the tree. Even when it rained, the sloth stayed there. One day, the howler monkey asked, “Why are you so slow?” The sloth did not answer. Then other animals came and asked why the sloth was so quiet and so boring. The anteater asked too, and the jaguar asked why the sloth was so lazy. The sloth thought and thought for a long, long time. At last, the sloth said it was true that it was slow and quiet, but it was not lazy. The sloth said it liked to live in peace and do things slowly, slowly. Then the sloth yawned and said, “That’s just how I am.”

Marisol said she would paint the ocean, and other children said they would paint fish and the sky. But when Marisol looked for blue paint, she could not find any. She wondered how she could paint the sky without blue. The bell rang, and she had to stop for the day. On the bus ride home, she kept thinking about the missing blue paint. That night, she dreamed of a sky full of many colors. The next morning, it was raining, and the sky was not blue. His grandparents gave him a warm red scarf for class, but it did not help. Everyone had ideas about why he was not doing well. They tried tape and scissors too, but he still could not get it right. Then he met a new friend who wanted a blue ocean for a boat. The red crayon could not make blue, so his friend did it instead. After that, the crayon drew many blue things, like bluebells, blue jeans, and blue whales. People were happy with his work, and he started making bigger and better pictures, including a green lizard. In the end, he was working on a big new project and enjoying a perfect day.

summaries.summary: Our skin is beautiful, strong, and important just the way it is. Skin gets its color from something called melanin inside our bodies. Melanin helps protect skin from the sun. Some people have more melanin and some have less, so skin can be many shades from dark to light. The story says color words like black and white are sometimes used to describe people, and there are many groups of people in the world, like black, indigenous, asian, white, arab, pacific islander, african american, latinx, and biracial. Color does not tell us what a person is like on the inside. A long time ago, some white people made up the idea of race and said white people were better. That was not true or fair. When people believe this story and make unfair rules, that is called racism. Racism can happen in big ways and small ways, but people can work for racial justice by telling the truth, speaking up, and changing unfair rules.

summaries.summary: Harriet Tubman was a woman who led people to freedom on the Underground Railroad. One dark night in 1851, she hid outside a cabin and whistled “Go Down Moses.” Ten slaves came out to follow her north. Harriet watched the North Star to find the way. When clouds hid the star, she used Daddy Ben’s lesson and felt the moss on the trees to know which way was north. Harriet remembered her childhood as a slave in Maryland. She was born Aramenta Ross, called Minty, and later took the name Harriet. She worked hard, had little food, and was not allowed to learn to read. As a girl, she was hurt by a heavy weight and after that she would fall asleep without warning. Daddy Ben taught her how to hide, what food to eat, and how to find north. Later, Harriet escaped, found safe houses, and became free in Pennsylvania.

Harriet Tubman was born a slave on a tobacco plantation in Maryland. She lived with her family in a small cabin and worked long hours. She helped her mother, carried water, and picked bugs off tobacco plants. When she was seven, she worked for Mrs. Cook and Mr. Cook, and she was whipped and made to do hard jobs. In the fields, Harriet watched birds fly north and wished to be free. When she was a teenager, a slave ran away, and a thrown weight hit Harriet instead. After that, she had sleep spells, but she still wanted to escape. Her father, Daddy Ben, taught her how to hide in the woods, eat safe plants and berries, run quietly, and follow the North Star. When Harriet grew up and married John Tubman, she told him she wanted freedom. After she learned she had been sold, she left at night with food in a handkerchief and ran into the woods.

Harriet Tubman ran for hours after escaping. She crossed the Maryland border, stepped into icy water, and hid from slave catchers in a swamp log. At a safe house in Camden, Delaware, a quilt told her it was safe to knock. The people there fed her and let her sleep in the attic. Then she ran again and reached other safe houses. She even hid in a ditch covered with mud when slave hunters came near. At last Harriet crossed into Pennsylvania and became free in Philadelphia. She found a room, worked as a cook, and met William Still of the American Anti-Slavery Society. At secret meetings, she learned that her sister’s family needed help escaping from Baltimore. Harriet said she would go for them. The men were surprised, because no women conductors worked on the Underground Railroad, but Harriet would not stop. She chose to keep helping people escape, just like Moses led people to freedom.

Harriet Tubman returned to Maryland to save her parents, Daddy Ben and Old Rit. They were now old, but Harriet wanted them to know freedom. In 1857, she dressed like an old woman and went back to them. She found an old horse and wagon, and that night Daddy Ben and Old Rit climbed in under blankets. Harriet drove fast so they could leave Maryland by daylight and reach Delaware. A Quaker railroad agent helped by selling them train tickets. Daddy Ben and Old Rit could hardly believe they were leaving slavery after a lifetime. Harriet used the lessons her father had taught her to guide them north. Later, Harriet worked during the Civil War as a spy, scout, and nurse for the North. When the North won in 1865, the Underground Railroad stopped. Harriet then lived in Auburn, New York, cared for her parents, and later used money from the government to build a home for elderly black people.

In 1913, Harriet Tubman was very sick and stayed in bed. Visitors read the newspaper to her, and she heard about women fighting for the right to vote. She sent them the message, “Stand together.” Harriet had already spent many years helping others. She had made at least 19 trips south and helped more than 300 people escape slavery. She once said, “I've never run a train off the track and I've never lost a passenger.” Harriet died at age 93. People remembered her as the Moses of her people and as one of the bravest workers in the fight against slavery. Her life story showed her journey from enslaved child in Maryland to free woman, helper on the Underground Railroad, and leader who guided many people to safety.

summaries.summary: Pete felt nervous when he played a pilgrim in his class Thanksgiving play. His friend Callie told him to do his best, and Pete tried. He wore a pilgrim hat that his mom made for him and stood at the front of the cardboard Mayflower. The story then told about the pilgrims who left England in 1620 to begin a new life. Their trip on the big ship was long, rough, and dangerous, and many got very sick. After 65 days, they saw land and were happy. summaries.summary: Legend says tiny leprechauns visit once a year. On the night before St. Patrick’s Day, people try to catch one so he will grant a wish. To do this, they build a trap with a box, a bottle cap, glitter glue, tape, gold paint, rocks, and a rainbow slide. They close the drapes, dim the light, and wait quietly in the dark. Then they hear a sound and check the trap. But the leprechaun escapes. He leaves behind one shoe and a small note. The note says his name is Liam the Leprechaun and thanks the children for the shiny gold rocks and glitter, but says a cardboard box cannot trap him. The story ends by saying it is a shame he got away, but children should enjoy Saint Patrick’s Day and try again next year.

Then they hide, close the drapes, dim the light, and wait very still. Soon they hear something and look at the trap. The leprechaun is gone. He has escaped and could be anywhere. The children find his shoe, and inside it is a note. The note from Liam the Leprechaun says the trap was clever, but he cannot be caught by a cardboard box. The story ends by saying to enjoy Saint Patrick’s Day and try again next year.

Their job is to find a queen to mate with. Workers are the biggest group, with about 30,000 to 80,000 in a hive. They are small female bees with stingers. Workers do many jobs. They gather nectar, pollen, and water, make honey, feed baby bees, build and protect the hive, and make royal jelly for the queen.

summaries.summary: Camila Cream loved lima beans, but she did not eat them because her friends did not like them. On the first day of school, she worried about what to wear and tried on 42 outfits. When she put on a red dress, she saw that her whole body was covered with stripes. Her mother kept her home, and Dr. Bumble said she could go to school the next day. At school, the children laughed and called out different colors and shapes, and Camila kept changing into them. The principal said she had to stay home because she was too distracting. Her parents called more doctors, but the specialists and experts could not find a cure. News reporters came, and many helpers tried to fix her, but each one made her look even stranger. Finally, a kind old woman offered her plain lima beans. Camila admitted she really loved lima beans, ate them, and the stripes disappeared. After that, she ate lima beans whenever she wanted and never got stripes again.

At school, the other children laughed at her and shouted for more colors and patterns, and Camila changed every time they called out something new. Camila first said she did not like them, but then she told the truth and said she really loved them. After she ate the beans, all the strange things disappeared, and she became normal again.

summaries.summary: The Cat in the Hat takes Sally on a trip to the rain forest. He says the rain forest is steamy and wet because lots of rain falls there near the equator. He also tells about other kinds of rain forests, like seasonal rain forests, cloud rain forests, and mangrove rain forests. Then he explains that rain comes from transpiration, when plants give off water and warm air makes clouds. The Cat says the rain forest has four floors. On the top floor, very tall emergent trees grow, with buttress roots to hold them up. Harpy eagles and macaws live there. On the next floor, the green canopy is full of animals like howler monkeys, sloths, toucans, orchids, and tree frogs. Hummingbirds help flowers by carrying pollen. The understory is dark and has spider monkeys and ocelots. The forest floor is full of leaves, insects, snakes, jaguars, and people who have lived there for many years. In the end, the Cat says many trees are being cut down and asks people to save the rain forest.

Harpy eagles and colorful macaws live there. The second floor is the canopy, where treetops make a green roof. Epiphytes grow there, and animals such as howler monkeys, sloths, toucans, orchids, tree frogs, and hummingbirds live and eat there. Hummingbirds carry pollen from flower to flower. The third floor is the understory, where little sunlight gets through, so vines and ferns grow. Spider monkeys and ocelots live there. The fourth floor is the forest floor, where jaguars, snakes, insects, spiders, and people live among leaf litter. At the end, the Cat says millions of acres are being cut down and asks people not to cut the trees.

At Pig three’s place, she stood in her gi, bowed, and faced the wolf. She showed fast kicks and backflips, then split a pile of bricks. The wolf saw her strength and ran away. The pigs cheered, and they kept training at school.

The handsome prince sent her away because he did not like how she looked. Then the woman changed into an enchantress and turned the prince into a beast. She also cast a spell on everyone in the castle. She said the spell would break only if the prince learned to love and be loved before the last rose petal fell. In a nearby village, Belle lived with her father, Maurice. Maurice got lost in the forest, and Belle went to find him. She came to the castle, where the beast kept Maurice. Belle stayed instead of her father. At first she was sad and afraid, but she met Mrs. Potts, Lumiere, and Cogsworth. Belle and the beast spent time together, and he became kinder. When Belle returned to save him from Gaston, she said she loved him. The beast changed back into a prince, and everyone in the castle became human again.

The camp rules said to wear life preservers, stay where the camp could still be seen, and never go out in bad weather. Felix and Harry were in a hurry, so they forgot the life preservers and rowed away from shore. Soon the wind pushed them farther out, and they could not get back. It got dark, cold, and rainy, and the boat rocked hard. Then the boat broke apart, and the boys fell into the water. They were tired and could not see the shore. Just when they were sinking, something lifted them up and carried them back to land. When they looked back at the lake, they thought they saw a huge turtle with a long neck diving under the water.

On the third day, he adds three yummy cupcakes. On the fourth day, he adds four far out surfboards. On the fifth day, he adds five onion rings. On the sixth day, he adds six skateboards rolling. On the seventh day, he adds seven concert tickets. On the eighth day, he adds eight guitar strumming. On the ninth day, he adds nine ugly sweaters. On the tenth day, he adds ten slots of sleeping. On the 11th day, he adds 11 balls of bouncing. On the 12th day, he adds 12 friends are rockin. Each new day repeats the earlier gifts, so the list gets longer and longer. Every line ends with the word Groovy.

video_title: It’s Christmas, David | Ms. Ocasio Reads… | Story Time | Bed Time Read Aloud For Kids | Full Story

summaries.summary: At Christmas time, everyone keeps telling David, “No, David.” They say no peeking, no snitching, and no opening toys early because Santa is watching. They tell him to be patient and to hurry up, and they warn him about the naughty list and a lump of coal. David also gets many rules at dinner with his grandmother, like sitting up straight, using the right fork, and keeping his elbows off the table. Later, he is told to go to sleep and that there will be no Christmas for him. Then a note from Santa says, “Sorry you were naughty.” After that, David wakes up and learns he was dreaming. It is really Christmas, and there is a new note that says, “Merry Christmas.”

Christmas has come, and Santa’s real note says, “Merry Christmas.”

video_title: Christmas Read Aloud Story for Kids | Ms. Ocasio Reads... Needles the Forgotten Christmas Tree

summaries.summary: At a Christmas tree farm, a small tree named Needles waited for the day he would become a Christmas tree. The other trees laughed at him because he was short and had fewer branches. When the Tree Farm Workers cut down the trees and brought them to the lot, Needles stood with the others, but many families passed him by. For 10 days, people chose the bigger trees, and Needles was left alone. Still, he kept telling himself he would be somebody’s Christmas tree. At last, the lot owner gave the last tree to a friend. The worker took Needles to the friend’s house, but the family already had a Christmas tree. The father moved Needles outside, then later put him on the curb with a sign that said “free tree.” On Christmas Eve, Emily and her mother found him. Emily loved him, and her family decorated him with lights and ornaments. Needles finally became a happy Christmas tree.

Needles was a little tree at a Christmas tree farm. He wanted to be chosen for Christmas, but the bigger trees laughed at him because he was small. When the workers took the trees to the lot, Needles hoped families would still pick him. Many moms, dads, and children looked at the trees, but they said Needles was too short or did not have enough branches. After 10 days, he was the only tree left. He stayed hopeful, and then the lot owner gave him to a friend. The worker brought Needles to the friend’s house, but the family already had a tree inside. The father set Needles outside, and later he was put on the curb with a “free tree” sign. Near Christmas Eve, Emily and her mother found him. Emily said he was the most beautiful tree she had ever seen. They took him home, decorated him, and placed him by the window. Needles was proud and happy.

video_title: The Proudest Blue by Ibtihaj Muhammad | Kids Book Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Mama holds out a pink hijab, but Asia shakes her head because she wants the bright blue one. The blue looks like the ocean and the sky. The next day, the younger sister gets a new backpack and light-up shoes for her first day of school. She walks with Asia, who wears her blue hijab and takes her hand to cross the street. At school, the younger sister tells other children that Asia’s hijab is a scarf, and then says, “hijab” more clearly. Mama had said the first day of wearing hijab is important and means being strong. Later, a boy laughs and says mean words about Asia’s hijab. The younger sister draws a picture of two princesses in hijab having a picnic by the ocean. At break time, more mean words are said, but Mama says to drop hurtful words because they belong to the person who said them. After school, the sisters meet again, walk home together, and the younger sister wants to show Mama her picture and her own hijab drawing.

Asia chooses a blue hijab instead of the pink one Mama offers. The blue is compared to the ocean and the sky, and it is Asia’s first day wearing hijab. The next day, her younger sister goes to school with a new backpack and shoes that light up. She feels proud to walk beside Asia, who takes her hand and helps her cross the street. At school, the younger sister hears another girl whisper about Asia’s hijab. She says the word out loud and remembers Mama saying the first day of hijab is important and shows strength. Soon, a boy laughs at Asia, and later another boy says he will pull the “tablecloth” off her head. Asia and her friends turn away and go play tag. The younger sister draws a picture of two hijab-wearing princesses having a picnic. After school, she finds Asia waiting for her. They cross the road together, and she plans to show Mama the drawing and how she put a hijab on the princess in her picture.

video_title: RAMADAN by Hannah Eliot  | Kids Book Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Ramadan begins when the crescent moon first appears in the sky. It lasts for one whole month. During Ramadan, Muslims think about what is important, feel thankful, and help other people. They eat and drink only when it is dark outside before the sun comes up. Each day they have a big meal called sahoor to get energy. In the evening, when the sun goes down, family and friends gather to break the fast. They eat a date first, then share a meal called iftar. People still go to work, school, and play, but they also spend time with family, pray, and do good deeds. When the crescent moon appears again, Ramadan ends. Then people celebrate for three days with a feast called idolfitter, also called the sweet festival. They eat, pray, and give gifts.

In the ninth month of the year, Muslims celebrate Ramadan when the crescent moon appears. Ramadan is a special month that lasts for one whole month. People fast by eating and drinking only before sunrise and after sunset. In the morning, they eat sahoor, a big meal that gives them energy for the day. At night, they meet with family and friends and eat a date and then iftar. During Ramadan, mothers and fathers still go to work, and children still go to school, play, and see friends. All month long, people think about what matters most. They spend time with family, pray, and help others. When the crescent moon appears again, Ramadan ends. Then people celebrate idolfitter, the sweet festival, for three days with food, prayer, and gifts.

When the crescent moon appears again, Ramadan is over. People celebrate for three days with idolfitter, the sweet festival. They eat, pray, and give gifts to each other.

The man was the night gardener and asked for help because there were so many trees in the park. William worked with him under the full moon. In the morning, William saw happy families and a gift from the night gardener. Later, the leaves changed, fell, and the topiary disappeared, but the town and William were changed by what had happened.

They danced by moonlight and fell in love.

That night, Bruce’s family goes to bed sad and secretly wishes Bruce were more cheerful, adventurous, and full of pizzaz. They prefer to snuffle around with their noses, which does not fit a parade. They also refuse to wear majorette uniforms, even when enough uniforms are found for them. The story says pigs do not care about parade floats, even ones about The Three Little Pigs or Wilbur from Charlotte's Web. Instead, they only like root beer floats. The pigs also play bad music, choosing sad country songs instead of marching band music. Finally, they would not hold the giant balloons, so the balloons might drift away. Because of all these problems, the story says a pig parade is a terrible idea.

The story begins by asking the reader to imagine a pig parade, which seems like it should be fun. It says people might picture many pigs marching together in a big parade. Then it explains why this would fail. Pigs hate marching and would rather snuffle around the Barnyard looking for food. They also will not wear majorette uniforms, even if someone finds enough for all of them. The story says pigs do not care about parade floats, including a Three Little Pigs float or a Wilbur float. They only care about root beer floats. When given instruments, pigs would not play cheerful parade music. Instead, they would play sad country ballads. They also would not help hold the giant balloons, so the balloons could float away or hit buildings. In the end, the story says a pig parade is a terrible idea, but a panda bear parade would be fantastic.

video_title: Bruce and the Legend of Soggy Hollow 🎃 by Ryan T Higgins 🎃 Halloween Storytime 📖 Kids #Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Bruce was a bear who did not like holidays, and he especially did not like Halloween. Every year, he grumped about tricks, treats, and visitors at his door. This year, Bruce’s family had an idea. They decided to act out a scary story called the legend of Soggy Hollow. They got dress-ups and asked friends to help. Then the story began. Long ago, a soldier lost his horse and became known as the Horseless Horsemen of Soggy Hollow. Later, a school teacher named Bruce moved to town. He was kind and gave students treats, sang, and danced, and he liked Miss Camila van muffl. One night, he went to ask her to marry him, but he got scared on the way. Miss van muffl said yes, and Bruce was happy. Then the Horseless Horsemen came close, and Bruce ran through the woods. After the chase, Bruce gave out candy, Camila said, “My hero,” and the old story was still told on cold nights.

video_title: 🍄 Alice in Wonderland 👑 by Lewis Carroll 📚 #Read Aloud for Kids

summaries.summary: Alice sat with her sister by a riverbank when a white rabbit ran past and said he would be late. Alice followed him and fell down a rabbit hole. She landed in a hall with many doors and a glass table with a key. The key opened a tiny door, but Alice was too big to fit. She drank from a bottle that said “drink me” and became small, but then she could not reach the key. She ate a cake that said “eat me” and grew very tall. Alice cried and made a pool of tears. The White Rabbit dropped gloves and a fan, and when Alice used the fan she became small again and fell into the pool of Tears. There she met the duck, Dodo, Lori, iglet, mouse, and other creatures. They did a caucus race, and everyone won. Alice later met the Caterpillar, who told her how the mushroom could make her grow taller or shorter. She changed size, visited the Duchess, saw the Cheshire Cat, met the Hatter and March Hare, and went to the Queen of Hearts’ croquet game and trial. When Alice spoke up, the cards flew at her, and she woke up on the riverbank beside her sister.

Alice was resting with her sister when a White Rabbit hurried by. She followed him and fell far down a rabbit hole. At the bottom, she found a hall with doors and a key on a table. She could not open the doors at first. A small door opened with the key, but she was too big to go through. Then Alice drank a bottle marked “drink me” and became tiny. After that she ate a cake marked “eat me” and grew so large that her head touched the roof. She cried until tears made a pool, and the White Rabbit’s fan made her small again. In the water, Alice met many strange animals, and the Dodo led a caucus race so they could dry off. Alice gave out sweets as prizes. Later, the Caterpillar asked who she was and showed her the mushroom that could change her size. Alice then went to the Duchess’s house, where a baby turned into a pig. She met the Cheshire Cat, the Hatter, and the March Hare, and then went to the Queen of Hearts’ croquet game. The Queen shouted “Off with his head!” many times. At the trial, Alice spoke against the rules, the Queen grew angry, and the cards flew at her. Alice woke up by the riverbank and told her sister about her curious dream.

video_title: 🍄 Alice in Wonderland 👑 by Lewis Carroll 📚 #Read Aloud for Kids

summaries.summary: Alice sat with her sister by a riverbank when a white rabbit hurried past, saying, “Oh dear! I shall be too late.” Alice followed it and fell down a rabbit hole. She landed in a hall with locked doors and a glass table with a key. After finding a tiny hidden door, she drank a bottle marked “drink me” and shrank so she could fit, but the key was too far away. Then she ate a cake marked “eat me” and grew very large. Alice cried, and her tears made a pool. The White Rabbit dropped gloves and a fan, and when Alice used the fan, she shrank again and fell into the Pool of Tears. There she met a duck, a Dodo, a Lori, an iglet, a mouse, and other creatures. They held a caucus race, and the Dodo said everyone had won. Alice gave out sweets, but the animals ran away, leaving her alone.

Alice walked on and met a caterpillar sitting on a mushroom. The caterpillar asked who she was, but Alice said she did not know because she had changed size so many times. The caterpillar told her that one side of the mushroom would make her grow taller and the other side would make her grow shorter. Alice nibbled the mushroom pieces and changed size until she could use the right piece to become smaller. She went inside a tiny house and found a Duchess singing to a baby while a cook stirred soup. The Duchess gave the baby to Alice and went off to play croquet with the queen. Outside, the baby grunted and changed into a pig, so Alice set it down and it trotted away. Then Alice saw the Cheshire Cat in a tree. The cat told her that the Hatter and the March Hare were both mad and said, “We’re all mad here,” before disappearing.

Alice found the March Hare, the Hatter, and the Dormouse sitting at a long table. They asked riddles and moved from place to place. Alice took the March Hare’s seat. The Dormouse talked about three little sisters who lived in a well and ate molasses. When Alice began to speak, the Hatter told her not to talk because she had said, “I don’t think.” Alice thought the tea party was very rude and called it the stupidest party she had ever been to. After that, she came to a beautiful park where the King and Queen of Hearts arrived with soldiers and the White Rabbit. The Queen made them play croquet, but the game was very strange. The balls were hedgehogs, the mallets were flamingos, and the arches were made by soldiers. The Queen grew angry and kept shouting, “Off with his head!” or “Off with her head!” Alice saw the Cheshire Cat again, and when the Queen ordered its head cut off, the cat disappeared.

The Queen sent Alice to meet the Griffin and the Mock Turtle. The Mock Turtle said he had once been a real turtle and had gone to school in the ocean. The Griffin and the Mock Turtle showed Alice how to dance the lobster quadrille. Then the Mock Turtle sang a song about beautiful soup. After that, someone shouted that the trial was beginning, and the Griffin took Alice to court. The King and Queen of Hearts sat on their thrones, and the Knave of Hearts was under arrest. The White Rabbit read the charge that the Queen of Hearts had made some tarts and the Knave had stolen them. The Hatter was called as a witness, then the cook, and then Alice. The King said Alice’s name was very important, and he read a rule that all persons more than a mile high must leave the court. Alice said he had made the rule up. Bruce did not eat eggs raw. He liked to cook them into fancy recipes from the internet. One day he found a recipe for hardboiled goose eggs with honey salmon sauce. He got salmon, honey, and eggs, and he went home to cook. But the fire in his stove went out, so he went to get more wood. When he came back, he found that the eggs had turned into goslings. Bruce did not want goslings. He took them back to their nest, but Mrs. Goose was away. The goslings followed him home, and Bruce could not make them leave. As time passed, the goslings grew up. In winter, Bruce and the geese packed bags, took a bus, and migrated to Miami together. Now they spend winter at the beach.

summaries.summary: Bear cannot sleep. He tosses, turns, moans, and stares at the wall in his lair. Mouse comes in to check the fire and says it is winter in the woods, so bears hibernate. Mouse makes mint tea, but Bear still cannot sleep. Then Badger and Hare come in and say they heard Bear talking. Bear tries to snuggle down, but he is still awake. Mouse turns down the lamp, Badger builds up the fire, and Hare pours milk into Bear’s tin cup. Gopher and Mole arrive and say it is bedtime for bears. Raven and another friend come in, and they all sing a lullaby, but Bear still cannot sleep. At last Bear says he is bored and will tell a story. He begins a story he has never told before, and just before the end he starts to snore. When the sun comes up, the friends cannot sleep, but Bear snores on.

In the library, Mrs. Barry reminded her that libraries need quiet voices. Penelope tried to help by pushing the book cart, signing students in on the computer, and helping at the reference desk, but she still used a loud voice. The library became very messy and noisy. Penelope felt sad and thought she was not right for the job. Then she stopped and remembered that not all library voices are quiet. She got a new idea, went back to work, and soon students came to listen. In the end, Penelope smiled and invited everyone to come back for Penelope story time the next day.

video_title: Farmhouse

summaries.summary: At the end of a road, over a hill, there was a house where 12 children were born and raised. They crawled in the front hall, posed on the stairs, and grew taller beside the marks on the wall. They made flower patterns with paint, and they were scolded when they painted the cat and lied. They read books about planets and stars in their rooms and dreamed at night. They also worked on the farm. They milked champion cows, fed calves, cleaned stalls, and piled hay. They fished in the glittering stream, picked apples, and dragged in mud from the fields. They helped their mother with chores, set the table, cared for a feverish child, and sewed buttons and socks. Spring came each year, and rain leaked through the roof. One by one, the children grew up and left for school, work, farms, nursing, stars, and babies. The youngest child left last with her sister to go to the sea. After that, the house slumped, the rooms filled with rain and plants, and later the storyteller found its old papers and memories.

She asked, “Mr. snowman, will you be my friend?” The snowman said yes and told her his name was Puddles. Puddles said he was made with friendship snow and would teach her how to be a good friend. When spring came, Puddles had to go away and told Jojo to keep a heart and remember she was a good friend. Jojo later made new friends, including black kitty and Ned, and Puddles returned every winter.

summaries.summary: As the moon stayed high above the treetops, Dad bear woke his little fisherman early and said they had to beat the Sun. The two bears got ready and went on their trip. Dad bear took the long way around the mountain, through the valley and into the tall birch trees. They stopped at the edge of a cliff to look at the mountains, then kept going until they reached their fishing spot. The fish did not bite, and the bobbers stayed still while time passed. Little Bear got bored and flicked pebbles into the water. When the sun began to go down, Dad bear said it had been an amazing day. Little Bear said they had not caught anything, but Dad bear explained that fishing was not only about catching fish. He said they had caught the stars, the mountains, the wheat, the cicadas, the honeysuckle, and the wind. He said the best thing he caught was Little Bear.

Dad bear woke Little Bear before sunrise and told him they needed to leave early to beat the Sun. Little Bear stretched and yawned, and then the two bears started out together. At last, they reached their fishing place, but no fish would bite. Their bobbers did not move, and Little Bear became bored. He played with pebbles while Dad bear waited. By sunset, Dad bear said the day had been amazing. Little Bear wondered why, because they had not caught any fish. Dad bear laughed and said it was called fishing, not catching. He told Little Bear they had caught many wonderful things in the world, and the best thing he caught all day was Little Bear.

Mommy gave the old man an apple from Morgan’s lunchbox, a bottle of water, and one dollar. The man said thank you, and Morgan felt happy. At school, Daddy was there to meet him after his night job. Morgan was excited and joined his class. In math, he shared a red pencil with Jacob, who had lost his. Later, Morgan shared a favorite book with Olivia. In art class, he shared art pencils and taught the class to draw smiling Hearts. His teacher gave him a star. When Mommy and Daddy picked him up, Miss Wilson said Morgan was a great friend. On the way home, Morgan saw the old man again and said he loved to share.

summaries.summary: Mr. Malouf loved to play tricks all day long. His mother told him that one day he would stop fooling around and grow old. Mr. Malouf did not believe her. Then one day, he really did get old, and he was not goofy anymore. He sat in his chair feeling grumpy, and a single bright blue hair grew on his head. He tried to cut it off with clippers, but they broke. Then he put on a hat to hide it. Later, three children walked by and teased him. When he sneezed, the blue hair popped through the hat. One child pulled off her own hat, and blue hair fell down her back too. Mr. Malouf was surprised. He waited for the children to come back, and he planned a prank. He hid in the bushes and shouted, and the children laughed. They kept playing this trick on each other many times, and Mr. Malouf stayed silly even when he was old.

summaries.summary: Three monks named Hok, Lok, and Siew walked down a mountain road and talked about happiness. They came to a village where people were tired, scared, and did not trust one another. The villagers shut their windows and would not answer the monks’ knocks. Siew said they would show the village how to make stone soup. The monks made a fire, filled a pot with water, and put in three smooth stones. A little girl watched them and helped find the stones. When she told her mother, the mother gave the girl a bigger pot. Soon the other villagers came out to watch. The monks talked about salt, pepper, carrots, onions, and more. Each time, someone ran to get an ingredient and put it in the soup. At last, everyone shared rice, buns, tea, cakes, and more. They ate together, told stories, and let the monks sleep in their homes. In the morning, they said goodbye, and the villagers said sharing had made them richer.

Hok, Lok, and Siew traveled together and asked what makes one happy. When they reached a village, they saw that the people were lonely and did not welcome strangers. No one opened their door for the monks. Siew decided to make stone soup. The monks built a fire and put a small pot of water on it. A brave little girl helped them find three round stones, and then she brought her mother’s bigger pot. Her mother wanted to learn how to make the soup. As the monks stirred, the villagers looked out their windows and came closer. Hok and Siew asked for salt, pepper, carrots, onions, and mushrooms. The villagers brought these, then noodles, cabbages, dumplings, bean curd, yams, and many other foods. The pot grew fuller and the smell grew better as more people gave. When the soup was ready, everyone shared a feast with rice, buns, tea, and sweets. They celebrated together, slept in warm homes, and said goodbye in the spring morning.

But years passed, and they did not come back for birthdays, Día de los Muertos, or Navidad. One day Alex packed a suitcase and left for Nueva York first. Later, Areli started kindergarten and learned new things at school. Then Abuela told her that it was Areli’s turn to leave. Areli said goodbye to her cousins, friends, mountains, and chickens. A kind man took her to America. There, Mamá and Papá cried and hugged her, and Alex was happy to see her. New York was bigger and louder than Mexico, and Areli had to learn English and face teasing at school because she was born in Mexico and was not yet a citizen.

Carmela wore her birthday bracelets, and they jingled as she moved. Her brother did not want her to follow him, and he kept telling her she was annoying. Carmela found a dandelion and wanted to make a wish, but she did not know what to wish for. She helped her brother with the laundry and kept imagining many things, like candy, her mom in a hotel bed, and her dad getting his papers fixed. Then her brother went into a friend’s house, and Carmela sat on the curb. She thought about turning him into animals and looked at the dandelion again. On the way home, she fell and crushed the dandelion. Her brother helped her, then took her to an abandoned farmhouse near the sea. He told her to close her eyes and make her wish. When she opened them, she saw white spores floating in the air like wishes. He said not to tell the wish, and Carmela took off her bracelets and went home with him.

On the way home, Carmela falls off her scooter and sees that her dandelion is crushed. Upset, she follows her brother to an abandoned farmhouse by the ocean, where he tells her to close her eyes and make a wish. She sees white dandelion spores in the wind and then goes home with him.

Carmela’s birthday begins with pancakes, candles, and a wish. She wants to go with her big brother, and that wish comes true. They travel through busy streets and stop at places like the Laundromat, Miss Maria’s vegetable stand, the locksmith shop, the bodega, and the pharmacy. Carmela tries to talk, but her brother mostly ignores her and gets upset by the sound of her bracelets. Carmela picks a dandelion and thinks it is important, because it is where wishes go. She lies and says she already made a wish. While helping wash clothes and waiting during errands, she imagines many things, including candy, her mother in a hotel bed, and her father getting his papers fixed so he can come home. When her brother leaves to visit a friend, Carmela sits alone and imagines turning him into a rat, a cockroach, or a wheelbarrow of manure. On the way back, she crashes her scooter and sees her dandelion crushed. Her brother takes her to an abandoned farmhouse near the sea, where she closes her eyes, makes a new wish, and watches the dandelion spores float into the sky.

summaries.summary: Daisy’s papi has a motorcycle, and she waits for him when his gray truck comes home from work. He is a carpenter, and his hands are rough from building homes. Even when he is tired, he still takes Daisy for a ride. Today he will show her the new houses he is working on. Daisy puts on her helmet, and Papi asks, “¿Lista?” Daisy says, “¡Sí!” They ride through the city as the sun goes down and the motorcycle shines in the light. They pass Abuelita’s church, Tortillería la Estrella, Joy’s Market, and the library. They also see murals, old houses, and new homes being built where citrus groves used to be. Daisy hears the sounds of the city and feels that it will stay with her.

When Papi arrives home from work, Daisy brings both helmets outside. Papi is a carpenter, and his clothes are full of sawdust. He puts Daisy on the motorcycle seat and tightens her helmet carefully. Daisy and Papi ride through their city together. They pass places she knows, like Abuelita’s church, Joy’s Market, Mr. García’s library, and la panadería. They also pass murals about the city’s history and the new houses where citrus groves once stood. They stop seeing Don Rudy’s Raspados, but the shop is empty and closed, so Daisy and Papi keep going. Daisy hears many sounds and sees many streets, and she knows the city will always be part of her, even when it changes.

They pass Abuelito and Abuelita’s old yellow house, and Daisy remembers the lemon tree there. They also pass barking dogs, Franky the Labradoodle, and Mercedes López running after her. Then they ride toward the new homes replacing the citrus groves. Workers wave to them, and Papi greets them. Daisy and Papi turn around the circle on Grand Boulevard and pretend they are in the old road race. They fly past the school, the post office, and the panadería before heading home.

summaries.summary: One day, when Baba picked the child up from school, the child did not run in for a hug. The child felt hurt because Kurt drew a picture of their friends and pointed to a person with eyes like two lines, saying it was the child. At home, Baba stood with the child in front of a mirror and said the child’s eyes rise to the skies and speak to the stars. Baba said the child’s eyes can see secrets and the future, just like his own. Baba also showed this with playful moments, like lifting the child high and saying, “Ready for takeoff!” Baba’s eyes were like Agong’s eyes too. Agong answered questions on early morning walks and held the child’s face at night. Di-Di also had these eyes, and when he woke up, the child made silly faces and sang until he laughed. In the end, the child says these eyes are also their own, full of light, vision, and power.

summaries.summary: Before sunrise, Dad wakes the child quietly so Mom can keep sleeping. Dad has already made sandwiches and packed the car. The child helps carry the tackle box, and they drive through dark, quiet roads to Lake Street to buy minnows at the bait store. Dad says he has a second job and must work that morning, so they still need to fish for food because everything in America costs a lot of money. At the pond, Dad holds the child’s hand and says, “Step where I step.” The child makes a small fire from dry twigs and lights it with one match. Dad asks the child to put a minnow on the hook, but the child says no because the fish is small. Dad is not upset. He tells about fishing in Vietnam with his brother, who did not come home from the war. Soon Dad catches crappie, and the child helps put them in the bucket. They go home with enough fish for dinner.

summaries.summary: Amy can do many things, but she cannot make the perfect bao. Her mom, dad, and grandma make soft, fluffy bao that Amy loves to eat. Today, Amy wants to make the best bao ever. Her dad makes the dough in the morning and kneads it. Amy helps, and the dough rises and gets bigger. Her mom makes the filling with garlic, mushrooms, pepper, salt, and ginger. Then everyone starts making bao. Amy’s first bao is too small, and her second is not quite right either. It is hard to know how much filling to use and how to pinch the dough shut. Amy watches her family make bao and tries to copy them, but her bao still leak or have holes. Then Amy has an idea. Her grandma cuts the dough into smaller pieces for Amy’s small hands. Now Amy can roll, fill, and pinch the bao better. She makes perfect bao, and later they are steamed and eaten.

Amy wants to make the world’s most perfect bao. At first, she has trouble. Her bao are too small, too big, too empty, or too full. They sometimes fall apart before she can eat them. Then Amy notices that the dough pieces are made for grown-up hands. She tells her grandma, and grandma cuts the dough into smaller pieces. summaries.summary: The child tells us about eyes that kiss in the corners and glow like warm tea. At first, the child says some people have big eyes and long lashes, but their own eyes are different. The child’s eyes are like Mama’s. When Mama comes home from work, her eyes crinkle into crescent moons. She hugs the child, tickles them, and tucks them into bed at night. The child also says Mama’s eyes are like Amah’s eyes. Amah’s eyes do not work like they used to, but she can still see into the child’s heart and read the child’s mind. Her eyes hold many stories, and the child imagines Guanyin, the Monkey King, lychee trees, and mountains by the sea. The child then says Amah’s eyes are like Mei-Mei’s eyes too. Mei-Mei waits at the window, smiles with two teeth, and follows the child around. In the end, the child says their own eyes are like all of theirs and are beautiful.

Baapa bought him a green umbrella and purple shoes with crimson soles and linings. Little Sambha put on his fine clothes and went for a walk in the jungle. There he met many tigers. Each tiger said it would eat him up, and each time Little Sambha gave away one of his things to stay safe. He gave away his coat, then his trousers, then his shoes, and then his umbrella. After that, he had nothing left and cried. Soon he heard a loud noise and saw the tigers arguing about which one was the grandest. They fought, rolled, and spun around the tree until they melted into a pool of butter. Baapa took the butter home, Maata made pancakes, and the family ate a big supper.

That night, Squirrel worries, but the next morning many flowers have grown, and there are enough flowers for everyone.

summaries.summary: This story is an alphabet book about many Black heroes, leaders, and artists. It starts with A for Advocate, where women like Stacy Abrams, Kandi Brown, and Jackson use their voices and vote. B is for brave, and Rosa Parks takes a stand by staying in her seat and changing history. C is for Creative, with Maya Angelou, Jean Michelle Basat, and Lorraine Hansbury making art, words, and plays. D is for dream, and Martin Luther King Jr. marches in Selma and says, “I have a dream.” E is for equality, and Ruby Bridges walks through crowds so she can learn. F, G, H, and I show freedom fighters, gospel singers, hair, and inventors. The book keeps going through the alphabet, ending with Z for zest and Cab Callaway.

The story names many people who helped make history. Rosa Parks is brave and does not move from her seat. Martin Luther King Jr. marches and speaks about a dream for freedom. Ruby Bridges goes to school even with shouting crowds around her. Malcolm X fights for rights. Mahalia Jackson sings gospel songs, and Black hair is shown as a crown through many styles. Inventors like Mark Dean, Marie Van Britton Brown, and Granville T. Woods build new things. Harriet Tubman helps enslaved people escape on the Underground Railroad. The story also says Barack Obama and Kamala Harris were first as President and Vice President. Other letters talk about teachers, songs, rights, winners, youth, and zest. The alphabet ends by telling children they can help make history too.

summaries.summary: Cassie Louise Lightfoot is eight years old and lives with her family in a building roof she calls Tar Beach. One night she lies on the roof and looks at the stars, the skyscrapers, and the George Washington Bridge. She remembers that Daddy worked on the bridge and told her it is the longest and most beautiful bridge in the world. Cassie says she can fly, and she thinks that if she flies over something, it can be hers forever. She wants the bridge to be her prized possession. Daddy also works on a new Union building, but he cannot join the union because Grandpa was not a member. Cassie thinks that if she flies over the building, it can belong to Daddy. Then he would not have to work so hard, and Mommy would not cry when he looks for work. On Tar Beach, Mommy cooks peanuts and chicken, Daddy brings watermelon, and the Honey neighbors play cards. Cassie plans to fly with Bibi to the union building, because anyone can fly if they have somewhere to go that they cannot reach any other way.

summaries.summary: At night, the moon rises and the Flying Fox wakes up to look for food. It is a bat, not a fox. Flying foxes sleep in the day and fly at night. They like fruit, especially ripe figs, and they also lick nectar from flowers. The pollen sticks to them and helps plants grow. The story then tells about Stellaluna, a baby fruit bat who gets lost one night when an owl swoops down. She falls into a forest and lands in a bird nest. The baby birds are surprised. Stellaluna is hungry, but she does not want the bugs the bird mother brings. Later she eats a grasshopper. She learns to live like the birds, but she still hangs by her feet. When she tries to fly like them, she feels clumsy and flies away by day. At last, other bats find her and show her she is a bat. Stellaluna brings the birds to meet her bat family, and they stay friends even though they are different.

summaries.summary: Babushka lived alone in a little house in the country and was known for painting beautiful eggs. Every year, her eggs won first prize at the Easter Festival in Moscow. One day after a snowstorm, she went outside to feed the wild caribou and saw a goose fall from the sky. She put the goose in a basket lined with a warm quilt and named her Rashenka. Babushka cared for Rashenka, and the goose grew strong. Rashenka laid an egg each morning, but one day she jumped on Babushka’s work table and knocked over the basket of painted eggs. The eggs broke, and both Babushka and Rashenka felt sad. The next morning, Babushka found a shining egg in Rashenka’s basket. She cooked the egg for breakfast and admired its beauty. Soon she had enough eggs for the festival, where the judges chose her eggs as the most beautiful. Babushka won first prize, a feather bed quilt, and went home happy. Later, she found a new egg in Rashenka’s basket and saw that it was hatching. A special gosling came out, and Rashenka stayed with Babushka.

Rashenka had given Babushka a special gift, and the little goose stayed with her.
