Later he returned, but Borreguita tricked him again. She told him about cheese, and at night she led him to the pond. He saw a round shape in the water and thought it was cheese, but it was only a reflection. When he jumped in, the image broke and he got wet, while Borreguita escaped. The next day she fooled him again by pretending to hold up a mountain under a rock ledge. Coyote helped by holding it up with his own feet, and Borreguita ran away. At last, Borreguita tricked him one more time and knocked him back, so Coyote never bothered her again.

summaries.summary: Many years ago, there was a small boy in a tribe who was called Little Gopher. He could not ride and shoot like the other boys, but he loved to decorate stones with berry juice. The wise shaman saw that Little Gopher had a special gift and told him his path would be different from the warriors. When Little Gopher went to the hills alone, he had a dream vision. A young Indian maiden and an old grandfather came to him and gave him tools for painting. The maiden showed him a pure white buckskin and told him to find one like it. After the dream ended, Little Gopher made brushes and paints and began painting hunts and visions. He found a white buckskin, but he could not make the colors of the sunset. One evening, a voice said he would find the colors because he had been faithful. The next night, sunset-colored brushes appeared, and he painted quickly. In the morning, the brushes had grown into bright flowers, and the people gave him a new name: He who brought the sunset to the earth.

The next sunset, brushes full of bright paint were waiting for him, and he painted the buckskin. Later, those brushes grew into colorful plants, and the people called him He who brought the sunset to the earth.

At the city gate, Manyara ran out in fear after seeing a monster. Nyasha went inside and found Nyoka, who changed into the king and chose her to be his wife. A great feast was held, and Mufaro was glad that Nyasha became queen.

He judged the turkey art on Thanksgiving Day, but then he disappeared. He had blended in with the other turkey art, found his fee, and left a note. The townspeople still had no turkey, but they were thankful for their shredded wheat. They learned that a plump and perky turkey can be very clever.

summaries.summary: One morning, a child says they are not going to get up today. The alarm rings and the birds peep, but the bed is warm and the pillows are deep. They stay in bed and keep sleeping. People try many ways to wake the child. They tickle their feet, shake the bed, and pour cold water on their head. The neighbors try too, but it does not help. The child also refuses breakfast and says to give the egg back to the hen. Even strawberries, marshmallow dip, pineapple butterscotch, dogs, roosters, goats, geese, police, newspapers, Marines, TV, peas, beans, and a brass band cannot make them get up. At the end, the helper understands, and the child stays in bed while the egg is given away.

summaries.summary: Otis and the little calf liked to play Follow the Leader with all the Farm Friends. They marched around the apple tree, the barn, the hill, the pond, the cornfield, the meadow, and Mud Creek. Everyone played together except the bull. The bull lived alone in a pasture and scared the other animals. Otis once brought him a red apple and asked him to play, but the bull snorted, glared, and charged at the fence, so Otis stayed away from him after that. One day a storm came. The sky turned green, the wind stopped, and the farmer shouted that a tornado was coming. Otis opened the stalls and let the calf, pig, sheep, horse, and cow out of the barn. Then he heard the bull crying in his pen. Otis rushed back, broke the gate, and led the bull to Mud Creek. The animals hid there until the tornado passed. After the storm, the farm needed repairs, and the bull joined the other animals in Follow the Leader.

Otis and the little calf led their Farm Friends in a game of Follow the Leader. Later, dark storm clouds came over the farm. The farmer shouted, “It’s coming fast! Get down in the cellar,” and Otis saw a tornado heading toward the farm. Otis opened the calf’s stall, then the pig’s, sheep’s, horse’s, and cow’s doors. He led them out to Mud Creek. Then he heard the bull in trouble. Otis raced back, broke open the bull pen gate, and brought the bull to safety too. After the tornado passed, the animals came out, saw the damaged farm, and played together again with the bull in the line.

summaries.summary: A little old lady who was not afraid of anything went out from her cottage one windy afternoon to gather herbs, spices, nuts, and seeds in the forest. She stayed out so long that it became dark. On the path home, she met two big shoes that went clomp clomp. She told them to get out of her way and kept walking. Then she met a pair of pants that went wiggle wiggle, a shirt that went shake shake, two white gloves that went clap clap, and a tall black hat that went nod nod. Each time, she said she was not afraid and walked faster. Near her cottage, she found a very big orange pumpkin head that went boo boo. This time she ran home and locked her door. Later, she opened the door and saw all the things again. The pumpkin head said they came to scare her, but she was not afraid. She whispered to the pumpkin head, and the next morning the pumpkin head and the other things were in her garden, scaring away the crows.

summaries.summary: Eugene loved the aquarium on Saturday. She watched the glittery fish and, most of all, the sharks. She pretended to swim like them and wanted to know what it would be like to live under the sea. In the summer, her mother took her to the beach in Atlantic City, and Eugene dove into the water. She imagined sharks, sea stars, and ocean currents, and she saw sharks as beautiful. Since the sharks were only in her mind, she decided to learn all she could about them. Eugene read books about whale sharks, nurse sharks, tiger sharks, and lemon sharks. She joined the Queens County aquarium society and filled her notebooks with shark drawings and facts. Her mother also gave her a small aquarium, and Eugene kept fish and snails in her room. As she grew older, people told her to stop thinking about sharks, but Eugene studied zoology, became a scientist, found new fish, saw a wild shark, and later trained sharks. In the end, she proved sharks are smart and should be protected and loved.

Eugene put gum in her ears, dove into the water, and looked for fish. She thought sharks were beautiful, even when others called them scary. Eugene then read many books about sharks and joined the Queens County aquarium society. Her mother surprised her with a small aquarium, and Eugene filled it with guppies, clown fish, and coral red snails. Later, people told her to choose other work, but Eugene studied zoology and learned about fish in her laboratory. She traveled to the Red Sea, found new fish, met a wild shark, and was not afraid. People called her the Shark Lady. She also trained sharks and learned they could remember. Eugene showed that sharks are not mindless killers and that they deserve care.

video_title: Storms Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Storms happen in the atmosphere, the blanket of air around Earth. When the air changes fast and hard, we call it weather, and very violent weather is a storm. Thunderstorms are powerful storms that can bring huge amounts of rain, hail, lightning, and thunder. They begin when warm, wet air rises from the ground and meets cool, dry air. Tiny water drops form clouds, and the cloud can grow very tall and wide. Inside the storm, water drops bump together and grow bigger. Then heavy rain or hail falls, and strong winds blow up and down inside the storm cell. Some thunderstorms stand alone, but many join in a squall line. Thunderstorms help move heat high into the sky and bring water to dry land. They can also make hail, strong gust fronts, and dangerous lightning that can start fires and hurt people.

Hail is made of balls of ice that fall during some thunderstorms. It starts with tiny dust and ice pieces that freeze to water drops. The storm winds toss the ice up and down, and more water freezes on it. The hailstones grow bigger and bigger until they become too heavy and fall to the ground. Some hailstones are small like peas, and some are as big as baseballs or grapefruits. Hail can smash grasses and small plants into the ground and ruin crops. It can hurt chickens, rabbits, squirrels, cows, and horses. Hail can also damage roofs, windows, cars, and farm machines left outside. Thunderstorms can also make gust fronts with strong cold winds. These winds can blow dust, hurt homes and crops, and be very dangerous for airplanes if they happen near takeoff or landing.

Lightning is an electrical flash inside a thunderstorm. As the storm grows, electricity builds up in the clouds. When the charge gets strong enough, the electricity jumps through the air. Lightning can flash inside one cloud, from one cloud to another, or between the cloud and the ground. Thunder is the loud sound made when lightning heats the air very quickly. If lightning is close, thunder sounds like a sharp crack. If it is far away, it sounds like a rumble. Because light travels faster than sound, people see lightning before they hear thunder. By counting the seconds between the flash and the sound and dividing by five, people can tell how many miles away the lightning is. Lightning can start fires, damage power lines, and cause blackouts. To stay safe, people should go indoors, stay away from trees, water, and metal, and crouch low if they are outside.

Sometimes a thunderstorm gives birth to a tornado. First, the wind blows hard, trees bend, and rain, hail, lightning, and thunder fill the sky. Then spinning winds inside the storm make a funnel-shaped cloud that reaches down to the ground. When it touches Earth, dirt flies up and the tornado turns dark. The funnel can move across the ground, bouncing up and down and leaving marks behind it. It can travel very fast and pick up loose things as it goes. Tornado winds can blow at more than 200 miles an hour and can knock down houses and carry away furniture. Tornadoes usually do not last long. As they clog with dirt and air, they grow weaker, narrow, and finally vanish. If a tornado is coming, people should go indoors, stay away from windows, and hide in a cellar or a small middle room.

Hurricanes are the biggest and deadliest storms on Earth. They form in late summer over warm tropical seas, where water evaporates and gives heat to the air. Thunderstorms grow there and can become hurricanes. A hurricane can stretch over hundreds of miles, and its winds can blow very fast. When a hurricane reaches land, it pushes ocean water up into a high dome. Big waves crash on top of this water, and the storm surge washes away beaches and can carry boats inland. The strong winds bend trees and can pull them out of the ground. In the center of the storm is the eye, where the wind stops and the sky may look calm for a while. But the storm is not over, and the wind soon returns from the other side. Today satellites, radar, and computers track hurricanes so forecasters can warn people. The story ends by saying that storms still make people feel awe and wonder.

summaries.summary: Abella is the narrator’s grandma. She speaks mostly Spanish, and she and the narrator go places together. One day they go to the park and see many birds around the bread they bought. Abella imagines the birds lifting her up so she can fly. The narrator calls to her, and Abella answers and leaps into the sky. They fly over the city, parks, streets, buses, factories, trains, and the Sea. They see ships, fruit from Abella’s home country, and the Statue of Liberty. Abella remembers coming to this country for the first time. They fly to the airport, then to Tio Pablo and Tia Alisa’s store for lemonada. They rest in the clouds, look at shapes in the sky, and fly over their house and the building where the narrator’s father works. At the end, they return to the park by the lake, and Abella invites the narrator on another adventure.

summaries.summary: The story begins when the speaker sees someone in a storm of hurt, unfairness, anger, and sadness. The sky grows dark, and the speaker listens with a hand on the heart to find the answer. The speaker says love is compassion and tenderness. In the middle, the speaker says love can help someone share what is important, understand that no one is perfect, and try to make things better when something is wrong. Love can also remember people who were loved before and notice small kind acts like a smile or helping hand. At the end, the speaker says all creatures share the world and the same Stardust. When clouds come for others and for the speaker, the heart leads the way, and love helps everyone weather the storm and Light Up the Sky together.

summaries.summary: A freight train races toward Chicago. At first, one train says, “First one to Chicago wins!” The other train says it must load its freight first. It loads lumber, bricks, a gondola, a steel coil car, a gas tank car, and a gravel bin. Then it opens the hatch, checks the hopper catch, and goes fast. The train carries a freezer car full of ice cream bars and sees cold mountain ahead. It takes an auto rack through a tunnel and out into the snow. It pushes through and keeps going. It also carries a boxcar full of food like wheat, eggs, tomatoes, peppers, and cheese. Trucks ride on piggyback cars, and cattle stand on the track, so the cows move out of the way. The freight cars roll on the side track and the train wins the race to Chicago.

Then he put on his mask and cape and used a Spanish accent to sing about Scapito Fresquito. Mama and the girls watched TV, but Skippy John Jones was not thinking Siamese. He went into his closet and found a place full of chihuahuas and his old amigos, the lost Chimichangas. They told him a Babalito was in their house, and they rolled him into a three-bean burrito. They took him to the doghouse, where he fought the Babalito, stuffed the little bubbly toe into his pants, and brought him down. Then Skippy John Jones went back to his room, wrapped in his blankie, talking to his bobble head and still thinking Chihuahua.

summaries.summary: The tub people were seven wooden figures who stood in a line on the edge of the bathtub: father, mother, grandmother, doctor, policeman, child, and dog. Every bath time, the father played sea captain and took the mother, grandmother, and child for rides on the floating soap. The policeman and doctor had water races, and the child cheered. When bath time ended, they always lined up again. One evening, the water rushed down the drain too soon. The soap spun in a whirlpool, and the child was carried away. The father could not save him. The mother looked into the drain, and all the tub people felt sad. That night and the next night, they called for their child, but he did not answer. Later, a big man fixed the drain and pulled the child back out. The tub people smiled, but the child was put into a tool box. After that, they waited until they were moved to a new room and placed on a soft bed, where they became seven again and played new games together.

He rode the soap with the mother, the grandmother, and the child, while the others watched. The child sometimes slid off the soap and called, “Help! Help!” and the father rescued him. The policeman and the doctor liked water races, and the grandmother told the child to hush. When bath time was over, they lined up again. One night, the bathwater rushed down the drain before they were ready. The soap spun over the drain, and the child disappeared into it. The mother looked into the drain, and the tub people grew very sad. They called for the child every evening, but he did not come back. Then big people found a problem in the drain. A man opened it, shone a light, and used a wire. The child popped out wet and tired. The tub people smiled, but the man took the child away in his tool box. Later, they were carried to a new room and placed on a bed, where they played and lined up together again.

summaries.summary: The days grow short and the nights grow long. It gets cold, and winter is coming. Leaves fall from the trees, and there are no berries or seeds left. Birds and animals get ready in different ways. Bluebirds and Orioles fly south to warm, sunny places with food. In spring, they fly back north. Monarch butterflies also migrate. They gather in a tree by the hundreds, stay there all night, and fly south in the morning. Some bats go south, but some stay in caves and hibernate all winter without eating. Woodchucks hibernate too. In fall, a woodchuck eats grass, twigs, and leaves, grows fat, and sleeps in a long tunnel for many months. Some animals, like pikas and squirrels, store food for winter. Other animals must hunt all winter for food. When spring comes, the days grow longer and the weather gets warmer.

A woodchuck eats a lot in fall, gets fat, and crawls into a tunnel to sleep for four months. Pikas do not hibernate. They gather grass in summer, dry it on stones, and hide it under rocks. In winter they eat that grass. Squirrels bury nuts in the ground and dig them up later. Some animals, like mice, deer, rabbits, and foxes, must hunt for food in the snow. People can help by feeding birds and wild animals and by making feeders and birdhouses. Then spring comes, and it gets warmer again.

The child also fights like a champ, loves like a heart, climbs like a ladder, and rises like the air and wind. The child pushes, pulls, pours, and falls like rain. The child dreams like the moon, learns like a student, swells like water, and burns like fire. Even in winter, the child keeps trying. Sometimes the child cries, but still tries again. The story says people do not have to be the same. They may look different and sometimes disagree, but they all have worth. In the end, they should live with love, help each other, stay together, and remember: “I am enough.”

In spring, he woke with wide eyes. He felt the sun and saw little buds on the bare trees and tiny leaves opening. He cried, “Welcome!” and thought the leaves welcomed him.

After that, Kevin was ready to try something new.

video_title: 🏹🔥The Rough-Face Girl🔥🏹Native American Cinderella Read Aloud for Kids

summaries.summary: Long ago, by Lake Ontario, there was a great wigwam where an invisible being lived with his sister. Many women wanted to marry him, but his sister said only someone who could see him could become his wife. In one village, a poor man had three daughters. The two older girls were cruel to their youngest sister and made her sit by the fire until her hands, arms, face, and hair were burned and scarred. The older sisters tried to marry the invisible being, but his sister asked them questions about his bow and sled runner, and they guessed wrong. Then the rough-faced girl asked for beads, buckskin, and moccasins, and she made her own dress from birch bark. People laughed at her, but she kept walking. The sister of the invisible being saw her kind heart, answered her questions, and welcomed her. The invisible being arrived, married her, and after she bathed in the lake, her scars disappeared and her beauty returned.

His sister asked what his bow and sled runner were made of, but they did not know the answers and had to go home. The youngest daughter then made a necklace from broken shells and clothing from birch bark. Even though people laughed at her, she went to the lake shore. The sister of the invisible being saw her good heart, let her in, and accepted her answers. The invisible being came, and the two were married after she bathed and became beautiful again.

Later, Kyrie's father came home, and they all ate porridge. One year later, a little troll saw Kyrie and asked about the sleeping cat, and Kyrie said it had grown into a big cat with seven kittens, so the troll ran away.

summaries.summary: Many children write letters to Santa with funny wishes. Teddy asks for a bike or a helicopter, the moon, a zoo, a bottle of Happiness, a genie, and green hair. Other children ask for magical shields, a swimming pool, a park ranger hat, a river or sea, Santa’s sleigh, 20 billion dollars, a spaceship, a tiger, a robot, x-ray eyes, bionic legs, a cloud, a doll’s house, and the best present in the world. Dad says he wants anything but socks. After many days of waiting, Christmas Eve comes. The story says this is the time to try to catch Santa, but he is very busy and will not stay long. It tells children to think ahead, ask Santa questions, tell him they are trying to be good, and leave gifts like drawings, cookies, and homemade decorations. It also says not to use wild tricks, but to be clever, gentle, and patient.

The story gives children clues for catching Santa on Christmas Eve. It says to write Santa a note and fill it with glitter so he leaves a glitter trail. Children can scatter carrots in the yard or on the windowsill to see if the reindeer come. They can bake cookies, draw arrows to the room, and hang bells and chimes above the cookies so Santa makes noise and wakes them up. The story tells children to wait patiently by singing Christmas songs and reading books about Santa. It also says to ask Mom and Dad, and even grandma and grandpa, if they ever tried to catch Santa. When it gets dark, Santa and his reindeer start their rounds. Families should look out the window and listen for Santa sounds like sleigh bells, reindeer in the distance, elves giggling, and ho ho ho. If children get sleepy, they should leave the Christmas tree lights on, put out Santa riddles, and let a gentle puppy watch the room. Before sleeping, they should peek out the window one last time.

The story shows that children may catch Santa, only glimpse him, or find Santa’s bin instead. It says to plan for all of these things. If Santa comes, he may see the glitter note, the carrots, the cookies, the arrows, and the lights. The story says Rudolph’s bright nose cannot help him from the roof, so the tree lights help Santa see. Children are told to leave a note saying to wake them up for help with the riddles. Santa is said to be unable to resist these clues. The story ends this part by saying good luck catching Santa and Merry Christmas. If children do not catch him this time, there is always next year.

After Christmas, some children write back to Santa and thank him for their presents. Eve says Santa is the best and thanks him for her new toy car. She says she wanted a pony but is very happy with her doll’s house, and she wishes him Happy Christmas. Another child sends Santa a picture and says thank you for the presents, and hopes to catch him next year. Another child thanks Santa for amazing presents and says see you next year. The last letter thanks Santa for fantastic presents and says the writer likes his beard. It also says the cat likes its present too, and shows a drawing of the cat. Dad thanks Santa for the socks, even though earlier he said he wanted anything but socks. The letters end with thanks and Christmas wishes for Santa.

The story then explains how to prepare for Christmas Eve, how to look for Santa, and how to wait for him. video_title: 🦨👃My School Stinks👃🦨 Funny Back to School Read Aloud for Kids

summaries.summary: A child starts at a new school and feels worried. Mom and Dad tell them to take deep breaths and think happy thoughts, and they also say the child is old enough to walk to school alone, so the child draws a map. At school, the child thinks there has been a mistake because the deskmate stinks, the locker buddy bites, and the teacher feels unbearable. The child says the classmates are wild animals, and Mom says all little kids are wild animals. The child feels sick, but Mom and Dad do not believe it. On the next day, the child is hurt by monkeys at recess and visits Nurse Patricia, who pulls out quills. The child says the deep breaths and happy thoughts still are not working. The child does not want to go back, but has to return. Mrs. Fuzzy bottom is the only one who understands.

The child keeps writing about Wild Wood Elementary and all the strange things there. Betsy chews up the pencils, George looks through the child’s hair for bugs, and Charlie eats the science experiment. One day Miss Fuzzy bottom is missing, and the child wonders if Sammy took her, but Sammy says he is still digesting breakfast from last week. Charlie asks the child to eat lunch with him, and the child worries about being lunch. Dad and Mom both say they will not pick the child up before lunch. Later, the class runs relay races, but the team loses and the child lets Camila go first at the water fountain. By the time they get back, everyone has left, and Charlie is waiting. The child runs away without homework, and Mr. Grizzly is not happy. After that, the child gets the job of closet cleaner instead of line leader.

While cleaning the closet, the child finds four dead cockroaches and gives them to Sammy for lunch. Sammy says the child can have his dessert for the rest of the week because he will not be hungry. The child thinks about giving one dessert to Charlie because Charlie is always hungry. The next day the class runs races again and wins. The child gives Charlie a cupcake, but Charlie bites the child’s finger, so Nurse Molly puts on one bandage. The child also says you cannot get rabies from a crocodile. Then the child finds a note from Charlie saying sorry for biting the finger and saying he is a nervous spider. Charlie asks if they can be friends. The child thinks maybe deep breaths and happy thoughts should be told to Charlie.

At lunch, the hyenas laugh at the child’s small teeth. Charlie stands up for the child, and the hyenas are surprised when they see Charlie’s teeth. Later, Charlie and Ralph help the child clean the closet. While they are inside, they hear a scary noise and come out smelling very bad. Mom does not understand how a skunk got into the storage closet, and the child says she will find out at open house. After that, the child learns that the scary scratchy noise was only Miss Fuzzy bottom. The child and the class throw her a welcome home party and give her extra treats, but she seems to want to go back to the closet. The child then writes that there are three things to love about Wildwood Elementary: Betsy sharpens all the pencils, George keeps the child lice free, and Charlie is the best friend.

The child uses a drawn map to walk to school alone, and at school the child thinks the desk mate, locker buddy, and teacher are all terrible. The child keeps telling Mom and Dad about the strange classmates and feeling sick, but they do not believe it. Then the child is hurt by monkeys during recess and Nurse Patricia removes quills. Later, the child has to go back to school and says Mrs. Fuzzy bottom is the only one who understands. Many odd things happen after that: Betsy chews pencils, George searches hair for bugs, Charlie eats the science experiment, and Miss Fuzzy bottom disappears for a while. The child worries about Charlie, but Charlie later apologizes, helps in the closet, and stands up for the child at lunch. In the end, Miss Fuzzy bottom returns, and the child says Wildwood Elementary has become a place with friends, good pencils, and Charlie.

summaries.summary: In a small village near the Moroccan desert lived a young potter named Amir. His father made famous pots, but Amir wanted to make the most beautiful pot of all. He worked hard, used gold dust, and put his shiny pot in the town square. People admired it for a while, but an old herb seller said beauty alone would not last. A desert fox and a bird found that the pot was empty, and soon the wind made it tip over and crack. Amir made another pot with jewels and silver, but it was empty too. A sandstorm blew it away. Then the old herb woman told Amir that a pot must have a purpose. Amir made a simple clay pot, filled it with water, and left it for travelers. People came to drink, and his father said the pot now shone from the inside out. Amir understood that kindness mattered more than glitter.

summaries.summary: Mrs Bobbin was very tired and had a bad headache, but she finished sewing a beautiful gown for the duchess. Her daughter Irene wanted to help, so she packed the dress in a big box, dressed warmly, and carried it out into the snow. The wind was strong and kept pushing her, but Irene kept going because the gown had to reach the palace. The wind tore the box open, and the dress flew away. Irene searched for it, fell into the snow, and became lost as night came. At last she saw the light of the palace below. The box turned into a sled, and Irene slid down until she found the gown caught in a tree. She put it back in the box and brought it to the palace. The duchess and servants cheered, and Irene stayed there for dinner. The next morning, Mrs Bobbin found Irene returning in a sleigh, safe and smiling, with gifts and a note from the duchess.

summaries.summary: Mr. Spivy was angry and scared when he saw the broom acting in strange ways. He called it wicked and told others it was dangerous. But the broom kept working hard on the widow Mina Shaw’s farm. It swept the road and even played the piano with one note at a time. One day, two of the Spivy boys and their dog bothered the broom on the dirt road. The boys kicked stones into its path, called it names, and tapped it with sticks. The broom finally turned and knocked both boys down. When the dog chased and bit at it, the broom was still not harmed. That evening, Mr. Spivy and three other men came to the widow’s house with rope and a stake. Mina said they should take the broom away. The men tied it up, burned it, and turned it to ashes. After that, people found the dog safe in a tree, and life seemed normal again.

After the broom was burned, Mina Shaw told her neighbors that she had seen the broom’s ghost. She said it was white like snow and carried an axe through the woods at night. Mr. Spivy did not believe her at first. Then, on the nights of a full moon, he saw the ghost himself. It came from the woods and circled his house. Each night it came closer, and on the third night it tapped the axe on his door. The next morning, Mr. and Mrs. Spivy packed their wagon with their best things and their eight children. Mr. Spivy asked Mina to leave too, but she stayed in her farmhouse. As the wagon drove away, she waved goodbye. Mr. Spivy called her a brave woman. That evening, Mina fell asleep in her chair by the fire after listening to music from the piano. A gentle tap woke her, and she saw the broom, not a ghost, but white from the paint she had given it. The broom bowed, put a log on the fire, and played another tune.

The broom lived on Mina Shaw’s farm and did many jobs. It was especially happy when it could sweep. Sometimes it went onto the dirt road between Mina Shaw’s farm and the Spivby farm. One afternoon, the Spivby boys and their dog found the broom working there. They tried to stop it by kicking stones back into its path and teasing it. When that did not work, they hit its handle with sticks. The broom then knocked both boys on the head, and they cried. The dog ran after the broom and bit at its bristles. Later, Mr. Spivby came with three men, a stake, and rope. They said the broom had beaten the boys and hurt the dog. Mina opened the closet where the broom slept and let them take it. The men tied it to the stake, covered it with straw, and Mr. Spivby burned it. Afterward, the dog was found safe in a tree, and the farm became quiet again.

video_title: 🚌The Magic School Bus, Inside the Human Body, children’s story, read aloud.  By Joanna Cole

summaries.summary: Miss Frizzle showed the class a film strip about the human body, and the children knew another strange adventure was coming. The next day, she made them do an experiment and then took them on a class trip to the Science Museum to see how food gives the body energy. They rode in the old school bus and stopped at a park for lunch. When it was time to leave, Arnold was still at the picnic table eating cheesy wheezys, so he stayed behind. Miss Frizzle pressed a strange button, and the bus began shrinking and spinning. The class landed inside a human body and traveled down the esophagus into the stomach, then into the small intestine. Miss Frizzle showed them how food moves into the blood through tiny villi. The children rode red blood cells through the blood, into the heart, up to the brain, and along the nerves and muscles. At the end, they were blown back to school through Arnold’s nose.

Miss Frizzle told the class they were going to the Science Museum to learn how the body gets energy from food. They rode the old school bus and stopped for lunch at a park. When the class got ready to leave, Arnold was still outside eating cheesy wheezys, so he did not get back on the bus. Miss Frizzle pushed a button, and the bus shrank and spun until it landed inside a human body. The class went down the esophagus, into the stomach, and then into the small intestine. Miss Frizzle showed them the villi, where food goes into the blood. They became very small and traveled with red blood cells, which carry oxygen, and saw white blood cells chasing germs. The bus and the children moved through the heart, the lungs, and back into the blood. Then they reached the brain, climbed down the spine, and followed nerves to the leg muscles. Finally, they were blown out through the nasal cavity and back to school when Arnold blew his nose.

summaries.summary: Tim carved his first pumpkin and named the Jack-o-Lantern Jack. He liked Jack very much and kept him for a while, but Mom said the pumpkin would rot and needed to go outside. Tim carried Jack to the garden and left him there. As the days passed, Jack changed. He got wrinkled, then moldy, and then flat. Winter snow covered him, and Tim forgot about him. Later, when the snow melted, Tim found only a little pumpkin skin, a stem, and some seeds. He covered the remains with dirt and said goodbye. In spring, a green sprout grew where Jack had been. Tim watered it and watched it grow into a pumpkin vine. Yellow flowers came and went, and then a small green pumpkin appeared. By Halloween, the pumpkins were orange, and Tim made one into a new Jack-o-Lantern and welcomed Jack back.

The plant grew long vines and yellow flowers, and later a small green pumpkin appeared. More pumpkins grew as summer went on. When frost came in October, Tim picked the pumpkins and put them on the porch. By Halloween, they were bright orange. Tim gave away all but one pumpkin, carved a new face, and said, “Welcome back, Jack.”

video_title: 🎧💥Too Much! An Overwhelming Day for help supporting children with sensory needs, story read aloud

summaries.summary: An alarm clock beeps, and the child feels upset by the loud sound and bright sunlight. Washing is hard because the washcloth feels rough and the water is cold. At breakfast, the child does not want crunchy food and chooses soft bananas instead. Then the child gets dressed, but the shirt has a sharp, itchy tag and the coat feels too tight. At the playground, friends crowd close, someone hugs the child, and everything feels too loud, too bright, too itchy, and too tight. The child does not want to play because it all feels like too much. Later, the child asks for a gentle hug and feels brave. The child learns to say what is needed, like quiet time, a dark place, a soft shirt, and personal space. With deep breaths and a held hand, the child feels thankful and calm.

summaries.summary: On a bright Christmas Eve, Fletcher the rabbit saw that the rabbits had moved to a new burrow. He worried that Father Christmas would not find the new home. Fletcher began to collect sticks and make a trail of arrows through the wood. Squirrel saw him and helped. Soon birds came down from the trees, and then the mice joined in too. Together, they finished the trail to the rabbit’s new burrow. The rabbits’ home was warm and smelled like blackberry pie. The friends sat by the fire, ate pie, and sang Christmas songs. Then snow fell softly, and the arrows disappeared. Fletcher became worried again. He asked everyone to stay awake and help Father Christmas find the burrow. But one by one, the animals fell asleep. Father Christmas came anyway. The next morning, the rabbits were happy because Father Christmas had found them, and all their friends came to share the bright, warm burrow.

In the morning, the rabbits were glad because their friends had brought gifts and because everyone fit in the burrow for a happy Christmas.

At Teiti, Moana gave the heart to Teay, who became Teiti again. The world was balanced, and Moana returned home as a daughter, a leader, and a wayfinder.

video_title: THOSE DARN SQUIRRELS FLY SOUTH  Read Aloud ~ Bedtime Story Read Along Books  ~ Kids Books Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Old man Bookwire lived by a beautiful forest, but he was a grump. He scolded fireflies, clouds, and lilacs. In summer, he painted the colorful birds in his yard, and sometimes he painted squirrels by accident. Then fall came, and the birds flew south for the winter. Bookwire thought he would be alone, but the squirrels had built flying machines and followed the birds. They flew in gyrocopters, gliders, and a zeppelin. The birds waved goodbye, and the squirrels flew after them. They traveled through night, rain, and turbulence until they reached a warm beach in Santa Vaca. There they had a fiesta, swam, ate mangoes, and danced. Later, Bookwire got a phone call from Santa Vaca. He missed the birds and squirrels, so he drove his old car to the beach. The squirrels hugged him, and he laughed for the first time in a long time. He painted the birds there, but the hot sun made him too tired. The squirrels gave him water, and everyone drove home together.

Bookwire lived at the edge of town in a forest full of birds and squirrels. He was often cross and complained about many things. During summer, he painted the birds that came to his yard. When fall arrived, the birds flew south. The squirrels did not want to stay behind, because they wanted to see where the birds went. So they made flying machines from pine cones, leaves, and even an old shopping bag. When the frost came, the birds left, and the squirrels took off too. They flew behind the Flugel bird for many days and nights. At last they reached a warm beach and landed with a crunch. The squirrels were happy and had a big party with swimming, mangoes, music, and dancing. After some time, Bookwire got a call from Santa Vaca. He missed the birds and squirrels, so he loaded his paints into his old car and drove slowly to the beach. The squirrels welcomed him, he painted the birds, and then the hot sun made him faint. The squirrels helped him and drove him home.

summaries.summary: Big Bear walked through the autumn woods while the wind blew all around him. First, leaves flew off the trees when Bear sneezed. Bear said the wind did not do it, and he tried to nail the leaves back with a hammer and tacks. Then he came to an apple tree. When he sneezed again, the branches shook and the apples fell to the ground. Bear put the apples back on the branch. After that, Bear went to the lake and saw twenty geese. When he sneezed, the geese flew away with loud honks and flapping wings. The wind kept saying it did these things because it was fall. At last, the wind told Bear that it whips leaves off trees, drops apples, scares geese south, and makes Bear sneeze. Bear listened and went to his den. The door slammed shut, and Bear hid in bed and turned out the light.

Bear stacked the apples back on the branch. Next, Bear came to the lake where twenty geese were resting. When Bear sneezed, the geese flew away to the south. The wind and Bear argued about what caused each thing. Finally, the wind said it did all of it as the autumn breeze. Bear understood, went to his den in the forest glen, and shut the door. He got into bed, covered his head, and turned off the light on the windy night.

summaries.summary: Every morning Sarah watches from the window as her mom goes to work and waves from the bus stop. She also sees Saul open his store and put bad fruits and vegetables in a box by the side of the store. One day Sarah sees an old man take an apple from the box and eat around the bad spots. Grandma says he may be poor and hungry. Sarah thinks about him at school and saves her snack cookie for him. She asks Mom to leave it near Saul’s store. Later the man finds the cookie and eats it. Sarah tells her friends, and they wrap more cookies. Her teacher says this is called sadaka, giving to someone who has less. Sarah and Mom also leave juice and a sandwich for the man. Soon Sarah sees his face and thinks she knows him. At a Shabbat and Hanukkah party, she learns his name is Morris Berger. After that, food is left for him every day.

He even slid down a coal shoot and became so dirty that he looked like a black dog with white spots. Soon Harry felt tired and hungry, and he wondered if his family thought he had really run away. So he hurried back home. At the house, his family did not know him at first. Harry tried his old tricks, but they still said he was not Harry. Then he dug up the scrubbing brush and showed it to them. The family gave him a bath, and when they scrubbed him, they finally knew it was Harry. Afterward, he was white again with black spots, and he went to sleep happily.

Mr. McGee could not steer, so he asked the moose to step aside and then yelled, “Duck!” Their skis snagged on a spruce log, and Mr. McGee and Dee flew into a ravine and got stuck across it. The moose returned, stepped on the skis, and made them spring up. Mr. McGee and Dee landed safely. Mr. McGee said they still needed a lesson and should let someone else use the skis for a while.

summaries.summary: A young man walked all day and all night until he was tired and hungry. He came to a big house and knocked on the door. A little old lady opened it, but she said she had no food to give him. The young man asked for something to do and said he could make soup from a stone. The old lady was surprised, but she let him use a pot. She filled it with water and put it on the fire. The young man dropped a round gray stone into the pot and asked for more things to make the soup better. One by one, the old lady added onions, carrots, beef bones, pepper, salt, butter, and barley. The soup bubbled and grew thicker and better. At last they ate it together. Before he left, the young man took the stone from the pot, put it in his pocket, and said he would cook it more tomorrow.

summaries.summary: Forever Green Forest was peaceful until Bruce, a big shaggy bear, came out of a canyon and stayed there. When he felt playful, he liked to tumble rocks down the hills. The rocks smashed logs and bushes and scared the rabbits and quail away. One day Bruce pushed a huge boulder off a bluff. It rolled fast and crashed near Roxy, a witch, and her cat, Clinker. Roxy was angry and ran to her cabin. There she baked a blueberry and honey pie and added a magic shrinking spell. She set the pie on a stump and waited. Bruce followed the smell, ate the pie, and laughed. Soon he became sleepy and fell asleep against a tree. While he slept, he shrank smaller and smaller until he was tiny. When he woke, rabbits and quail chased him, and he ran into the creek. Later, Roxy and Clinker found him, took him home, and kept him as a small pet bear.

summaries.summary: In the Kingdom of Didd, old King Derwin grew angry with the sky because the same four things kept falling every year: rain, sunshine, fog, and snow. Late one night, the King called his royal magicians. They made a strange new thing called oobleck and sent it into the sky. At dawn, green blobs began falling over the kingdom. Bartholomew warned the bell ringer and the trumpeter, but both became stuck in the sticky oobleck. The Captain of the Guards also tried it and got glued shut. Soon the whole kingdom was covered, and everyone was trapped. Bartholomew told the King that it was all his fault and that he should say, “I’m sorry.” The King did, and the oobleck melted away. After that, he rang the holiday bell and made a holiday for the rain, sunshine, fog, and snow.

By the end, everyone thanks him and says he made the show better. The egg learns that helping others is a talent too.

Horse, sheep, and deer prepare for cold weather by staying in their stables, eating the last leaves and berries, and growing thicker fur. Silent Night follows as frost, icicles, and snowflakes appear, covering windows, eaves, and the world in a quiet white mist.

It looks as afraid as the children do, so the narrator wants to hug it and help it feel safe.

summaries.summary: A new cafeteria lady comes to school. Her name is Wanda Belch. The kids tell wild stories about her. Eric says she drives a garbage truck. Freddy says she learned to cook on a pirate ship. Derek says kids once found sneakers and baseball caps in her tuna surprise. The children also imagine strange foods like mashed potato bugs, key slime pie, and furry fritter ficasi. They think Wanda uses odd things in her meals and never throws anything away. At lunch, the children are scared and line up for the cafe. But when they get inside, Wanda is not making a disgusting meal. She serves hamburgers and French fries. The food smells good and tastes great. The children eat happily, and there are homemade chocolate chip cookies for dessert. By the end, lunch becomes their favorite time of day, and they hope Wanda will even let them stay for dinner.

summaries.summary: There was once a peddler who sold caps. He wore many caps on his head: his own checked cap, then gray caps, brown caps, blue caps, and red caps on top. He walked through the streets calling, “Caps, caps for sale. 50 cents a cap.” One morning nobody bought any caps, so the peddler became hungry. He left town and walked into the country. He came to a big tree and sat down to rest. He leaned back carefully and then fell asleep. When he woke up, he felt his head and found only his checked cap. He looked everywhere, but the other caps were gone. Then he looked up and saw monkeys in the tree wearing his caps. The peddler asked for his caps back, but the monkeys copied him and said, “tus, tus, tous,” and other sounds. Finally, he threw down his own cap. Then the monkeys threw down all the caps. He put them back on his head and walked back to town, calling, “Caps, caps for sale. 50 cents a cap.”

For the third crop, Bear asked for both tops and bottoms, but Hair gave him the tops and bottoms and kept the middle. After that, Bear woke up and said he would farm for himself. Hair later bought back his land and opened a vegetable stand.

video_title: "Pocket Full of Colors: The Magical World of Mary Blair, Disney Artist Extraordinaire" Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Mary was a little girl who loved collecting colors instead of marbles or dolls. When her family moved out west, she said goodbye to her yellow house and kept her friend lemon with her. On the trip through the desert and into California, she noticed many new colors, like rust, Sienna, Azure, golden fruit, and steel gray buildings. She saved these shades in her sketchbook for later. Mary went to art school and met Lee, who showed her rosy pink and blushing red. Later, Mary worked at Walt Disney Studios, where the men in charge wanted only black and white. They changed or rejected many of her colorful ideas. Walt Disney liked her work and took her to South America, where Mary found even more colors. After she returned, she made new art for Disney films, but most of it was still turned down. Then Mary left and worked on other art jobs. Later, Walt asked her to help create a colorful ride about cultures from around the world. Mary agreed and became the leader of the project. The ride, It’s a Small World, was a great success.

Mary loved every color she saw. As a child, she collected shades from her home, her trip west, and the places she visited in California. She put them in her sketchbook and saved them for when she was older. At art school, she met Lee, and together they painted rainbows. During the Great Depression, Mary got a job at Walt Disney Studios, one of the first women to work there. At first, the men in charge only wanted black and white, so they changed many of Mary’s bright ideas, like emerald skies, flying magenta horses, and peach giraffes. Walt Disney admired her colors and took her to South America so she could find more. Mary returned with many new shades and used them in her concept art for movies like Cinderella, Alice in Wonderland, and Peter Pan. Some ideas were accepted, but many were still rejected. Mary left Disney and worked in other jobs, though she missed Walt. Then Walt called her again and asked her to create a colorful ride about the world. Mary said yes, but only if she could be in charge. She worked with her colors, and when the ride opened, people loved It’s a Small World.

Then one morning, a little girl named Lisa saw him and wanted him, but her mother said no because he was missing a button on one shoulder strap. That night, after the store closed, Corduroy climbed down from his shelf to look for the button. He rode an escalator, went to the furniture floor, and found a button on a mattress. When he pulled it, he fell and made a loud crash. The night watchman heard the noise, found Corduroy, and put him back on the toy shelf. In the morning, Lisa returned. She had saved money in her piggy bank and bought Corduroy. She carried him home, and in her room she sewed on a new button. Lisa said she wanted a friend, and Corduroy said he did too.

summaries.summary: In a small village in Ghana, an old man lived with his seven sons after their mother died. The boys were strong and handsome, but they argued all day. They fought about the crops, the weather, and even dinner, so family meals often lasted until morning. One day the old man died, and the village chief told the brothers that their father had left them an inheritance. The brothers began fighting at once over who should get everything. The chief stopped them and gave them a task: by moonrise, they had to turn silk thread into gold or lose their home. At first they could not do it, but then they talked calmly and decided to work together. They made beautiful multicolored cloth from the thread and sold it to the king's treasurer for a bag of gold. The chief then gave them their inheritance, and the brothers taught the village how to make the cloth too.

An old man in Ghana had seven sons, but after their mother died, the brothers spent their days quarreling. They argued from morning to night about farming, the weather, and food. Their father died, and the village chief called them to hear about the inheritance. The brothers shouted and pushed each other because each one wanted everything. The chief told them that their father had left his property to be shared equally, but first they must make gold from silk thread before moonrise. If they failed, they would be sent away. When the brothers returned home, they sat together quietly for the first time and began to make a plan. They decided to weave the thread into cloth with many colors. Working side by side, they made cloth that looked beautiful in the sunlight. They sold it in the marketplace to the king's treasurer for gold. After that, they told the chief they had finished the task, and he gave them their inheritance.

When their father died, the village chief told them that the inheritance would be shared equally, but only if they could turn silk thread into gold by nightfall. The brothers were given different colors of thread and told not to fight again. At home, they stopped arguing and began to talk and plan together. They decided to weave the thread into special cloth because they could not find any gold in it. All seven brothers worked together to build a loom and weave bright cloth with stripes and shapes. They carried the cloth to the marketplace, where many villagers admired it. The king's treasurer bought all of it for a bag of gold. The brothers returned to the chief, who praised them and gave them their father's property.

The king's treasurer bought it for gold. When the brothers returned, the chief said they had learned the lesson their father wanted them to learn, and he gave them their inheritance.

summaries.summary: Susie’s mother and father go away, and Miss Mugs comes to stay with Susie. Miss Mugs is nice, but she is always in a hurry. She tells Susie to hurry up and get ready for school. On the way, Miss Mugs hurries past the milkman and makes a mess with milk. Then she hurries past a lady with three little cats and one big dog and makes another mess. The milkman and the lady both tell her not to hurry so much. Miss Mugs keeps rushing and falls into a hole by a sign that says, “Danger Men At Work.” Susie gets a policeman to pull her out with a rope. Miss Mugs hurries again, gets lifted by a steam shovel, and then walks under a ladder and gets glue all over her. Susie helps, but Miss Mugs keeps saying “hurry,” so Susie stops helping. At last, everyone helps pull her free. Miss Mugs learns to walk slowly and goes home slowly.

Soon she does not see a warning sign for men at work and falls down into a hole. Susie calls a policeman, and he pulls Miss Mugs out with a rope. But Miss Mugs still hurries. She gets lifted up by a steam shovel, and later she walks under a ladder and gets a pot of glue dumped over her head. Susie and the others help, but Miss Mugs keeps saying “hurry,” so Susie stops. summaries.summary: A person goes to the barber shop for a fresh cut. When it is their turn, they sit in the chair and wear a cape like royalty. The barber gives them a tight fade, a high low, or a bald cut, and the fresh cut makes them feel strong and confident. The story says the barber works slowly and carefully with a razor, shaving cream, and other tools to make clean lines and neat sides. People in the shop notice the result, and the person in the chair feels amazing when they see the cut in the handheld mirror. The barber also uses alcohol or witch hazel, which stings a little. At the end, the person removes the cape, pays the barber, and leaves the shop feeling magnificent, flawless, and like royalty.

The story begins with someone coming into the barber shop looking plain, like clay or marble, and then sitting down for a fresh cut. The barber puts a cape on them and shapes their hair with care. The cut can be a tight fade, a dark Caesar, waves, a fa hawk, locks, cornrows, or a shape up with tapered sides and a crisp line. As the barber works, the person starts to feel better and more important. The story says the cut can make someone feel ready for school, tests, and the whole day ahead. People in the shop seem impressed, and the person in the mirror looks proud of the new style. After the barber finishes, the person gets brushed off, pays the barber, and leaves feeling wonderful, like they are wearing a crown.

The person in the chair sees their new look in a handheld mirror and smiles a big smile. Everyone in the shop seems to notice how fresh the cut is. When the barber finishes and brushes off the hair, the person pays him and leaves. They go out feeling like a star, magnificent, and like royalty.

Together they went beyond the dark woods, and Vlad found courage. He learned he did not need to hide to feel good about himself.

video_title: 50 Below Zero

summaries.summary: In the middle of the night, Jason kept waking up and hearing strange sounds. Each time, he found his father sleepwalking in a different place. First, his father was on top of the refrigerator in the kitchen. Then Jason found him sleeping in the bathtub. After that, he found him asleep on top of the car in the garage. Each time Jason called, “Papa, wake up,” and his father jumped up, ran around three times, and went back to bed. Jason said the house was going crazy, and he was very tired. Later, Jason saw his father’s footprints going out into the snow on a very cold night. Jason worried his father would freeze, so he put on many warm clothes, followed the footprints, and found him by a tree. Jason could not lift him, so he got a sled and pulled him home. He then tied his father’s big toe to the bed so the sleepwalking would stop.

video_title: Duck in the Fridge

summaries.summary: One night, Daddy found a duck in the fridge. Then three more ducks appeared, and soon the ducks were everywhere. Daddy could not brush his teeth, put on his pajamas, or go to sleep. He gave the ducks crackers, but they ate them all and ordered pizza. Daddy called 1-1800 Duck Be Gone for help. First they sent two hairy sheep, but the ducks were not scared. Then he ordered a bigger kit with dogs, but that did not work either. The dogs played cards, and the ducks and sheep made a band. Daddy kept trying, but each new kit only brought more animals and more noise. At last, he found Mother Goose and started to read it. The ducks, sheep, dogs, and cows all liked the stories. Daddy said everyone should go to sleep, and they did. After that, he read Mother Goose every night, and everyone got sleep.

Daddy told his child why he always reads Mother Goose before bed. When Daddy was a kid, he found a duck in the fridge. The duck came out and said, 'Hi there!' Then three more ducks appeared. The company sent a box with two hairy sheep, but the ducks were not afraid. Daddy ordered another kit, but it had dogs that played cards instead of scaring the ducks. Then he got a crate with cattle, but the cows did not help either. The animals made music and parties, and Daddy still could not sleep. Then he noticed Mother Goose and started reading it. The animals listened, laughed, and asked for more. Daddy said they could hear more tomorrow if they all went to sleep. They did, and the same thing happened the next night. So Daddy read Mother Goose every night.

video_title: Groundhug Day

summaries.summary: Moose is planning a big Valentine’s Day party for two weeks away. Squirrel, Bunny, and Porcupine help with ideas like balloons, cards, and hugs. Then Bunny says there is a problem: tomorrow is Groundhog Day, and if Groundhog sees his shadow, he will go back into his hole for six more weeks and miss the party. Moose and his friends make a plan to stop that from happening. Squirrel wants to change the calendar, and Porcupine says he will blindfold Groundhog. But the animals argue all night and do not notice morning coming. Groundhog wakes up, sees his shadow, and goes back into his hole. Moose asks why, and the friends learn that Groundhog is afraid of shadows. They show him dancing leaf shadows, cloud shadows, silhouettes, and shadow puppets. Groundhog enjoys them all. At the end, he still goes back to his warm hole, but he gives the others a nose kiss and they call it Ground Hug Day.

summaries.summary: A troll lived under a bridge in mud and trash. He was very hungry and waited for animals to cross above him. One day he heard clip-clop sounds and climbed up to stop a little goat. The goat said his name was Billy Goat Gruff and told the troll he was too small to eat. He also said his big brother would come later and would be bigger and tastier. The troll let him pass. Then the second Billy Goat Gruff came. He said the same thing, and again the troll let him cross after hearing about the bigger brother. At last, the third Billy Goat Gruff arrived. The troll tried to threaten him, but the big goat lowered his horns and rammed the troll. The troll flew off the bridge and down the waterfalls. The three goats went to the grassy ridge and stayed there eating grass.

Under a bridge lived a troll who was always listening for feet and hooves. He was hungry and wanted to eat whatever crossed his bridge. First, a small goat came across. The troll wanted to eat him, but the goat said he was too little and told the troll that his brother would come soon and be bigger. The troll believed him and let him go. Then the second Billy Goat Gruff crossed. He also said his big brother would be much fatter and tastier, so the troll let him pass too. The troll waited in the dark for the third goat. When the biggest Billy Goat Gruff came, the troll tried to scare him and said he would eat him up. But the big goat lowered his horns and knocked the troll off the bridge. The troll fell into the river and over the waterfalls. The three brothers stayed on the grassy ridge and ate all they wanted.

There was a bridge, and a troll lived below it in a messy place. He waited for animals to walk across so he could eat them. When he heard clip-clop, he jumped up and found the first Billy Goat Gruff. The little goat said he was too small and told the troll that his bigger brother would come later. The troll let him cross. Next came the second Billy Goat Gruff. He said the same thing, and the troll let him go too. The troll then waited for the third brother, who was the biggest of all. When the big goat reached the bridge, the troll said he would eat him, but the goat did not move away. Instead, he pushed the troll with his horns. The troll flew off the bridge, down the rapids, and over the waterfalls. The three Billy Goats Gruff ended up together on the grassy ridge, where they could eat grass safely.

A hungry troll lived under a bridge and listened for sounds of hooves and feet. He wanted to eat anyone who crossed. One day the first Billy Goat Gruff came to the bridge. The troll called out and said he would eat him, but the little goat said he was too small and promised that his big brother would come soon. The troll let him pass. Then the second Billy Goat Gruff crossed. He also told the troll to wait for the bigger brother, so the troll let him go too. The troll waited with great hope. At last, the third Billy Goat Gruff came. The troll tried to threaten him, but the big goat lowered his horns and knocked the troll into the water. The troll went over the waterfalls and disappeared. The three goats stayed on the grassy ridge and ate there for the rest of the story.

Once there was a bridge with a troll living beneath it. The troll was hungry and wanted to eat animals that crossed above him. He heard the first Billy Goat Gruff and jumped up to stop him. The goat said he was too small and told the troll that a bigger brother would come later, so the troll let him cross. Then the second Billy Goat Gruff arrived and said the same thing. The troll let him go too because he wanted the bigger brother. After that, the third Billy Goat Gruff came to the bridge. The troll said he would eat him, but the big goat did not run away. He lowered his horns and pushed the troll off the bridge. The troll fell into the river and over the waterfalls. The three Billy Goats Gruff were left on the grassy ridge, where they stayed and ate grass.

The first Billy Goat Gruff came along, and the troll shouted that he would eat him up. The little goat said he was too small and told the troll that his big brother would follow later. He rammed the troll off the bridge and sent him over the waterfalls into the river. The three brothers then stayed on the grassy ridge, where they could eat as much as they wanted.

A troll lived below a bridge and listened for footsteps, hooves, and paws because he wanted food. He was very hungry when the first Billy Goat Gruff crossed. The troll came up and said he would eat the goat, but the first goat said he was small and offered a secret: his big brother was coming soon and would be much tastier. The troll let him cross. Then the second Billy Goat Gruff came, and the troll again talked about eating him. The second goat gave the same kind of secret and was also allowed to pass. The troll waited eagerly for the third brother. When the biggest goat arrived, the troll said he would eat him too, but the goat did not run away. Instead, he lowered his horns and stamped his hoof, then charged the troll and knocked him into the rapids and over the waterfalls. After that, the three Billy Goats Gruff were safe on the grassy ridge and still there today.

summaries.summary: Calvin was a starling born in a very big family under an old barn. While his brothers, sisters, and cousins found worms, grass, dirt, and water, Calvin found a book. He learned to read and spent his days in the library, where he read about pirates, dinosaurs, planets, wind, and butterflies. The other starlings called him names, and Calvin felt sad. When fall came, it was time to fly south, but Calvin could not fly. His family left, then came back and tied him with string and scraps of cloth so they could carry him along. While they flew, Calvin saw places he had read about. Later, Calvin heard bad weather coming and warned everyone about a hurricane. His family listened and hid in a cave. The storm passed, and the starlings were safe. They celebrated Calvin, and then Calvin discovered he could fly too. Together, they flew south.

Calvin the starling lived with many brothers, sisters, and cousins in an old barn. He was different from the others because he loved books. After he discovered a book, he learned to read and spent summer in the library instead of learning bird things with Mr. Wingstead. He read about dinosaurs, volcanoes, rainbows, whales, the planets, and many other wonders. His cousins teased him, but Calvin stayed with his books. When the leaves turned orange, it was time for the starlings to migrate south. Calvin could not fly, so his family tied him up and carried him with them. During the trip, Calvin saw rivers, mountains, and towns he knew from reading. Then strong winds came, and Calvin remembered a weather book. He warned the flock that a hurricane was coming and told them to get into a cave. The storm hit, but the family stayed safe. Afterward, they held a party for Calvin, and then he flapped his wings and learned that he could fly.

At the old barn, Calvin the starling was born with a huge family. His brothers and sisters found ordinary things, but Calvin found a book and loved it right away. He read all summer in the library while the other young starlings learned to swoop, hover, and fly. Calvin learned many facts from books and dreamed of stories and adventure. The other starlings made fun of him, and he felt lonely. When autumn came, the family had to head south, but Calvin still could not fly. His family came back and tied him with cloth and string so they could carry him in the air. As they traveled, Calvin recognized places from his books. Then the wind grew hard, and Calvin warned them that a hurricane was coming. The flock followed him into a cave, and the storm passed over them. After they came out safely, they celebrated Calvin with food and songs. Calvin was so happy that he flapped his wings and flew at last.

Calvin was a starling who loved reading more than anything else. He lived under the eaves of an old barn with a very large family. While other baby starlings discovered worms and insects, Calvin discovered a book. He spent his summer in the library, reading about dinosaurs, pirates, weather, and the world. His cousins teased him, but Calvin kept reading. When fall came, the family needed to migrate south, but Calvin could not fly. His brothers, sisters, and cousins tied him with string and scraps of cloth and carried him in the air. Calvin saw rivers, mountains, and towns he had read about. Then the wind changed, and Calvin knew a hurricane was coming. He told his family to go into a cave. They did, and the storm passed safely by. The family was happy and thanked Calvin at a big party. After all that excitement, Calvin flapped his wings and found that he could fly, so the whole family flew south together.

The storm came, but they were safe. After the storm, the starlings gave Calvin a party, and Calvin flapped his wings so much that he finally learned to fly. Then they all continued south together.

summaries.summary: In the village of La Paz, everyone and everything sang all day long. The dogs barked, mothers sang, engines hummed, and fountains made music. The village was so noisy that people could not hear, sleep, or think. They fired the mayor and then voted for Don Pepe, who promised peace and quiet. After he won, new laws told people not to sing in public, then not to sing at home, and then not to sing at all. Soon La Paz became completely silent. Some people left, some learned to hum, and others were glad to rest. Seven quiet years passed. Then a merry gallito and his family came to a mango tree. The next morning the rooster sang, but the mayor said singing was not allowed. Don Pepe tried to stop him by cutting down the tree, taking away his hen and chicks, putting him in a cage, and covering him with a blanket. Still, the gallito kept singing. At last, the village gathered to listen, and the rooster said a song lives on as long as someone sings it.

Long ago, La Paz was a village full of song. People sang in the shower, animals made noise, and the whole place was loud from morning to night. Because it was so noisy, the people had trouble hearing, sleeping, and thinking. They fired the mayor and elected Don Pepe, who said he would bring quiet. He made many rules, and soon no one could sing at all. The village became silent, and some people moved away while others only hummed. After seven years, a gallito and his family came to a mango tree in the village. The next morning the rooster sang, and Don Pepe told him to stop because singing was against the law. The gallito said he would still sing, even if the tree was cut down, his family was gone, or he was put in a cage. Don Pepe kept trying to silence him, but the rooster sang again and again. Finally, the mayor asked why he kept singing, and the gallito said he sang for those who could not sing. Then he said songs do not die as long as someone sings them.

The village of La Paz was once very noisy because everyone and everything had a song. The noise made it hard for people to hear or sleep, so they fired the mayor. Then they chose Don Pepe as mayor because he promised quiet. He made stricter and stricter rules until no singing was allowed at all. La Paz became silent, and many people left. Some stayed and hummed. Seven years later, a gallito and his family arrived and settled in a mango tree. When the rooster sang in the morning, Don Pepe said it was against the law. He tried to stop the gallito by cutting the tree, removing his hen and chicks, putting him in a cage, and covering the cage with a blanket. Each time, the gallito said he would still sing and then sang: Kee-kee-ree-KEE! The mayor finally begged him to stop, but the gallito said he sang for others who had forgotten how. He said dead roosters do not sing, but a song never dies if someone keeps singing it.

summaries.summary: Matty loves glue at home with Dad and Mom, but his art teacher says, “Too much glue never dries” and “Glue raindrops, not puddles!” In art class, Matty uses the fullest glue bottles and makes a big sticky mess with sequins and googly eyes. Then he rolls onto the table and glues himself to it. He cannot get up, and his teacher worries because school will end soon. Noah, Izzy, and Owen try to help by lassoing him, but the ropes snap. Luke and Grace bring a tow truck, but it explodes. The school nurse checks him and cannot send him home early. The principal leaves a note on Matty’s belly. Then Matty sees his teacher huffing and puffing and whispers a plan to Hailey and Owen. They use a huge paper fan, and the glue finally dries. When Matty’s dad arrives, he peels Matty off the table and calls him a masterpiece. At home, Dad opens the dried glue shape, fixes it, and hangs it on the fridge.

At school, Matty is warned not to use too much glue, but he loves glue because he and his dad make glue glasses, glue mustaches, and glue bouncy balls at home. In art class, Matty pours out lots of glue, and the table becomes a gooey mess with sequins and googly eyes. He then jumps onto the table and rolls around, so he gets stuck. His teacher says there is too much glue and calls for help. Noah, Izzy, and Owen try to rope Matty like a rodeo pony, but the lassoes break. Luke and Grace bring a tow truck, but it breaks too. The nurse checks Matty and cannot send him home. The principal puts a note on his belly and leaves. Matty notices his teacher, Hailey, and Owen use a big fan to dry the glue. The glue dries at last. Matty’s dad comes in, peels him off the table, and says he is a masterpiece. Later, Dad opens the glue shape, repairs it, and puts it on the fridge.

video_title: 'The Three Questions' read by Meryl Streep

summaries.summary: Nikolai was a boy who wanted to be a good person, but he did not always know what to do. He asked his friends three questions: when is the best time to do things, who is the most important one, and what is the right thing to do? Sonya, Gogol, and Pushkin each gave answers, but Nikolai was not sure they were right. So he went to see Leo, an old turtle living high in the mountains. Leo was digging a garden, and Nikolai helped him finish the work. Then a storm came. Nikolai heard a panda calling for help, carried her to Leo’s house, and made a splint for her hurt leg. He then found the panda’s baby in the forest and brought the little one back safe and warm. The next morning, Leo explained that the answers were in Nikolai’s actions: the right time was the time he was helping, the important ones were the people with him, and the right thing was to do good for them.

Nikolai often felt uncertain about how to act. He told his friends that he wanted to be good, and he asked them three questions. Sonya said to plan ahead, Gogol said to watch closely, and Pushkin said to have help from a pack. Then Nikolai asked who was most important. Sonya, Gogol, and Pushkin each gave a different answer. When he asked what the right thing was, they answered with flying, having fun, and fighting. Nikolai thought for a long time, then decided to visit Leo, a very old turtle. In the mountains, Leo was digging a garden. Nikolai helped him dig until the rows were finished. After that, a storm began, and Nikolai heard a panda cry for help. He carried the injured panda to safety and fixed her leg with bamboo. Then he found her baby, brought the child inside, and kept it warm. In the morning, Leo told Nikolai that his questions had been answered by helping others.

summaries.summary: Once there were three little pigs who lived on a farm. One day the farmer and his wife moved to Florida, and the pigs had to leave. The first pig bought potato chips and built a straw house. The second pig bought sody-pop and built a stick house. The third pig spent all her money on bricks and mortar and built a strong brick house. The first two pigs finished first and relaxed in their homes. The third pig worked hard until her house was big and beautiful. Then a hungry wolf came to town. He found the straw house first and blew it down with a huff and a puff. The first pig ran away on a scooter. The wolf then blew down the stick house, and the second pig rode away on a bike. At the brick house, the wolf could not blow it down. The pigs helped him when he was tired, and all three pigs lived together in the brick house.

The first pig chose straw and built a straw house. The second pig chose sticks and built a stick house. The third pig chose bricks and built a brick house. Soon a wolf came to town, but he could not get food at the donut shop, the hot dog stand, or the pizza parlor. He went to the straw house and said he would blow it down. He huffed and puffed, and the house fell. The first pig escaped on a scooter. Then the wolf blew down the stick house, and the second pig got away on a bike. He came to the brick house and tried very hard, but the house stayed standing. The pigs saw the wolf fall down tired. They gave him chips and sody-pop, and he stayed with them after that.

summaries.summary: Seymour the hamster starts with a perfect life in his cage. He has seeds, soft wood shavings, and room to run. Then Little Girl brings him an exercise wheel, a water bottle, and yogurt drops. Seymour loves running on his shiny FuzzyBoy 360 wheel every night. One night, Pearl the Cat tells him he runs a lot but never leaves the cage. Pearl says there is a sunroom and a staircase made of sunflower seeds, and she warns him about Hoover. Seymour cannot stop thinking about these things. He makes a plan called Operation Tasty Treat and escapes by using the wheel and a sunflower seed to open the lid. But Pearl was lying. The staircase is only carpet, and the sunroom has no yogurt drops. Seymour gets chased by Pearl and Hoover and hides under the sofa. At last, Little Girl finds him, and Seymour is safe again in his cage, happy with his seeds and room to run.

Seymour is a hamster who thinks his cage is the best place ever. Each night he enjoys his seeds, his cozy bedding, and his exercise wheel. Little Girl visits him, cleans his cage, and gives him yogurt drops. Then Pearl the Cat starts talking about the world outside the cage. She says there is a sunroom and a staircase made of sunflower seeds. Seymour wants to see them, so he plans an escape. On Night Ten, he moves his seed dish, pushes the wheel, and uses a sunflower seed to stop it from spinning so he can climb out. He gets outside, but Pearl has lied to him. The staircase is just carpet, and the sunroom has no yogurt drops. Pearl, Hoover, and Buck make a lot of trouble, and Seymour runs away under the sofa. He thinks he may be lost forever, but Little Girl comes and finds him. Seymour is kissed on the nose and goes back to his cage.

He feels trapped and scared, but Little Girl finally comes to him. Seymour is safe again, and he returns to his happy cage life.
